Industry News: Jensen Huang Is Gone. Now What?

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 22 min read (4420 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: WIRED

⏱️ ~22 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that I don’t go into any given week at WIRED assuming I’ll be thinking much about extramarital affairs.
  • Sources indicate that these thoughts, of course, were prompted by Jensen Huang.
  • WIRED’s senior correspondent Lauren Goode has spent years reporting on Nvidia and Huang, including interviewing the man himself on multiple occasions.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that I don’t go into any given week at WIRED assuming I’ll be thinking much about extramarital affairs. But last week, they were the only thing on my mind.

Sources indicate that these thoughts, of course, were prompted by Jensen Huang. In the span of a few completely insane days, the billionaire CEO and cofounder of Nvidia went from being a globally influential Silicon Valley executive to a lesson in exactly what not to do if you want to keep your job, and the extraordinary power that comes with it. It’s a damn mess—for Huang and his family, sure, but also for Nvidia, the AI industry the manufacturer is instrumental in powering, and the entirety of the global economy.

WIRED’s senior correspondent Lauren Goode has spent years reporting on Nvidia and Huang, including interviewing the man himself on multiple occasions. She also spent last week breaking news about his downfall, despite being in Europe on vacation. (Sorry, Lauren. You can have those PTO days back.) So at the end of a very long week for WIRED’s newsroom, I called Lauren to talk about what she makes of Huang’s ouster, what it means for AI, and where this all goes next. We also made a bet about Huang’s future—one involving a meal he recently made semi-famous.

This interview has been edited for length and clarity.

KATIE DRUMMOND: Lauren, first of all, thank you for your tirelessness these past few days. The last time I saw you, we were both in Miami for WIRED’s significant event, and you were getting on a red-eye that night to go to Europe for vacation, which didn’t exactly go as planned. When you saw that first story about Jensen’s affair on Sunday, what did you think? What went through your mind?

LAUREN GOODE: Oof. The story first started bubbling up a while ago because The New York Times, and a lot of credit is due to The New York Times here, first reported on Nvidia’s relationship, if you want to call it that, with this company Megaspeed, back in the fall of 2025.

Sources indicate that it was a very unusual story. And for some reason it just didn’t capture the attention of people the way that more recent reporting that we and others have been doing has.

Anyone who’s sort of been paying attention to that story, or had some sources in the industry, were starting to hear things. But the fact that the affair with this person, who goes by Alice Huang, was confirmed, that’s the kind of story that always captures people’s attention in a different way.

There are few things people love to read about more than extramarital affairs, especially when they involve powerful people. The reason it wasn’t surprising to you, was it because of that previous reporting and what you had been hearing here and there? Or was there another reason that you saw that story and thought, “OK, actually some of this is not shocking to me”?

It was both. I don’t know if you remember, Katie, but in the fall of 2024 we were doing a WIRED outing, a few of us hanging out, and we started chatting about whether or not we thought a lot of the most powerful people in Silicon Valley had girlfriends or extramarital affairs or situations. Because there are some people in Silicon Valley who are actually quite open about that. I remember us talking about it at the time, and there’s part of me that always kind of assumes that there are elements of their personal lives that we’re never going to have a full window into.

Not that we were talking about Jensen that evening, but it’s always been in my mind. Then, yes, I think being on the ground in Silicon Valley, you often hear things. But a lot of times there’s a certain threshold that things have to cross in order for us as journalists to consider something reportable or something worth chasing down as reportable.

I think an key distinction is that people cheat, people have affairs all the time, Silicon Valley or otherwise.

What tips this over into newsworthiness is, A) the Chinese espionage of it all, and B) the affair with a subordinate.

You reported that Jensen’s resignation—which really, to be clear, is the board of Nvidia ousting him—probably had more to do with the alleged affair with a subordinate than this other extramarital relationship, which is tied up in espionage allegations. A source told you this. Can you explain why that affair would tip the balance for the board?

It has been revealed that I just think it’s vital to note that this doesn’t seem like it was simply a moral decision. Someone had posted on X that “I can't believe the board caved to moral pressure.” To me, this doesn’t seem like it’s a moral issue.

Recent findings suggest that I think if you’re looking at the three things that could have led to serious scrutiny of Jensen Huang’s behavior, there’s: One, extramarital affairs. Two, alleged extramarital affairs with subordinates within his own tech giant. And three, an extramarital affair with an alleged Chinese operative, which puts Jensen Huang in this position where the board and the investigators who are looking into this are trying to determine what he knew and when he knew it, and basically whether he was aware of the fact that chips were making their way into China.

In a recent development, this isn’t just about the fact that someone had a girlfriend outside of their marriage. I think what is still to be revealed here could in fact be very, very serious in nature.

Now, you also reported on Monday, in a fantastic scoop for WIRED, that Jensen hired a crisis comms firm a year ago. In October 2025 he hired a fixer, Risa Heller, who is very well known for working with high-profile men who are facing allegations of sexual misconduct, among other things. I’m talking about Anthony Weiner, Mario Batali, writer Jeffrey Toobin. Tell us a little bit about that story and what you found out.

I really feel like with everything else going on this week, I could have gone without ever hearing about all of those stories again.

Oh, you don’t want to hear about Anthony Weiner all the time?

No, it turns out. I had kind of forgotten that. I was like, “I think I blocked that from my memory.” And Jeff Toobin—what a throwback.

Recent findings suggest that but this firm, it’s a really interesting firm run by this woman named Risa Heller. They have offices in Upcoming York and LA, and yes, they have this reputation for dealing with a lot of sexual misconduct cases, as well as other types of corporate and personal PR needs for high-profile people.

Recent findings suggest that A source had told me a while ago, and I’m not gonna timestamp it, but a while ago that it had been rumored that Jensen Huang had hired this firm. So immediately my antenna went up, and I was like, “Wait, what?”.

I thought it was curious, but I didn’t know exactly what the nature of the contract was or when they had been hired, and then eventually through more reporting, I was able to get confirmation of some of the details.

What we know is that this firm, Heller, started working with Jensen Huang sometime in 2025, and ostensibly, Huang and his family had hired Heller for their own personal PR outside of Nvidia’s walls. This is because when you’re someone like Jensen Huang, you have a lot going on. You have a family office. You do a lot of work with philanthropy. You’re hosting personal events. He’s also been grooming his adult children to take over these higher profile roles within Nvidia, so some of the PR might have ostensibly been to work on creating more of a public-facing image for his kids.

We do know, though, based on more reporting, that as of October 2025, and then closer to the end of the year, Nvidia’s internal teams had been instructed to start looping this outside crisis firm, Heller, into all press inquiries, all communications related to Jensen.

That was definitely a change from the prior terms of his working relationship with Heller, and also timing-wise coincided with that first New York Times story I mentioned. I think that it was published on October 9th, 2025, and first highlighted Megaspeed and what appeared to be a very close relationship between Jensen Huang and Alice Huang.

I can’t decide if he should get his money back for hiring this crisis comms firm, because this crisis has certainly not been contained, or if the fact that this is now coming up a year later suggests that maybe they did their job quite well for a while.

Well, first of all, I don’t think he needs the money back.

… on how his assets get divided, yes. Or if maybe they won’t divorce. You know, it’s also a very Silicon Valley thing not to necessarily do that.

I also think it’s possible that Jensen himself was not totally upfront with this firm when he hired them. Or, if they knew something was up, they may not have known all of the details. So if that is the case, hypothetically, then you can’t necessarily do everything you would typically do in terms of reputation management. TL;DR, it didn’t work out so well for him in the end.

In a recent development, no, things are not going well for Jensen. Now, Nvidia has named an interim CEO to replace him. Surprise, surprise, to both of us and women everywhere, she’s a woman.

What do we know about Colette Kress, who is the interim CEO of Nvidia?

It has been revealed that well, we know that when we emailed Jensen this summer to say, “Hey, Jensen, who do you think the most powerful women in Silicon Valley are?” He didn't mention Colette. Jensen mentioned Dina Powell from Meta and Ruth Porat from Google, both really high-ranking women, presidents of those companies.

And then [SpaceX president and COO] Gwynne Shotwell, because I prompted him. But no Colette, and that struck me as interesting at the time, too, though I didn’t press him on that. And then we did end up giving Colette a nod in our big feature that we did about high-ranking women in Silicon Valley.

Sources indicate that colette has been with Nvidia since 2013. Prior to that, she worked at Cisco, Microsoft. She’s CFO. She’s a financial whiz. She’s the person who appears on earnings calls with him every quarter.

She actually does a lot of the speaking, because she’s a person who has really, really deep knowledge of Nvidia’s complex financials. She’s the person who gives guidance for the next quarter. She’s CFO of arguably the world’s most key organization. I think it makes sense that she would be slotted into this role.

In a recent development, nvidia doesn’t really have a traditional hierarchy. They don’t have a traditional chief operating officer, for example. You know, when Steve Jobs was at the end of his tenure and he was very sick, Tim Cook, who was the operations whiz at Apple for many years prior, was basically groomed to be the CEO.

According to recent reports, nvidia doesn’t have someone like that. So it makes sense for now that Colette is the person who would slot in, because part of Nvidia’s goal has to be, at this point, easing the stock market. I don’t know if you’ve been following, but, I mean, it’s pretty bad out there.

I would say that, against my will, I am seeing a lot about Nvidia stock not doing well. I have not looked at my 401(k). I try really hard not to because I’m a control freak, and I simply cannot control how many affairs this man is having and what impact that has on my finances.

These things, though, help paint a picture of Jensen’s character and the way he ran the company. The fact that Nvidia did not do succession planning. There was no hierarchy; he had dozens of direct reports. There was no successor waiting in the wings. What do those things combined tell us about Jensen and Nvidia?

As I understand it, Katie, even you have had to do a succession strategy, right?

Industry observers note that yes, without revealing too many details, Condé Nast, like most normal companies, has people in senior leadership roles do succession planning. They take it really seriously. It’s an annual exercise that we do, and my understanding is that that is very par for the course at most companies, at any company, and particularly a company of Nvidia’s stature and importance on a global scale. The idea that there would not be a formal succession plan is shocking to me.

According to recent reports, it is shocking, and it’s shocking not just from the perspective that Jensen perhaps didn’t do that or didn’t have a super well-formulated one, but that the board wouldn’t demand that. I’ve heard a few different theories floated as to why this is. One theory is that Jensen may have had a lot of the insecurities that come with being a cofounder, CEO, someone who’s been living and breathing this company, his baby, since 1993, and not necessarily wanting to stuff the ranks with people who are just as capable, if not more capable in some measures, than himself, right?

Like you don’t create an environment in which someone could theoretically replace you that easily. So that’s one theory. The other theory is that—and Jensen himself has said this, both to me and other people in interviews too—he truly believed that keeping a flat org was better for the flow of information, that once you start to create a structure that’s too hierarchical, then any kind of changes that happen in the manufacturer, any kind of new information that comes out, even in some kind of white paper, fundamentally changes the direction of the way the industry is going.

I mean, think about the way people inside the AI industry probably reacted when they first saw the famous Transformer paper in 2017 and mentioned, “Oh my gosh, this is going to change everything.” If you’re a major, fat, bloated, slow organization, you’re probably five years behind on your AI strategy. If you’re lean at the top, you can basically say, “Let’s go. We’re going in this direction now,” and you won’t encounter a lot of barriers to doing that. So that helps explain the flat org. It doesn’t necessarily explain the lack of a succession blueprint.

The third theory that’s been floated to me is that maybe in some, I don’t know, alternate universe, he really did think that his children, one of his two children, who are both working within Nvidia, would one day be the inevitable successors.

According to recent reports, you have met Jensen several times. You’ve corresponded with him, you’ve interviewed him, you published a cover story for WIRED that featured an excellent interview with him. You published an edition of our newsletter, Backchannel, at the end of last week with a little bit about this. In it you talk about one experience you had interviewing Jensen at a conference. You wrote, “Huang was domineering, evaded some of my questions, and immediately after our session concluded, did an impromptu Q&A session with a much more adoring crowd than me.” You describe him as obsessed with controlling the narrative.

According to recent reports, again, we’re coming back to this theme of control. I’m curious to hear a little bit more about that observation, this idea of Jensen as fixated on storytelling and the stories that were told about Nvidia and about AI.

In a recent development, that particular interview was July of 2024, and Nvidia had invited me to interview Jensen again at the SIGGRAPH Conference in Denver, which is this whole confab of computer graphics nerds. It’s a really fun conference.

During the preparation for it, when I got on the call with some Nvidia comms executives, Madison Huang, Jensen’s daughter, appeared on the call and she basically took the lead and said, “Here’s this cluster of slides that when you’re on stage, Jensen’s going to be referencing, and he’s gonna have a lot to say about each slide, and it would be great if you could tee him up at this point.”.

And I remarked, “Well, wait a second. This is not a standard journalistic interview. Like, what’s going on here?” The whole thing felt very strange, but I made it clear I planned to ask him the questions I really felt I needed to ask him as a journalist. It was just very clear he did not want to answer a lot of my questions, and that he was going to just own the stage and reference his slides. I remember that he talked about how he made a little Jensen AI of himself, and the crowd was all, “Ha! Jensen AI,” and I was like, “What is happening?”.

It was so strange. Afterwards, he did this impromptu Q&A with the crowd. A bunch of people rushed the stage. I could see someone from his PR team being like, “What just happened? What is he doing?” Not standard operating procedure. I thought, wow. It felt to me like Jensen Huang was just riding high on this wave, this AI wave and this incredible success that Nvidia was experiencing and the way the AI industry was growing.

But it occurred to me that he was really, really obsessive with controlling the narrative, and it reminded me of something that he’d remarked the first time we’d ever spoken, which was that he really admired the CEO of Adobe because he felt that the CEO of Adobe was a very good storyteller, and that he never had a pitch deck when he first pitched Nvidia as a manufacturer because he just thought it was better to tell a story.

Industry observers note that storytelling is so important in terms of establishing the culture of a tech giant. He was very good at creating his own story, his own image of himself as this founder CEO who was utterly obsessed with his own company and really passionate about everything.

I guess we know where some of that passion led him.

Industry observers note that we do indeed. It’s interesting that you talk about Jensen as a crowd favorite, because he did very much become that. He’s incredibly charismatic. He’s a great public speaker. He can really own a room. He can spin a great yarn. You describe in the cover story about Jensen, that you were “Jensen-pilled” after spending time with him, because he is so compelling.

That was interesting to me this week, in seeing how many leaders in Silicon Valley came out in support of him, despite these very, very troubling allegations, which to be clear, again, go beyond having an affair. This is beyond moral decision-making. Regardless of that, everyone from Elon Musk to Jason Calacanis came out guns blazing for Jensen.

Recent findings suggest that do you think that speaks to how revered he is in the industry, or do you think that that speaks to the fact that he is mission-critical for the industry’s ongoing growth? Are these defenses of Jensen essentially self-interested on the part of industry leaders?

Sources indicate that I don't think they’re all self-interested. There are at least three layers to this, and one is that there are executives and lower-level tech workers who have worked for Jensen directly, and who came away from the experience with not a great taste in their mouths. They left feeling uninspired, and they actually saw a more egotistical side of him that they didn’t like, an obsessive side. There have been stories reported by other outlets about how he has sometimes berated some of his top lieutenants in front of other people. There’s almost a Dr. Jensen and Mr. Huang narrative here. He’s got two sides to him. But he’s very smart and almost can come across as sort of mensch-y. I think people really admire him.

Then I think, yes, there are people who probably own Nvidia stock, they’re industry watchers, they’re tech enthusiasts, and they see him perhaps still as a kind of our generation’s rock star who also happens to be keeping the economy afloat with his organization.

So there are varying levels of interest there in terms of people who just either wish this didn’t happen, or really wish in some alternate universe he would be reinstated, which would be shocking to me at this point.

Sources indicate that I will say WIRED had a great scoop last week, much credit to our amazing journalists, of Nvidia employees who would like to see Jensen back. There is a great deal of reverence for him, in a way that I have to admit gave me acute flashbacks to 2023, when Sam Altman was ousted at OpenAI. Very different circumstances, but yet again, a woman was installed to clean up that mess, and employees revolted and called for Sam to come back. I mean, these allegations are much more significant and serious and consequential. That said, the jury’s still out on whether Jensen makes a comeback in two weeks.

Recent findings suggest that really? You think there’s a possibility?

Industry observers note that wow. OK. I would be very surprised. We should make a bet.

Oh, Lauren. I was going to say dinner the next time I’m in San Francisco.

Dinner sounds good. Let’s do it. You know what? Whoever loses the bet has to buy dinner at Proposition Chicken, which according to, was it the Daily … ?

The Daily Mail reported that Proposition Chicken, which is a slightly elevated fast food chicken place in San Francisco, was being delivered to Jensen Huang’s house in Pacific Heights the other day.

OK. I’m in. Two weeks from today, we will see.

I want to ask you lastly about ripple effects. Nvidia has invested in or bought outright plenty of AI startups. It finances a lot of the build-out happening in this industry. I have been stomping around the Fresh York office all week screaming things like, “The global economy, the global economy!” I mean, this is much bigger than just this firm, right? So what are the industry effects that we should all be watching out for from here?

What I’ve heard so far from people is that in the short term—even though we’re seeing this dip right now—there’s still just such incredible demand for Nvidia chips, and they blueprint everything basically 18 to 24 months out in terms of producing those chips, that I don’t think we’ll see any really serious softness in Nvidia in the short term.

But I think that the long tail of Nvidia is going to be interesting, because another CEO could come in with a totally different approach to how Nvidia spends its capital and how it also makes investments in outside companies.

In a recent development, would a new CEO come in right now and make the kind of investment in CoreWeave or Perplexity, for example, that Jensen decided to? Quite possibly no. Would the new CEO come in and decide to spend so much on, let’s say, Nvidia’s healthcare division? We don’t really know. Would the new CEO come in and be as much of an open source booster as Jensen Huang had become? We don’t really know.

It’s just hard to say. The guys at Hugging Face are probably quite happy that they got in when they did.

Another thing that Jensen had set Nvidia on the path of in the past couple years was really investing in what they’re doing with CPUs as well as GPUs, which is an area that Intel and AMD are in, as well as Arm.

Was that the right path to set the manufacturer on, to over-index a little bit on CPUs for now because of the ways that the AI industry is shifting from training on high-powered GPUs to inference computing on slightly lower-powered CPUs? I think it was a smart move, but let’s see how that shakes out.

I don’t know if you remember, Katie, but back in 2008, shortly after the collapse of Lehman Brothers, a venture capitalist at Sequoia sent around a pitch deck to all of that firm’s portfolio companies that became very famous in the industry, and it’s called “RIP Good Times.”.

Industry observers note that in that pitch deck, this very prescient VC basically laid out all of the things that they wanted their portfolio companies to do, which meant saving a lot of cash. Like, this is a gird-your-loins moment. I think if we see something like that kind of mentality start to develop in Silicon Valley in the coming weeks and months, then I think that’s a very substantial indication that people are genuinely worried about what this Nvidia tumble means.

I am going to ask you to make one final prediction.

Industry observers note that OK. I’m very bad at predictions, by the way, but please.

Two years ago, you said, “Huang is the man of the hour. The year. Maybe even the decade.” I would argue that that decade has been cut short, but I also think that someone like Jensen doesn’t just go quietly into the night. If he’s not reinstalled at Nvidia, and I’m wrong, and I’m buying your chicken in two weeks, where does someone like that go? Where do you expect we will see Jensen pop up in a year, in two years?

There’s a glib answer and it’s either Jensen goes to jail, or Jensen starts a podcast. I’m sure he’s hoping right now it’s the podcast outcome.

It has been revealed that realistically, let’s say that he’s not implicated in the end result of any kind of federal investigation. And let’s say he’s not reinstated. In either case, I don’t think this is the last we’re going to hear from Jensen Huang.

Tech Report: Eisenkot condemns Netanyahu’s ‘racist’ campaign against Israel’s Arab citizens

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Prime ministerial hopeful calls Arab minority ‘an integral part of the Israeli story’ as he seeks to form government.
  • Israeli prime ministerial hopeful Gadi Eisenkot condemned a “racist and aggressive campaign of delegitimisation” against the country’s Arab citizens, after the caretaker prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, accused Arab parties of electoral fraud without evidence.
  • Industry observers note that netanyahu has repeatedly targeted Arab parties and Palestinian citizens of Israel after his party received a disappointing electoral showing, accusing them of manipulating the election and being linked to Hamas.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Prime ministerial hopeful calls Arab minority ‘an integral part of the Israeli story’ as he seeks to form government.

Israeli prime ministerial hopeful Gadi Eisenkot condemned a “racist and aggressive campaign of delegitimisation” against the country’s Arab citizens, after the caretaker prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, accused Arab parties of electoral fraud without evidence.

Industry observers note that netanyahu has repeatedly targeted Arab parties and Palestinian citizens of Israel after his party received a disappointing electoral showing, accusing them of manipulating the election and being linked to Hamas. Israeli electoral authorities have rejected these claims as not being backed by evidence.

Arab citizens of Israel, the vast majority of them of Palestinian descent, comprise more than 20% of the country’s population.

Shin Bet, Israel’s internal security branch, sought to question four Arab lawmakers, including the Arab-majority Ra’am party head, Mansour Abbas, leading to accusations that the security agency had become politicised.

Sources indicate that “Arab citizens of Israel are an integral part of the Israeli story. The attempt to marginalise them and vilify them collectively is a profound violation of the principles of statesmanship,” Eisenkot remarked in a statement on Friday.

Eisenkot’s statement was a rare instance of a prominent Jewish political leader taking a strong stand in defence of Arab Israelis.

According to recent reports, the statement also reflected political realities in Israel, as Arab parties found themselves kingmakers after the latest election. The two Arab-majority parties, Ra’am and the Joint List, secured 19 seats in the October election.

They have the potential to help Eisenkot form a governing coalition and become Israel’s next prime minister. If Eisenkot cannot form a coalition within 28 days, with a possible 14-day extension, the mandate to form a government would pass to another lawmaker, potentially Netanyahu.

It has been revealed that eisenkot has to balance the competing interests of several parties if he hopes to form a coalition. Rightwing elements of the opposition have pledged to drop their support of the prospective PM if he cooperates with Arab parties.

His statement on Friday portrayed a more statesman-like approach to ruling than his more rightwing, demagogic opponents who have used Arab parties and citizens as political scapegoats over the last three years.

“[Arab citizens] have been subjected to a racist and aggressive campaign of delegitimisation, fuelled by the outgoing prime minister and those around him for political purposes,” Eisenkot remarked in his statement.

“The prime minister of Israel is the prime minister of all Israeli citizens, including those who did not vote for him,” he added.

Netanyahu and his allies have repeatedly criticised leaders of Arab parties for refusing to describe Hamas as a “terror group” after its unprecedented 7 October 2023 attack on Israel.

All leaders of Arab parties have condemned the attack, in which Arab Israelis – descendants of Palestinians who remained in what became Israel in 1948 – were also among those killed.

In a speech, Netanyahu falsely claimed that the two Arab lists sought to establish either an “Islamic state” or a “nationalist Palestinian state”.

During the same ceremony, the national security minister, Itamar Ben Gvir, heckled Joint List’s leader, Yousef Jabareen, during his oath of allegiance, accusing him of having “pledged allegiance to Hamas”.

Nvidia privately confirmed it could track chips to fight smuggling, even as industry publicly questioned feasibility

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Representatives from Nvidia told Illinois representative Bill Foster that it would be technically possible to implement the anti-smuggling measures called for in the Chip Security Act, Foster told MIT Technology Review in an interview on Thursday, even while an industry group claimed they were “potentially infeasible.”.
  • Foster, a Democrat who serves on the Committee on Science, Space, and Technology, is a cosponsor of the act, which would introduce geotracking requirements to verify the location of advanced AI chips in order to prevent their smuggling to China.
  • Recent findings suggest that when the Chip Security Act was introduced, in May 2025, lawmakers noted the technology to implement it existed, something Nvidia has not publicly confirmed.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Representatives from Nvidia told Illinois representative Bill Foster that it would be technically possible to implement the anti-smuggling measures called for in the Chip Security Act, Foster told MIT Technology Review in an interview on Thursday, even while an industry group claimed they were “potentially infeasible.”.

Foster, a Democrat who serves on the Committee on Science, Space, and Technology, is a cosponsor of the act, which would introduce geotracking requirements to verify the location of advanced AI chips in order to prevent their smuggling to China. It is one of three chip-security bills under consideration for inclusion in the Senate’s National Defense Authorization Act, each of which is drawing renewed attention after Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s resignation and reported affair with an alleged Chinese spy.

Recent findings suggest that when the Chip Security Act was introduced, in May 2025, lawmakers noted the technology to implement it existed, something Nvidia has not publicly confirmed. In March 2026, the Semiconductor Industry Association, of which Nvidia is a member, explicitly opposed the bill and wrote that its mandates for chip tracking were “new, untested, and potentially infeasible.”.

But privately, Nvidia representatives working with Foster told the lawmaker that the firm could implement them.

“They never put anything in writing,” Foster says, but during technical discussions on the possibility of such safeguards, their reaction was “yeah, of course we can do this.” This private acknowledgment to Foster goes further than anything Nvidia has previously made public.

Other technology Nvidia has built for its customers suggests that the company can indeed offer accurate tracking of its chips’ locations. In December 2025, for example, it announced a new tool called Fleet Intelligence that would allow customers to monitor how its advanced chips were performing across different data center locations. In doing so, the tool could indicate which country chips were in, Nvidia confirmed to Reuters, but the company would not elaborate on whether this technology could be used to prevent smuggling.

Nvidia did not respond to requests for comment or confirmation of Foster’s characterization.

In early October, when lawmakers were reportedly increasingly concerned about Nvidia’s role in smuggling, MIT Technology Review asked the tech giant if Fleet Intelligence could be used to prevent the practice. It declined to answer directly, instead sending a statement: “Governments and media have found insignificant diversion of controlled US products—a drop in the bucket compared to the ocean of domestic compute China already has.”.

The recent fallout at Nvidia involves a number of people and companies alleged to be involved in chip smuggling. Alice Huang, with whom Jensen Huang reportedly had an affair, runs Megaspeed, a Singaporean firm now under investigation for smuggling advanced GPUs to China. A US Commerce Department inquiry into the organization was reportedly halted after invention by Nvidia. Megaspeed reportedly bought chips from Supermicro, a company that packages Nvidia’s chips onto servers.

It has been revealed that the Chip Security Act as drafted would require a mechanism to track the locations of chips, either by inspections of facilities, attestations by companies, or ping-based location mechanisms. The ping-based technique, the hardest option to circumvent, would require the GPU to send a signal of its location when it comes online. In September, the Center for Security and Emerging Technology found it would be the most cost-effective option.

Foster said he did not ask Nvidia’s representatives why they weren’t voluntarily adopting such chip-tracking tools if they could technically do so.

But if the requirements of the bill pass as part of the Senate’s National Defense Authorization Act, the new tracking mechanisms would only tell investigators where the chips are, not offer a way to disconnect them if it’s revealed they have been smuggled. Foster told MIT Technology Review he intends to introduce new, stricter legislation in the new year that would offer a workaround. The new rule would require licenses to operate advanced GPUs, and before a GPU could connect, its valid license would need to be verified.

In the meantime, the controversy at Nvidia, Foster notes, has fueled support among his colleagues for the rules in the bill: “There will be a lot of political pressure, in the wake of everything that’s happened, on the companies to actually do a very good job of the geographic validation of where the chip actually is.”.

France wracked by more pension protests amid rising violence on the streets.

According to recent reports, schiappa responded to her critics in a tweet on Saturday, saying: “Defending the right of women to have control of their bodies, that’s everywhere and all the time. In France, women are free. With all due respect to the detractors and hypocrites.”.

French Interior Minister, Gérald Darmanin came to Schiappa’s defense during an interview with French news channel CNews on Sunday calling her a “woman of character.”.

“I wanted to say that Marlene Schiappa is a courageous female politician who has her character and who has her style which is not mine, but I respect,” he remarked.

James Webb telescope finds ice older than the star it orbits

📅 14 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1126 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Ars Technica

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, beta Pictoris is a young star, roughly 20 million years old, and located about 64 light-years away from Earth.
  • It has been revealed that the water ice is glassy rather than crystalline, and it is mixed with carbon dioxide in roughly the same proportions we see in comets of our own Solar System.
  • According to recent reports, beta Pictoris is one of the best studied stars in the sky.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, beta Pictoris is a young star, roughly 20 million years old, and located about 64 light-years away from Earth. It is surrounded by a vast disk of dust and rubble where planets are still forming—astronomers have already found three. In a new Science study, a team led by Sarah Betti, an astronomer at the Space Telescope Science Institute in Baltimore, used the James Webb Space Telescope to look for ice in this disk. Researchers found both water and carbon dioxide ice.

It has been revealed that the water ice is glassy rather than crystalline, and it is mixed with carbon dioxide in roughly the same proportions we see in comets of our own Solar System. This suggests ingredients necessary to form water-rich worlds might be common around young stars.

According to recent reports, beta Pictoris is one of the best studied stars in the sky. Its disk was among the first ever imaged, back in 1984, and we see it almost exactly edge-on, which makes it a natural laboratory for studying how planetary systems grow. It’s what astronomers call a debris disk, where the dust is constantly replenished by collisions among comets and planetesimals, small bodies that are the building blocks of planets.

Sources indicate that the outer parts of the disk are far enough from the star that water and other volatile molecules should freeze into solid ice. The disk holds a large reservoir of carbon monoxide gas, which ultraviolet light from the star should destroy within 50 to 300 years. For that gas to still be there, something must keep replenishing it—most likely it’s released from ice when volatile-rich comets collide. The properties of the planet Beta Pictoris b also suggest it formed from ice-rich material.

Yet despite plenty of reasons to suspect the system is full of ice, earlier searches have failed to find it. Attempts to detect water vapor found nothing, and a search for the telltale dip that water ice leaves in starlight at a wavelength of 3 micrometers also failed.

Industry observers note that according to theoretical models, ultraviolet radiation from the star can destroy small grains of pure ice faster than collisions can produce them. On the other hand, grains of dirty ice, mixed with other molecules, should survive longer.

Sources indicate that betti and her colleagues observed Beta Pictoris on December 7, 2023, using Webb’s Near Infrared Spectrograph (NIRSpec). They operated it in a mode that records a full spectrum, from 0.6 to 5.2 micrometers, for every point in the image. After subtracting the overwhelming glare of the star, the team measured how much starlight the disk’s dust reflects at each wavelength to look for the fingerprints of ices.

Water ice absorbs light strongly near 3 micrometers, while carbon dioxide ice absorbs either at 4.27 micrometers or 4.39 micrometers when it contains the heavier carbon-13 isotope. The team first mapped the water ice features across the disk and found they were strikingly uniform. They then extracted detailed spectra from two spots on opposite sides of the star, each roughly 100 astronomical units out.

Both spectra showed water and carbon dioxide ices, the latter in both its common form and the rarer carbon-13 version. But the shape of those features turned out to tell us more than the fact they were there.

The carbon dioxide features were shifted slightly toward shorter wavelengths and were much broader than those of pure carbon dioxide ice measured in the lab. The team indicates in the paper that this is how carbon dioxide behaves when its molecules are trapped inside water ice. In other words, the two ices aren’t sitting side by side as separate grains—they are thoroughly mixed, which makes it the kind of dirty ice that models suggested could survive the star’s ultraviolet radiation.

In a recent development, the team calculated that there is slightly more than one carbon dioxide molecule for every 10 water molecules, meaning it’s about 11 percent of the ice. That falls within the 2.5 to 30 percent range measured in Solar System comets and the 7 to 20 percent seen in the ice of disks around other newborn stars. It means the ices of Beta Pictoris may have formed through the same processes as in our own Solar System, building up on dust grains in cold, dense, water-rich clouds during the earliest stages of star formation.

Industry observers note that the structure of the water ice also pointed in this direction. When water freezes at moderate temperatures, its molecules settle into an orderly crystal lattice, and crystalline ice produces a sharp peak in the spectrum just above 3 micrometers. That peak was absent at Beta Pictoris. The ice is almost entirely amorphous, a disordered, glass-like solid that forms when water molecules freeze so fast and so cold that they stick wherever they land. The team estimates that less than 7 percent of the water ice in the system is crystalline, which is somewhat surprising.

Industry observers note that models predicted that ice in debris disks should mostly be crystalline. For amorphous ice to stay in that form, it has to remain colder than about 100 Kelvin, or minus 173° Celsius. Otherwise, something has to keep breaking up its crystal structure, such as high-energy ultraviolet light, cosmic rays, or particles streaming from the star. Either way, the researchers concluded the ice most likely formed in the interstellar medium, long before the planets of Beta Pictoris began to take shape.

The remaining question was how the icy grains got spread so evenly across the disk.

The team argues that this even ice distribution requires frequent collisions among planetesimals. Each collision would release fresh icy dust, including ice that had been buried and protected deep inside the colliding bodies, replenishing what the starlight destroys. We already have evidence that such collisions do happen. Earlier infrared images revealed a curved, lopsided streak of dust in the southwestern arm of the disk, thought to be debris from a violent collision a little less than halfway out from the star.

Betti’s team’s findings support the idea that the disk’s carbon monoxide gas comes from colliding icy bodies and offer an explanation of how ice can survive in an environment constantly exposed to ultraviolet light. What the team could not do is determine exactly how much crystalline ice is present or rule out other molecules hiding in the mixture.

But if a young planetary system 64 light-years away may have started with much the same icy ingredients as ours, then primordial, interstellar ice might be a common ingredient of planetary systems in general. This means the raw materials for water-rich, potentially habitable worlds might be common, too.

According to recent reports, science, 2026. DOI: 10.1126/science.adw7770.

  • In a recent development, even by the diminished standards of today’s corporate governance, this was a shockingly foolish decision.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The self-styled visionaries of Silicon Valley, leaders like OpenAI chief executive Sam Altman and SpaceX boss Elon Musk, have built careers claiming to see the future. Long-term vision is currency: Meta’s Mark Zuckerberg built a 10-year road map for Facebook in 2016, and Google famously told investors before its public offering that it was unconcerned with short-term results. And yet there they all were, a mere five weeks before the midterm elections, gathered at the White House to smile for photos with President Trump and sign on to his “Super Intelligence” agenda.

In a recent development, even by the diminished standards of today’s corporate governance, this was a shockingly foolish decision. Despite dozens of polls showing a rising tide of anti-Trump sentiment and bipartisan rejection of AI and data centers, the futurists of the tech elite cast aside long-term corporate interests for short-term political favor. And now, their industry is very squarely in the newly introduced victors’ crosshairs.

For an industry obsessed with pattern recognition, their decision to lash themselves to President Trump has proved to be a catastrophic misreading of the political landscape. Now, not only have they jeopardized their companies’ fates, but they’ve also raised questions about their vision and judgment.

Recent findings suggest that the people who work for them are just as confused as the rest of us. Tech workers I’ve spoken to at OpenAI, Meta, and other firms have noted an absence of commentary from their leaders post-election. Zuckerberg has yet to address the results internally, while an employee at another AI firm said that “leadership has been pretty silent on Slack.” Most employees share concern about potential anti-data-center legislation and are curious how leadership will adjust to a Democratic Washington, DC. But more than anything, they don’t understand how their bosses didn’t see what was so blindingly obvious to everyone else.

Sources indicate that in Silicon Valley, the Gretzkyism “skate to where the puck is going, not where it has been” is a management maxim; it preaches anticipation and foresight over reactiveness to the present moment. Tech entrepreneurs love a good “pivot,” and companies that can’t change with the times get disrupted and die.

Which is why I find it so strange that Zuckerberg, OpenAI cofounder Greg Brockman, and so many of Silicon Valley’s other prominent AI leaders and venture capitalists have put themselves in a potentially inescapable political bind. In going all in on President Trump’s cultural and business agenda instead of playing both sides of the aisle as corporate America usually does, they’ve built identities they may not be able to pivot out of. Will anyone really believe that Palantir CEO Alex Karp is suddenly progressive after a year of promising “violence and death to our enemies” and telling investors that the organization is “completely anti-woke”?

I believe this is less a surprise than a very public exposure of a fundamental reality: that tech’s most visible leaders are not all-knowing visionary masterminds after all. Insights about social media or artificial intelligence do not make Zuckerberg or Altman experts on politics, the economy, or much else outside of technology. The instant gratification of presidential access, subsidies, and a say in their own regulation blinded them to the basics of political math that they clearly did not understand.

Sources indicate that there’s a reason the chief executives of Chase, Boeing, and other Fortune 500 staples don’t go on podcasts to talk about “masculine energy,” or call the president from the stage of a MAGA-friendly AI summit to label fears about AI a “hoax” and a “scam.” This is the learned wisdom of decades operating in an environment where the customer changes every four years but contracts run for 10. Most companies play to both sides of the aisle because they know that their business models and multibillion-dollar projects must outlast the current administration. Instead, Big Tech tied itself to Trump and made its most important goals and investments—many related to grid access and data center permits—immediate targets for Democrats.

Industry observers note that in tech, you can always sunset a feature or update some code. But in politics, there is no undo button for failures that change public perception. The tech elites’ decision to visibly align their businesses with a temporary movement has left them no credible way to pivot now that the climate has changed. As one Meta employee who has worked closely with Zuckerberg put it, “Mark is a long-term thinker, but he never charts a initiative of how to get there. It’s spray and pray and see what happens.” As for whether employees expect the organization to do a strategic postmortem? “Facebook has never really done that.”.

“Move fast and break things” might work in a startup, but it’s a terrible strategy for building reputational goodwill. Previous technological leaps, like the rollout of fiber-optic technology and wireless infrastructure, avoided partisan politics. But by kowtowing to the Trump administration, Silicon Valley made artificial intelligence a culture-war problem. Now, when citizens vote on data center proposals from California to Florida, they are no longer considering only technical or economic concerns, but political ones.

Sources indicate that tech leaders didn’t see this coming because they were too focused on the urgency of the AI race to understand how reputational damage could undermine the intangible goodwill—and ultimately the very tangible infrastructure—necessary to win it. The industry’s misreading of the moment has already punctured one myth Silicon Valley holds dear: that its leaders can always see what’s next.

Aaron Zamost is a tech communications consultant and a former executive at Square.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Dust off that Hitachi and put your Slack on “Do not disturb,” because AO3 is back online, baby.

After weeks off the internet due to an unspecified security incident, the Organization for Transformative Works (OTW), the nonprofit that runs the hugely popular fan fiction forum, unveiled on November 15 that service had been restored.

Industry observers note that “We understand that the wait and uncertainty surrounding AO3’s return have been difficult, and we apologize for the inconvenience,” the statement reads. “We greatly appreciate your support during the downtime, and continued patience as our volunteers work hard to return AO3 to its full functionality.”.

In a recent development, the news came as a pleasant surprise to AO3’s devoted fans, as the website had announced in late October that restoring service could take between two to four weeks. To that end, the OTW statement says that some of the site’s features, such as user icons and external work importing, have been temporarily disabled in order to expedite the site’s return. It also warned that users “may experience a delay before AO3 loads,” due to “high traffic.”.

Industry observers note that founded in 2007, AO3 is one of the most popular fan fiction forums on the internet, boasting more than 11 million users and over 18 million original works. Following its temporary shutdown, many devastated fans started sharing Google Docs of their favorite fanfics, sparking some concerns among authors worried about AI scraping and their work being posted to other websites without their permission. Others resorted to other platforms to get their Dramione or Hollanov fix, such as Tumblr, which reported a 75 percent jump in fresh sign-ups among users between the ages of 18 and 25, according to data shared with WIRED.

Throughout the 17-day shutdown, AO3 has remained vague about the causes of the security breach. In its statement announcing its return, OTW mentioned that while it has “no reason to believe that the user database was compromised,” it can’t rule out the possibility; the website recommends people change their passwords “as a precaution.” The site is also pairing with a security firm “to help prevent future incidents.”.

Though the suggestion prompted some concern on social media, for the most part fans are jubilant about the end of the “AO3 apocalypse,” as some have referred to the shutdown.

Sources indicate that “Ao3 returned on a Sunday,” one fan wrote in a tweet that has 1.2 million views. “Just like Jesus.”.

Iran has debuted drone attacks against a US military base in Bahrain, casting further doubt on peace talks between Tehran and Washington and raising the spectre of escalation.

Blasts sounded over the Gulf nation on Sunday in the second Iranian drone attack in three days in retaliation for US strikes in Iran.

Industry observers note that meanwhile, in Yemen, Iran’s Houthi allies advanced against pro-government forces in the south, opening a potential route to Aden. Iran also claimed that a mine sank an oil supertanker in the strait of Hormuz.

The developments deepened gloom about the chances of any diplomatic breakthrough in the region.

Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guards Corps said they debuted six drones targeting a US air defence radar at the Al-Rifaa helicopter base in retaliation for “hostile US actions”. Authorities in Bahrain said air defences intercepted the drones before they reached their targets.

At a press conference in Tehran the foreign ministry spokesperson, Esmaeil Baghaei, said Iran would continue to respond to any military aggression by the US or other states. Asked if the latest strikes indicated a change in Iranian direction as negotiations with the US have stalled, he said Iran was “not waiting for anyone” and was focused on its security.

US forces have conducted a series of strikes against Iranian targets in recent weeks, including Qeshm Island in the strait of Hormuz.

Donald Trump last week called them minor strikes and said Saudi Arabia and other Gulf states had cautioned him against large-scale combat operations.

However, the president also noted Washington was no longer seeking a deal with Iran and that he had instructed the vice-president, JD Vance, to switch his focus to alleged corruption and fraud in Democrat-run cities and states.

Vance – who blamed the Republicans’ loss of Congress in midterm elections on the Iran war – had requested a personal meeting with Iranian negotiators to discuss peace terms.

A conflict that began with joint US and Israeli attacks against Iran in February remains at an impasse, with the US maintaining a naval blockade and Iran its chokehold over the strait of Hormuz.

In a separate development, Iran’s Revolutionary Guards claimed that two ships hit mines in the strait of Hormuz and that one, an oil supertanker with 2m barrels of oil, sank. The ships suffered “massive explosions and fire”, mentioned the statement.

It has been revealed that there was no immediate independent verification. The US military recently claimed it had cleared all mines from main routes through the waterway.

The strikes against Bahrain suggested Iran has decided on a tit-for-tat response to US attacks.

Bahrain hosts significant US bases, including a forward base that was home to the US Fifth Fleet and US Naval Forces Central Command, operating as a central support hub for military operations in the Middle East.

Tehran repeatedly targeted the kingdom until September, when there was a lull in attacks. That ended on Friday when Iran debuted drones against a US radar facility. US Central Command said it shot down two drones without any injury or damage.

The attacks on Sunday prompted sirens and alerts from Bahrain’s authorities urging residents to seek shelter.

“It’s exactly what I was hoping wouldn’t happen: Iranian attacks starting again, with all the worry and uncertainty that go with them,” resident Hayat Ibrahim, 65, told Agence France Presse.

Bahrain’s foreign ministry called the resumption of attacks “heinous aggression” and a flagrant violation of international law.

Sources indicate that the kingdom rejected Tehran’s “flimsy pretexts and baseless claims” to target its territory, it remarked in a statement. “The kingdom also rejects the transformation of its territory into an arena for settling scores and holds Iran fully responsible for these attacks and their consequences.”.

Jordan, Egypt, Saudi Arabia, and Qatar condemned the attacks and expressed solidarity with Bahrain.

In Yemen, Saudi Arabia’s campaign against the Iranian-aligned Houthi rebels reeled when forces fighting on behalf of the Yemeni government retreated from the Bab el-Mandeb strait to defend ⁠Aden on the southern ​coast.

“The Southern Armed Forces announce the implementation of ‌a redeployment operation for its forces from Dhubab Airport and the Bab el-Mandeb area, west of Taiz Governorate,” the main military force fighting for Yemen’s government in the south stated in a statement.

The admission signalled the apparent failure of a six-week government counteroffensive to drive the Houthis from the mouth of the Red Sea to secure a key oil route.

A Houthi missile strike near Aden killed people and wounded 12 near Aden, AFP reported, citing military and government sources.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Astronauts who will helm the first crewed moon mission in five decades were revealed on Monday, queuing up the quartet to begin training for the historic Artemis II lunar flyby that is set to take off in November 2024.
  • The astronauts are NASA’s Reid Wiseman, Victor Glover and Christina Koch, and Jeremy Hansen of the Canadian Space Agency.
  • According to recent reports, wiseman is a 47-year-old decorated naval aviator and test pilot who was first selected to be a NASA astronaut in 2009.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Astronauts who will helm the first crewed moon mission in five decades were revealed on Monday, queuing up the quartet to begin training for the historic Artemis II lunar flyby that is set to take off in November 2024.

The astronauts are NASA’s Reid Wiseman, Victor Glover and Christina Koch, and Jeremy Hansen of the Canadian Space Agency.

According to recent reports, wiseman is a 47-year-old decorated naval aviator and test pilot who was first selected to be a NASA astronaut in 2009. A native of Baltimore, Maryland, he’s completed one prior spaceflight, a 165-day trip to the International Space Station that had debuted aboard a Russian Soyuz rocket in 2014. Most recently, Wiseman served as chief of the astronaut office before stepping down in November 2022, making him eligible for a flight assignment.

Wiseman will serve as commander of the Artemis II mission.

Hansen, 47, is a fighter pilot who was selected by the Canadian Space Agency for astronaut training in 2009. From London, Ontario, Hansen is one of only four active Canadian astronauts, and he recently became the first Canadian to be put in charge of training for a upcoming class of NASA astronauts.

He will be the first Canadian ever to travel to deep space.

Glover is a 46-year-old naval aviator who returned to Earth from his first spaceflight in 2021 after piloting the second crewed flight of SpaceX’s Crew Dragon spacecraft and spending nearly six months aboard the International Space Station.

Recent findings suggest that “It’s so much more than the four names that have been revealed,” Glover said during the Monday announcement at NASA Johnson Space Center in Houston. “We need to celebrate this moment in human history. … It is the next step in the journey that will get humanity to Mars.”.

In a recent development, glover, born in Pomona, California, served in several military squadrons in the United States and Japan in the 2000s, and he completed test pilot training with the US Air Force. When he was selected for the NASA astronaut corps in 2013, he was working in the US Senate as a legislative fellow. All told, Glover logged 3,000 flight hours in more than 40 aircraft, over 400 carrier arrested landings and 24 combat missions.

Glover’s first mission to space was as part of the SpaceX Crew-1 team, which launched to the International Space Station in November 2020 for a six-month stay on the orbiting laboratory.

Recent findings suggest that koch, 44, is a veteran of six spacewalks — including the first all-female spacewalk in 2019. She holds the record for the longest single spaceflight by a woman, with a total of 328 days in space. Koch is also an an electrical engineer who helped develop scientific instruments for multiple NASA mission. Koch, a native of Grand Rapids, Michigan, also spent a year at the South Pole, an arduous stay that could well prepare her for the intensity of a moon mission.

Industry observers note that the Artemis II mission will build on Artemis I, an uncrewed test mission that sent NASA’s Orion capsule on a 1.4 million-mile voyage to lap the moon that concluded in December. The space agency deemed that mission a success and is still working to review all the data collected.

In a recent development, if all goes to plan, Artemis II will take off around November 2024. The crew members, strapped inside the Orion spacecraft, will launch atop a NASA-developed Space Launch System rocket from NASA’s Kennedy Space Center in Florida.

The journey is expected to last about 10 days and will send the crew out beyond the moon, potentially further than any human has traveled in history, though the exact distance is yet to be determined.

The “exact distance beyond the Moon will depend on the day of liftoff and the relative distance of the Moon from the Earth at the time of the mission,” NASA spokesperson Kathryn Hambleton said via email.

After circling the moon, the spacecraft will return to Earth for a splashdown landing in the Pacific Ocean.

In a recent development, artemis II is expected to pave the way for the Artemis III mission later this decade, which NASA has vowed will put the first woman and person of color on the lunar surface. It will also mark the first time humans have touched down on the moon since the Apollo program ended in 1972.

The Artemis III mission is expected to take off later this decade. But much of the technology the mission will require, including spacesuits for walking on the moon and a lunar lander to ferry the astronauts to the moon’s surface, is still in development.

NASA is targeting a 2025 launch date for Artemis III, though the space agency’s inspector general has already said delays will likely push the mission to 2026 or later.

The space agency has been seeking to return people to the moon for more than a decade. The Artemis program was designed to pave the way to establishing a permanent lunar outpost, allowing astronauts to live and work deeper into space long term as NASA and its partners map a path to sending the first humans to Mars.

Vanessa Wyche, the director of NASA’s Johnson Space Center, declined to provide details to CNN about the selection process. But she emphasized the diversity of the Artemis II crew, which includes men and women rather than only a staff of White male test pilots as has been the case for historic missions of the past.

Industry observers note that “I can tell you, they still all have the right stuff,” Wyche stated. “We have requirements different than we did (when we) just had test pilots” on inaugural missions.

Koch said in an interview with CNN’s Ed Lavandera that the group found out they were selected a few weeks ago.

“We were all sent to a meeting that was on our calendars under a different pretext that didn’t sound as lofty as the one it was going to be,” Koch noted. “And accidentally two of us were very late to that meeting.”.

She stated the offer rendered her “speechless.”.

Recent findings suggest that “It truly is an honor,” she added. “It’s an honor — not to get myself in the space — but because it’s amazing to be a part of this team that’s going back to the moon and on to Mars.”.

An interview with the four astronauts will air on “CNN This Morning” on Tuesday, which starts at 6 am ET.

CNN’s Kristin Fisher contributed to this story.

#217. Industry News: Sony 27-inch Gaming Monitor with DualSense Charging Hook review: A piece of PC history

Industry News: Sony 27-inch Gaming Monitor with DualSense Charging Hook review: A piece of PC history

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1175 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Engadget

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It’s a perfectly adequate display with one unique hook.
  • It's an odd time for Sony to launch a PlayStation-branded gaming monitor, but hey, we'll take it.
  • At $349, the 27-inch Gaming Monitor with DualSense Charging Hook is a reasonably hot gaming accessory.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It’s a perfectly adequate display with one unique hook.

It's an odd time for Sony to launch a PlayStation-branded gaming monitor, but hey, we'll take it. News broke in March that Sony would no longer bring its first-party games to PC, reversing course after a six-year run on desktops and teeing up a summer of heartbreak in the video game world. On the heels of this decision, Sony debuted the 27-inch Gaming Monitor with DualSense Charging Hook, advertising it as a desktop-geared peripheral that's compatible with PC, PS5 and a lineup of PlayStation accessories. It's sleek, it's sturdy, it has a crisp QHD display that supports VRR and HDR, and it features a buttery screen that handles glare well.

At $349, the 27-inch Gaming Monitor with DualSense Charging Hook is a reasonably hot gaming accessory. But more than anything, it feels like a vestigial remnant of Sony's abandoned prepares to infiltrate the PC space.

The DualSense monitor has a 27-inch IPS display with QHD (2,560 x 1,440 pixels) resolution and a 240Hz refresh rate that supports VRR. Here we have the first sign that this thing was originally designed for PC play: The PS5 and PS5 Pro max out at 120Hz, and the monitor's 240Hz cap was included with PC play in mind.

It supports HDR on the spec sheet, but with a peak brightness of 350 nits and no advanced local dimming, you're mostly getting a broader range of colors rather than the eye-popping highlights the term might suggest. There's also a stereo speaker built into the display, and while its output is slightly tinny and lacking bass as you'd expect, it's perfectly acceptable. Put simply, this is a pretty standard gaming monitor in 2026.

In a recent development, as far as inputs go, there are two HDMI 2.1 ports, one DisplayPort 1.4, two USB-A slots, one USB-C connection and a 3.5mm audio output. They're tucked into a divot on the rear of the monitor and pointed downward, with a clever cable management hook that can be popped out from the stand's neck, keeping things as organized as possible.

It has been revealed that the monitor is compatible with PC, Mac, PS5 and PS5 Pro, plus it can hold and charge a DualSense or DualSense Edge gamepad. It also functions with the PlayStation Link adapter, which enables Sony's Pulse and Pulse Elite wireless headsets, Pulse Explore earbuds and Pulse Elevate wireless speakers (at least theoretically). The Pulse headset will hit the market this month, while the Elevate speakers were just recently delayed indefinitely, extending the last echoes of a grander desktop scheme.

It has been revealed that the DualSense charging dock swings down from behind the screen and hangs below the frame, and it's actually the star of the show. It's truly cute and also incredibly useful. Having a dedicated, out-of-the-way spot to store and charge an often-used gamepad is clutch.

The DualSense monitor is a noticeable upgrade from both the 27-inch Samsung 1440p/144Hz TN display and the 24-inch Alienware 1080p/240Hz IPS display that I at the moment use. This improvement applies not only to gaming scenarios, but also your standard PC use cases, like working, creating, watching YouTube, scrolling Reddit and streaming Real Housewives.

Sony's marketing positions the monitor as a display for your desktop PS5, but this is an uncommon console configuration and it's one that I don't personally have set up in my home. So, I tested out the monitor the way most players will use it, as a PC peripheral that happens to hold and charge my spare DualSense. This worked out exceedingly well for my gaming habits, considering I play Overwatch on PC and PS5, and I prefer to use a DualSense for both (keyboard and mouse players, don't come for me). However, outside of this one title, I tend to use the Wolverine V3 Pro for my Steam games, and there's no place to adorably dangle any non-DualSense gamepad from Sony's latest display. This is also true for literally every other monitor, of course.

I plugged in a set of Creative Pebble speakers and my PC, popped my favorite DualSense Edge on the dock, clipped a Logitech camera and Elgato light to the top of the monitor, and I was good to go. The display naturally rests parallel to the stand neck and it can be tilted upward about 30 degrees, but not downward. The tilt action is fluid and it sticks in place well. Shifting the screen vertically is less enjoyable but still easy: Hold a button at the back of the neck and the monitor clicks into place at varying levels. If you want to lower it more than 21mm from the top, you have to hide the charging dock first.

In a recent development, there's a large sliding glass door beside my desk, providing ample opportunity to test the monitor's glare-management abilities. The DualSense display has an eggshell-like coating that eats light like it's late for dinner, and it maintains a bright, crisp image even in a sun-drenched room. Things only improve in dimmer conditions, and the monitor's 240Hz refresh rate is a dream compared with my previous cap of 144Hz. With 1440p resolution, VRR and up to 240 fps in-game, I don't find myself longing for 4K visuals while playing Overwatch or any other game. Of course, I'm not coming from a 4K monitor, so I would say that.

The monitor also looks great on the desk, with a wide and thin metal base, sleek cylindrical stand neck and subtle branding. Maybe my previous display was just severely unstable, but I find the DualSense monitor to be surprisingly sturdy, especially considering its minimal design. Say you share a desk with someone who has a habit of idly bouncing their legs throughout the day, intermittently shaking the entire workspace and sometimes even knocking over your aesthetically placed Sanrio figurines. (A totally random, hypothetical example, of course). The Sony Gaming Monitor holds up well to this type of abuse, wobbling just slightly even under extreme leg-bouncing conditions. It's far more stable than my previous monitor, and it doesn't make plastic creaking noises when it does sway. All told, it's a sturdy piece of equipment.

Industry observers note that sony's 2026 PlayStation-branded gaming monitor is sleek, clever and cute, and at $349, it's a solid investment for anyone who even occasionally uses a PlayStation controller at the desk. My final read on the dock is that it's dope: It charges and stores the DualSense in a cool way, and provides a function that no other monitor will have. Even if you don't ever pull the charging dock down, this is a capable and clean display.

According to recent reports, sony clearly started building the 27-inch DualSense monitor before reversing its plans to take over the PC space, so in many ways, this peripheral exists as a physical reminder of a future that will never be. You could say it's already a piece of gaming history, something that feels more ephemeral by the day.

#215. More autonomy, fewer NDAs: Volunteers have new requests for brain implant trials

📅 13 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1117 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Technologyreview ↗ Open Full Page

More autonomy, fewer NDAs: Volunteers have new requests for brain implant trials

📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1117 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Technologyreview

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, scientists have been working on ways to decode brain activity for decades.
  • It has been revealed that the people who volunteer for trials of those devices play a vital role in that research, and they ought to be recognized for their contributions, notes Ian Burkhart, who had one implanted in his own brain back in 2014.
  • Recent findings suggest that ethics guidelines for clinical trials already exist.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, scientists have been working on ways to decode brain activity for decades. Teams have developed brain implants that can be used to control robotic limbs and computers, and even to “speak.”.

It has been revealed that the people who volunteer for trials of those devices play a vital role in that research, and they ought to be recognized for their contributions, notes Ian Burkhart, who had one implanted in his own brain back in 2014. He’s been working on a set of guidelines for researchers developing brain-computer interfaces (BCIs).

Recent findings suggest that ethics guidelines for clinical trials already exist. But BCI trials are different, states Jennifer Chandler, a professor of law and neuroethics at the University of Ottawa who also worked on the guidelines. “These are people who have a device embedded in their brain, are in trials sometimes for years and years … [and contribute] a significant investment of time, of the body, and of intellectual effort.”.

Burkhart was left paralyzed from the chest down following a diving accident in 2010, when he was 19 years old. Around four years later, he volunteered to become the first person to trial a brain implant designed for hand control.

According to recent reports, he had an array of 96 electrodes inserted into the part of his brain that controls movement. The electrodes were connected to a computer via a cable that essentially plugged into his head. Algorithms on the computer were designed to interpret those signals and deliver them to another sleeve of electrodes worn on Burkhart’s arm, allowing him to control it.

In a recent development, the first movements were small, but Burkhart was ultimately able to use the system to pour beads from bottles, move small and delicate objects, and even play Guitar Hero, if only during lab visits. It was a scientific breakthrough.

Burkhart took part in two years-long clinical trials over the seven-and-a-half-year period he had the electrode array implanted in his brain. “It was a fantastic experience,” he indicates. “But there’s certainly some things that, knowing what I know now, I would want to do a little differently.”.

In 2022, Burkhart cofounded BCI Pioneers Coalition—an organization through which people who have taken part in BCI trials can share their experiences, both with each other and with researchers. Over the last year, members of the group have been developing a set of guidelines based on those experiences. The idea is to help academics, clinicians, and companies run ethical trials that respect participants’ autonomy.

The guidelines, published on Tuesday, lay out a list of recommendations that fall within 13 categories. One, for example, focuses on recognizing and compensating trial participants. During the trials that Burkhart participated in, “I was going into the lab two or three days a week, for four hours at a time,” he recalls. “That’s [easily] a part-time job if you just count the hours you’re putting in.”.

Sources indicate that as the trial progressed, Burkhart says, he learned more and was able to give more constructive feedback on what was working and what wasn’t. He says he was a key member of the research team. Others who find themselves in a similar position might appreciate being listed as a coauthor on scientific publications or publicly named as a research collaborator, he says. Burkhart and his colleagues acknowledge that not everyone will want this, however.

The guidelines also address the thorny question of privacy. That’s important: The public will always be interested in cutting-edge biotechnologies like these—and the guidelines say researchers also have a duty to prepare participants for the possibility of media attention. In some cases, it might be difficult to completely conceal the identity of trial participants.

Recent findings suggest that things get even more complicated when it comes to the privacy of participants’ brain data. Research teams will need to access, analyze, and—at least temporarily—store this data. Burkhart wasn’t too bothered about that in his case, where scientists were collecting neural activity related to movement. But people who have brain implants designed for turning thoughts into words might feel differently.

The guidelines state that brain data “should be understood as the participant’s personal information.” They are pushing for participants to be able to access their own brain data whenever they want—something that has not always been possible—and want to make sure people aren’t prevented from sharing it with their own doctors because of embargoes or nondisclosure agreements (NDAs) designed to keep findings under wraps from competitors.

According to recent reports, “It’s not super common for there to be firm NDAs within a lot of the trials,” says Burkhart. “But it’s something where we want to make sure that that does not happen.”.

Industry observers note that the guidelines also address what comes after a trial. Around five years after Burkhart had his device implanted, the research team ran into some challenges with funding. When we last spoke a few years ago, he recalled how he was told he would have to have the implant removed and could have it put back in once the team had secured funding. (And we’re talking about brain surgery here.).

Recent findings suggest that ultimately, he kept the implant until 2021, when it was removed after an infection started to develop at the point where the cable led into his scalp. But losing the device after all those years was difficult; he’d regained the ability to move his arm—and then lost it again.

Rita Leggett, an Australian woman who had a device implanted in her brain to treat her epilepsy, has noted she felt she “became one” with her implant. When the firm that made it went bust two years later, the device was removed against her will—an act ethicists have described as a potential breach of human rights.

In a recent development, researchers should instead commit to maintaining brain devices for a “reasonable period” after a trial ends, according to the guidelines. Participants should be given plenty of time to prepare for the surgery to remove it. And researchers should set aside extra funds to support trial participants who have to do that.

Sources indicate that some of the guidelines are vague and may overlap with existing ethics standards. They don’t all spell out explicit solutions. They were also developed with feedback from a small group of individuals—the number of people living with BCIs is still very low. The team hopes to grow and expand on the guidelines over time. Burkhart also prepares to discuss them with researchers at an upcoming neuroscience conference.

Recent findings suggest that “This is a living document, and this is version one,” says Chandler. “It’s just the starting point.”.
