💡 Key Takeaways
  • A military-run court in Jordan sentenced three men to death on Sunday after they were convicted in connection with an attack at a church last month that killed nine people, the Jordanian Armed Forces said in a statement.
  • The shooting at a Greek Orthodox church, which also wounded about three dozen people, was one of the deadliest militant attacks in the country in years, and King Abdullah II vowed that it would be met with “the harshest retaliation.”.
  • It has been revealed that the three men were sentenced after being convicted of violating antiterrorism laws, according to the Jordanian military.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A military-run court in Jordan sentenced three men to death on Sunday after they were convicted in connection with an attack at a church last month that killed nine people, the Jordanian Armed Forces said in a statement.

The shooting at a Greek Orthodox church, which also wounded about three dozen people, was one of the deadliest militant attacks in the country in years, and King Abdullah II vowed that it would be met with “the harshest retaliation.”.

It has been revealed that the three men were sentenced after being convicted of violating antiterrorism laws, according to the Jordanian military. They were found guilty of carrying out deadly terrorist acts, possessing weapons and ammunition with the intent to commit terrorism, and promoting the ideas of a terrorist group.

That group was not named in the armed forces statement.

The sentences are subject to appeal, the military statement noted.

Recent findings suggest that the three men were arrested in late October in Jordan after a shootout with security forces during a predawn raid on their hide-out in an abandoned house in the southern province of Karak, where the church attack took place. Karak is home to a sizable Christian community.

According to recent reports, king Abdullah praised the arrests on social media. “No proponent of dark ideologies that divide Jordanians will be tolerated,” he wrote.

Jordanian officials have not said what motivated the shooting at the church. Shortly afterward, Prime Minister Jafar Hassan said it was “the result of terrorist takfiri ideology,” using an Arabic phrase that often describes Islamist extremists who declare other Muslims heretics.

Recent findings suggest that the sentencing on Sunday came a weeks after Jordan retaliated for the church attack with deadly airstrikes on Islamic State targets in southern Syria, a Jordanian government spokesman said at the time. The Jordanian military said it had been “targeting hide-outs of terrorist organizations,” without naming any specific group.

The airstrikes in Syria killed at least seven civilians, including three children, according to the Syrian civil defense rescue service, and the attack was condemned by Syrian officials.

Muslims make up more than 97 percent of the population in Jordan, and Christians make up about 2 percent, according to United States government estimates. The country’s Constitution declares Islam the state religion but safeguards the free exercise of religion and bars discrimination on religious grounds. Christian Jordanians are guaranteed seats in Parliament and have long served as cabinet ministers and ambassadors.

The Christian presence in Karak dates back more than 1,500 years, and there are multiple churches there to this day. Jordan also has vital biblical and Christian pilgrimage sites, including one along the Jordan River where Jesus was said to have been baptized.

In June, Jordan hanged six men convicted of terrorism-related or drug-trafficking charges. The executions came after a nine-year hiatus in executions and were condemned by the European Union and human rights groups, including the Death Penalty Information Center and Human Rights Watch.

Raja Abdulrahim contributed reporting.

Ephrat Livni is a Times reporter covering news around the world. She is based in New York.

#213. SpaceX returned its Starship rocket on Saturday—but there's a catch

📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Ars Technica ↗ Open Full Page

SpaceX returned its Starship rocket on Saturday—but there's a catch

📅 15 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (747 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Ars Technica

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that STARBASE, Texas—The black-and-silver ship fell out of the sky, emerging from the cloud deck near the very end of its flight.
  • Recent findings suggest that slowly, gently, haltingly, the Starship upper stage eased its way toward the waiting tower where two arms extended outward, awaiting expectantly.
  • Then, less than a minute after it came into view, the Starship upper stage was snagged by the launch tower, as snug as you like.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that STARBASE, Texas—The black-and-silver ship fell out of the sky, emerging from the cloud deck near the very end of its flight. Incongruously, the rocket flew horizontally until the last moment, when three Raptor rocket engines ignited and it swooped into a vertical position.

Recent findings suggest that slowly, gently, haltingly, the Starship upper stage eased its way toward the waiting tower where two arms extended outward, awaiting expectantly. The margins are so incredibly narrow. Two nubs on either side of the rocket, each protruding only about 1 foot, were the only purchase the rocket would have on the arms.

Then, less than a minute after it came into view, the Starship upper stage was snagged by the launch tower, as snug as you like. And so it was all over. SpaceX, nearly a quarter of a century after its founding, had just taken a hugely significant step toward developing and optimizing a massive, rapidly reusable rocket.

Industry observers note that this was a breathtaking feat; a brilliant technical achievement that required the best engineering minds to think through a million different difficult problems. And on Saturday evening, following a handful of practice runs into the Indian Ocean, they did it before the entire world.

Watching Starship launch from here a little less than a day earlier, and knowing it had orbited the planet multiple times, added to the sense of unreality in seeing this spaceship return to Earth under its own power and be captured by the tower.

It felt like stepping into the future. SpaceX has dazzled us before by landing rockets on barges and returning humans to space with Crew Dragon. But this flight took things to another level. Starships are huge. They carry a huge amount of energy coming back from orbit. And until a few years ago, it seemed beyond fantastical to think about capturing a rocket with what are essentially outsized chopsticks.

Humans have built reusable spacecraft that flew into orbit before. In the 1970s, flush with confidence after the triumphant Moon landings, NASA designed and built several Space Shuttles. They had solid rocket boosters that were fished from the ocean and reused. The large orange external tank was not recovered after each flight, but the orbiters went to space for two weeks, or even longer, before returning to Earth and landing on a runway.

The shuttles were engineering marvels. But during the return to Earth they acted as gliders, not igniting their engines. And their heat shields were delicate flowers, requiring painstaking refurbishment after each flight. At the outset of the shuttle program, the space agency contemplated sending dozens of humans into space at a time, and carrying cargo at a cost as low of $25 per pound.

Reality never matched these rosy projections. The crew space capped out at seven astronauts, and the cost-per-pound was closer to $25,000. Each orbiter cost an extraordinary amount of money to build; NASA only ever built five that went to space.

SpaceX has five Starships in an advanced state of development at Starbase today; and its factory houses the components for a dozen more. The company can currently manufacture a Starship upper stage in its South Texas Starfactory every three weeks. The factory was sized to produce a ship every three days. When SpaceX founder Elon Musk discussed these build targets in an interview five years ago, he sounded mad. But he no longer does.

The Space Shuttle was nearly a fully reusable space launch system, but it fell far short of low-cost rapid launch. Over 30 years the vehicle made 135 flights. Within a few years SpaceX aims to fly 135 times a year, then thousands of times.

Such was the significance of Saturday. SpaceX aspires to fundamentally change the relationship between humanity and the heavens. The first step is to get the entire rocket back. SpaceX has now returned both elements of a Starship rocket safely to its launch tower. It will take time to reach a high rate of success with such landings, but Saturday’s safe return offered a proof of concept.

The landings will come with increasing frequency; and so will the launches. Over time SpaceX will perfect the heat shield that is likely to be the most difficult aspect of rapid reuse. And eventually, as difficult as it may be to believe, what we experienced with amazement this weekend will become routine. One day, we will take this all for granted.

#210. Industry News: How to use your phone to find an Apple TV remote

Industry News: How to use your phone to find an Apple TV remote

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (779 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Engadget

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Here is how to find your remote without buying a fresh one.
  • Is there anyone in the world who owns a TV and hasn't lost the remote at least once?
  • Industry observers note that apple has a dedicated Remote app that will let you locate the device much like you'd use an AirTag.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Lost in the cushions again? Here is how to find your remote without buying a fresh one.

Is there anyone in the world who owns a TV and hasn't lost the remote at least once? Unlikely, right? Now that remotes are slimmer and more compact, it's an even more prevalent occurrence. Losing your Apple TV remote is just as easy, of course. It can slip between couch cushions, end up under the blankets or get left somewhere when someone gets up from the couch to grab some water. The good news, however, is that your smartphone can actually help you find your Apple TV remote anywhere in your home.

Industry observers note that apple has a dedicated Remote app that will let you locate the device much like you'd use an AirTag. To find a missing Apple TV remote, you just have to pop open the app and hunt for the "Locate Remote" button, which will then trigger a beeping sound from the remote itself if you have the 2026 Apple TV 4K model. That helps if the thing's buried under the cushions.

In a recent development, in the meantime, you could also use that same Remote app to turn your phone into a fully functional Apple TV controller. Android people have some workarounds too. As long as your phone is connected to the same Wi-Fi network as your Apple TV, you can regain control within minutes. You just have to know how.

Recent findings suggest that if you've dug through the couch cushions, turned over every blanket, looked under the sofa and checked your kid's toy bins and still haven't found the remote, it's time to bring out the major guns. And by big guns, we mean to launch the Apple TV Remote app. This tool requires an iPhone running iOS 17 or later, while the Apple TV must have tvOS 17 or later. You have to open the Control Center on your iPhone and then tap on the Apple TV Remote. From there, tap the device list, tap Find and follow the prompts on your iPhone to locate your remote. The onscreen circle grows and grows and the text changes from far to near to here in a techy game of Hot and Cold.

The new Siri Remote that Apple released with its refreshed Apple TV 4K in October 2026 has Precision Finding hardware, which means it's easier to find with onscreen directional arrows and live distance guidance. There's even a built-in speaker that plays a chime to locate it. Previous models only come with proximity searching, so you'll have to rely on your phone to find the remote.

In case your remote is nowhere to be found and not even the built-in location feature is of help, then you have to try out a different method. You could, of course, order a newly introduced remote, but that's not absolutely necessary, and a new Apple TV is supposed to last long enough that losing a remote shouldn't push you to replace the whole setup.

To use the Apple TV remote, you just need to access your iPhone's or iPad's Control Center. As we already discussed, you have to tap on the Apple TV Remote button and then on your Apple TV or smart TV that's AirPlay-compatible from the list. You might need to enter a four-digit passcode to confirm the connection.

It has been revealed that once that's set up, you can use your phone as a TV remote to do things like control volume, open and close the device, switch streaming apps, control playback and so on. Everything you can do with the actual, physical Apple Remote, you can do with this app.

According to recent reports, if you're an Android user, there's no official Apple-made remote app to use. There are, however, workarounds to replace your lost Apple TV remote without spending money. Third-party apps like Remote for Apple TV are available on the Google Play Store and replicate the core remote functionality of the physical remote. You'll need to download the app, ensure your Android phone is connected to the same Wi-Fi network as the Apple TV and type in the onscreen code for pairing. Then you use the digital remote to hunt for your next binge-worthy show.

In a recent development, see? Losing the Apple TV remote doesn't have to derail your viewing session. The Remote app is the fastest and most reliable solution whenever you can't find the remote and you really want to turn down the volume or swap the app. Once you can hear your own thoughts again, you can resume your search for the device.

Breaking: Revealed: Israel uploaded millions of photos to Amazon’s facial recognition platform to track Palestinians

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1547 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Theguardian

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Upload came as the Israeli military was increasing its reliance on Amazon’s cloud platform to meet the technological demands of its bombardment of Gaza.
  • The Israeli military uploaded 3.5m photos to Amazon’s cloud platform in order to use the US company’s facial recognition technology to analyse images of Palestinians, the Guardian can reveal.
  • Leaked documents show the expansive catalogue of images was moved into Amazon’s cloud in the early months of Israel’s devastating aerial bombardment and ground offensive in Gaza.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Upload came as the Israeli military was increasing its reliance on Amazon’s cloud platform to meet the technological demands of its bombardment of Gaza.

The Israeli military uploaded 3.5m photos to Amazon’s cloud platform in order to use the US company’s facial recognition technology to analyse images of Palestinians, the Guardian can reveal.

Leaked documents show the expansive catalogue of images was moved into Amazon’s cloud in the early months of Israel’s devastating aerial bombardment and ground offensive in Gaza.

The images were uploaded by a department of the Israeli military that holds a vast collection of photos covering the Palestinian populations in Gaza and the West Bank.

The department informed Amazon of the decision to upload the images in early 2024 so it could use Rekognition, the tech giant’s AI-powered image analysis platform for a facial recognition project.

The documents obtained by the Guardian form part of an investigation into the Israeli military’s reliance on the technology and infrastructure of Amazon’s cloud computing business to monitor Palestinians.

According to the files and interviews with military sources, Israel has in recent years migrated huge volumes of data – including sensitive intelligence material and information about Palestinians living under occupation – into Amazon’s datacentres.

The large set of images was moved into an Amazon datacentre near Tel Aviv by a department commonly known as Rolling Stone, which sits within a military software unit.

The department takes its name from a system widely used by the Israeli military that serves as a central repository of information about Palestinians living in Gaza and the West Bank.

At the time, the department was exploring using facial recognition technologies to analyse the extensive catalogues of images of Palestinians it holds, several sources with knowledge of its work said.

After Israel’s ground invasion of Gaza in October 2023, its military routinely collected images of Palestinians as they passed through checkpoints, often after they had been forcibly displaced by the bombing campaign.

It’s not clear whether the 3.5m images uploaded to Amazon’s Rekognition were captured at these checkpoints, which effectively served as pop-up surveillance posts.

However, a military source familiar with facial recognition efforts at the checkpoints said Amazon’s cloud infrastructure was used due to the “very large scale” of images collected at the sites.

Israel has long used facial recognition technology, particularly in its occupation of the West Bank. Face scanning is routine at checkpoints, while Israeli soldiers use custom-built smartphone apps to collect images of people living in the Palestinian territory.

It has been revealed that in the early stages of its campaign in Gaza, Israel used Rekognition to identify hostages captured by militants in the Hamas-led attack on southern Israel on 7 October 2023. The military also deployed facial recognition technology to identify people it suspected were militants.

The New York Times has previously reported how the military experimented with commercially available technology in Gaza to detect faces in crowds and in drone footage, at times wrongly flagging civilians as militants.

The new documents reveal the Israeli military’s use of Amazon technology, both for experiments with facial recognition and for a more far-reaching project to move its data on to the servers of the computing arm of the conglomerate founded by billionaire Jeff Bezos.

They also shed light on what the Israeli military is moving into the cloud and how it uses Amazon Web Services (AWS) infrastructure to support the collection and processing of Palestinians’ personal data, typically gathered indiscriminately, through intrusive means and without their consent.

The files suggest the ties between AWS and the Israeli military deepened during a period in which Israel has been accused of committing grave crimes in Gaza, including genocide – a charge denied by Israel, but supported by a UN commission of inquiry, Israeli human rights groups and genocide experts.

In a recent development, A spokesperson for AWS said it had no “visibility” into workloads held by its customers in its cloud. They added: “We respect the privacy of our customers, and we do not discuss our relationship without their consent.”.

In early 2024, a small group of Israeli soldiers worked from AWS’s offices in Tel Aviv, located on the 28th floor of one of Israel’s tallest skyscrapers.

The soldiers were exploring ways to use the firm’s cloud infrastructure to more effectively operate a facial recognition programme underway in Gaza, several military sources mentioned.

It’s not clear whether their work was made operational or if it related to the 3.5m images uploaded to Rekognition. The presence of the group at AWS’s offices, however, underscores the close relationship between the Israeli military and the cloud provider.

An AWS spokesperson said its customers “regularly visit our offices for briefings and meetings”. They added: “Any suggestion that these visits are anything other than routine customer engagement is wrong and unsubstantiated.”.

Sources indicate that the foundation of Israel’s relationship with Amazon is a sweeping 2021 contract known as Project Nimbus. Under the multibillion dollar deal, AWS and Google provide cloud services to a wide range of government and military clients.

The Guardian revealed last year that the Nimbus contract contains unusual terms that prohibit the US companies from restricting or suspending Israeli government and military use of their cloud services, even if Israel breaches their terms of service.

This would prevent the kind of unilateral action taken by Microsoft last year when it disabled the Israeli military’s access to technology used to operate a mass surveillance system uncovered by the Guardian and +972 Magazine.

As part of the Nimbus deal, AWS opened latest datacentres in Israel in early 2023, allowing the Israeli government and military clients to migrate data from their own servers, according to documents. A large proportion of data was also moved from AWS datacentres in Ireland.

A central component of the Nimbus contract, files show, was an obligation on AWS to provide the Israeli military with access to a segregated area within its Tel Aviv datacentres, fortified with enhanced digital and physical security measures.

This isolated area within the AWS cloud – used to store sensitive material relating to military operations and intelligence collection – was described by the company and its client as a “walled garden”.

The Israeli military’s reliance on AWS reflects its embrace in recent years of leading US tech companies to meet the technological demands of war with rapidly scalable storage, computing power and AI-driven services.

The role of AI in Israel’s offensive in Gaza has come under fresh scrutiny particularly after the release of NAZA, a Guardian-produced documentary about the remote surveillance and killing of Palestinian civilians.

The Rolling Stone department is among AWS’s most significant Israeli military clients, documents suggest. Its use of Rekognition in early 2024 to analyse 3.5m images came after it had expanded its use of AWS products and services to store and analyse its data.

Recent findings suggest that files show the department migrated significant volumes of the data it holds into the so-called “walled garden” in AWS’s cloud throughout 2023. A military source involved in this effort said it had planned to move all of its databases from the military servers into AWS’s cloud.

The source, who spoke on the condition of anonymity, mentioned: “The strategy [at Rolling Stone] was to migrate pictures, videos, all the confidential intelligence information – everything.”.

A spokesperson for the Israel Defence Forces (IDF) noted it “does not intend to comment on engagements or services related to operational needs”.

The Rolling Stone department oversees several expansive databases that collate data on Palestinians, including the system from which the branch takes its name.

Used by the military for decades, the Rolling Stone system is constantly updated and includes data such as basic personal and family details, property holdings, and information on checkpoint crossings, work permits, and criminal activity.

A soldier who provided testimony to Breaking the Silence, an Israeli NGO, in 2016 described Rolling Stone as “a computerised system where all the information relevant to the control of the Palestinian civilian population is centralised”.

As a result of Israel’s control of the population registries covering Gaza and the West Bank, the Rolling Stone department has amassed millions of Palestinians’ photographs taken for the identity cards issued to every resident when they turn 16 years old.

Sources familiar with its work said the images were routinely used for facial recognition programmes. These include Blue Wolf, a smartphone app Israeli soldiers use in the West Bank to scan Palestinians’ faces and access information about them, including whether they’ve been flagged as suspects for arrest.

Industry observers note that in Gaza, at temporary Israeli checkpoints established after the ground invasion, cameras trained on Palestinian people were used to capture their images as they approached the sites. Facial recognition was then used to match people to images held in Rolling Stone’s systems, sources mentioned.

Sources indicate that the checkpoints became notorious in Gaza as places where people were pulled aside and detained. Many were taken into Israeli custody and held incommunicado, amounting to enforced disappearances, according to several UN bodies and rights groups.

Documents suggest AWS’s cloud technology was used at times during 2024 to support the work of the checkpoints. Military insiders stated the checkpoints were referred to by Israeli soldiers as Nakaz – a Hebrew word for drainage.

Instagram Is Bringing Amazon Affiliate Links Directly to Reels and Posts

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (591 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: WIRED

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Instagram confirmed a change on Monday that may spell the end for users being nudged to visit a creator’s “link in bio.” At least when they’re promoting products sold on Amazon.
  • Starting today, creators and businesses can attach multiple Amazon affiliate links to their Instagram content—up to 30 per video or 20 per regular feed post.
  • Instagram’s parent company Meta dropped this shopping-focused change right before the holiday season really kicks off.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Instagram confirmed a change on Monday that may spell the end for users being nudged to visit a creator’s “link in bio.” At least when they’re promoting products sold on Amazon.

Starting today, creators and businesses can attach multiple Amazon affiliate links to their Instagram content—up to 30 per video or 20 per regular feed post. (Affiliate links let creators earn a commission on any resulting sales.) To participate in this Amazon program, creators must be US-based adults with a professional account that has over 1,000 followers.

Instagram’s parent company Meta dropped this shopping-focused change right before the holiday season really kicks off. As creators look to cash in on Amazon's sales, you might expect an avalanche of affiliate posts as you sip hot cocoa and scroll through Reels. But Instagram claims this won’t be the case.

Industry observers note that “We don’t expect a sudden influx of shopping content from this launch,” Instagram spokesperson Megan Buckley tells WIRED. “Instagram’s recommendation systems will continue to recommend content based on people’s interests and what we think they’ll enjoy and find valuable. This update makes creators’ product recommendations easier to shop.”.

In a recent development, for years, Instagram customers could attach a single external link to their bio information. This led to the rise of bundlers like Linktree, where creators could create simple one-page sites with multiple links to content, like shopping recommendations or news articles. In 2023, Instagram expanded the number of links allowed in profiles to five. This most recent update could change how it feels to scroll Instagram, moving more shopping nudges from Amazon storefronts hidden in the bio to direct links on the viral videos.

According to recent reports, in an example shared by Meta, a woman recording a Reel leans into her camera as she applies makeup. The caption reads: “My favorite lip tint these days!” Above the creator’s name, a small image tile pops up with the Amazon product. Tap the product and a page opens inside Instagram with the price. Tap one of the listed items, and Instagram will bump you over to the Amazon app or website to complete your purchase.

In a recent development, this change comes as social media shopping habits continue to expand and evolve. TikTok, one of Meta’s primary competitors, has been quite successful in expanding owners’ purchasing habits through the app. Around this time last year, an analytics firm estimated that $19 billion worth of products were sold globally through TikTok Shop, putting it roughly the same size as eBay. Unlike TikTok, however, Instagram will not take a cut of the sales (at least for now). Reddit is also experimenting with how users shop heading into this holiday season, recently announcing Reddit Reviews, which uses generative AI to summarize user sentiment about products.

It has been revealed that for over a decade, Instagram developers have searched for ways to streamline how consumers spend money through the app. In 2016, WIRED wrote about how the social media app added select commerce links from brands like Warby Parker, a fairly novel attempt at the time to get people to buy stuff through social media. A few years later, the Instagram experience morphed into something like a “digital mall” with in-app checkouts.

It has been revealed that this latest attempt moves links from creator bios and places them directly in users' feeds. While this could be a boon for creators, the platform’s implementation could annoy users, who are already inundated with ads online. We’ll see if this change clicks.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Accusations of incompetence follow retreat of Riyadh-backed forces in effort to relieve siege of Taiz and protect Aden.

Saudi Arabia has been accused by anti-Houthi forces over its military strategy after its Yemeni allies withdrew troops from the strategic Bab al-Mandab strait and pulled back forces from parts of Marib in the central part of the country.

The Saudi-backed government explained the repositioning by saying the strategic priority was to break the attritional siege on Taiz, Yemen’s third city, and to protect Aden, the southern port city in which the Saudi-backed and UN-recognised government is now based.

According to recent reports, many blame the Houthi advance on the absence of a consolidated military command and control among the disparate forces backing the Aden-based government. Saudi Arabia responded to the setback by sidelining the commander of its Yemen coalition, Lt Gen Fahd bin Abdulaziz al-Salman, and replacing him with the chief of staff, Gen Fayyad bin Hamed bin Ruqad al-Ruwaili.

Recent findings suggest that the Houthis’ steady advance towards the areas surrounding Bab al-Mandab, the narrow strait linking the Red Sea with the Indian Ocean on Yemen’s west coast, culminated on Sunday with a formal withdrawal of Yemen government forces, including some in the Southern Giants Brigades that had always been reluctant to defend territory outside the old southern Yemen. In 1990 Yemen had been divided in two, and many in the south want to return to a separated state.

The Saudi-backed government launched a fresh military campaign 42 days ago to drive the Houthis from Yemen but so far it has backfired.

The forces redeployed on Sunday have moved along the coast to al-Suqyah, 95 miles west of Aden, and inside the old Southern Yemen.

Industry observers note that the retreat seems to be acknowledgment of Houthi resilience and is all the more remarkable given the Saudi air superiority. More than 300,000 Yemeni civilians have been displaced.

Amr al-Bidh, special representative of the exiled Southern Transitional Council (STC) leader, Aidarous al-Zubaidi, a separatist anti-Houthi force that is opposed by Saudi Arabia, accused the Saudis of incompetence – and in effect warned Riyadh that unless it became more open to a southern state it would lack the cohesive forces required to prevent the Houthis becoming a permanent security threat.

Industry observers note that he said: “When there is no strategy and no plan, it is inevitable the Houthis would take advantage. The STC will defend the south to the last man but we are fighting with one hand behind our backs since January after Saudi Arabia attacks on the STC.

Sources indicate that “The STC forces retain a credible capability on the ground. But we need practical and political support from the region to counter the Houthis and create the basis for a negotiated settlement, one in which the pathway towards southern independence is fully recognised. We cannot continue like this or else the Houthis will keep expanding.”.

Industry observers note that the breadth of support for the STC, backed by the United Arab Emirates, however, remains disputed. The movement suffered a near fatal setback in January and since then some of the Giants Brigades have switched to backing Riyadh.

Saudi Arabia continues in effect to keep as many as 10 STC leaders hostage in Riyadh, and has refused to let al-Zubaidi to return from exile in Abu Dhabi. Al-Bidh argued the priority should be defensive, avoiding counteroffensives that backfire, improving command and control, and widening the coalition.

Al-Bidh stated reconciliation would require Riyadh to acknowledge the political declaration al-Zubaidi made about a timetable for a southern state in January, and that al-Zubaidi’s return would boost morale and help unify chaotic southern military factions.

He said a recent Yemeni government cabinet reshuffle, including a new information minister, was designed primarily to try draw southerners into fighting the Houthis and not to change policy toward the south.

In a recent development, he also urged the UK to use its diplomacy to bring in other actors rather than simply backing Riyadh. A group of southern Yemenis have written to the foreign secretary, Ed Miliband, seeking a review of UK policy. “We recognise that the longstanding advice from your office is to continue following the Saudi line while calling for unity among the anti-Houthi forces,” the letter mentioned. “But you must surely recognise that every time Britain calls for ‘the unity and territorial integrity of Yemen’, it is asking the southern people and their armed forces to fight for a political outcome in which they do not believe”.

It has been revealed that the former US special envoy to Yemen Tim Lenderking mentioned the US administration was treating Yemen like a sideshow adding “world powers do not understand the gravity of what it is at stake here”. He warned “the problem is only going to get bigger through apathy and lack of attention”.

Microsoft outage cause revealed: It was a perfect storm of problems

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (713 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Mashable

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • You're probably aware that Microsoft 365, the popular suite of products that includes Outlook, suffered a massive global outage last week.
  • Aside from wondering when their email would be working again, the number one question on everyone's mind was what in the world happened to keep Microsoft 365 down for so long?
  • In a statement shared with customers and on X, Microsoft explained there were actually three causes, which created a perfect storm.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

You're probably aware that Microsoft 365, the popular suite of products that includes Outlook, suffered a massive global outage last week. In fact, it was the worst outage of the year, by a sizable margin. The problem took the computer giant roughly 24 hours, over the course of two business days, to get everything back up and running.

Aside from wondering when their email would be working again, the number one question on everyone's mind was what in the world happened to keep Microsoft 365 down for so long?

Now, we know. In a statement shared with customers and on X, Microsoft explained there were actually three causes, which created a perfect storm.

First, a bug caused servers to become unresponsive in specific conditions; second, an issue with Microsoft Teams increased server traffic and created those conditions; and third, many additional servers were already offline from an unrelated issue.

According to recent reports, as Microsoft explained, on their own, neither problem would have caused such a large-scale problem. However, together, well, they kept one of the world's biggest tech companies scrambling for two days to fix their service.

In a social media post published on X, Microsoft's EVP of Copilot, Agents, and Platform Charles Lamanna explained the situation in detail.

According to Lamanna, a "latent defect" resulted in the firm's servers becoming "overwhelmed and unresponsive under certain load conditions." The defect that caused the problem was introduced to Microsoft's systems during a July 2026 upgrade as part of a fix for Microsoft 365 networking gateway servers.

For months, as Lamanna described it, the concern went undetected, and it didn't cause any problems under normal load during Microsoft's testing process.

Recent findings suggest that the second problem occurred when a surge in server load set off the defect. Lamanna notes that Microsoft maintains two independent network gateway systems for Microsoft 365 to handle outages and disruptions. However, 15 hours before the global Microsoft 365 outage, Teams "failed over" from the alternative networking gateway to the primary one, which supports Exchange Online. This wouldn't usually cause a problem, except for the newly introduced defect introduced by the July patch.

Finally, Microsoft's servers weren't operating at 100 percent at the time. According to Lamanna, it just so happened that nearly 14 percent of the server capacity for the networking gateway was out of service "due to an unrelated glitch from the previous day.".

Industry observers note that again, normally, this would have been routine maintenance. The service would still have sufficient capacity to work as normal.

All three issues occurring at once led to disaster.

"Taken together, the increased load and the reduced server capacity, caused the network gateway to encounter the latent bug from July," Lamanna writes. "This caused requests to build up until servers ultimately stopped responding. This occurred during the peak window of traffic in the United States.".

Recent findings suggest that recovery from the outage also took much longer than usual because servers were "immediately overwhelmed by waiting traffic and became unresponsive again." In addition, Microsoft was unable to roll back the code because the bug dated back to July. So, Microsoft essentially had to develop a patch within that short timeframe, which returned the code to its previous "good state.".

According to recent reports, the entire explanation from Microsoft is actually quite an interesting read and reveals that no matter how big the manufacturer is, massive tech challenges can still occur. Readers can check out Lamanna's entire post on X; Microsoft enterprise customers can also learn more in the Microsoft 365 Admin Center.

In a recent development, microsoft has since apologized for the outage. Businesses affected by the downtime can also file a claim with the company for credits due to the downtime.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Miguel Ángel Félix Gallardo, a notorious Mexican drug lord who helped build the foundations of the modern drug trade, died a prisoner at the age of 80 on Sunday, according to the Mexican authorities.

Recent findings suggest that mr. Félix Gallardo became internationally known in the 1980s after the United States Drug Enforcement Administration accused him of the kidnapping, torture and murder of an undercover agent, Enrique (Kiki) Salazar Camarena.

On Friday, after decades behind bars, Mr. Félix Gallardo was transferred from the Puente Grande prison complex to a private hospital in Guadalajara after a medical emergency, according to the Jalisco state secretary of public security. He died around 2 p.m. Sunday of multiple organ failure, the agency said in a statement, citing medical personnel who treated him.

A small religious ceremony will be held at the hospital in the presence of his relatives, according to Jorge Eduardo Montiel, a spokesman for the Secretary of Public Security of Jalisco state.

Sources indicate that when Mr. Félix Gallardo was arrested in 1989, he was described by the Mexican attorney general, Enrique Alvarez del Castillo, as the “No. 1 narcotics trafficker in Mexico.”.

Which Steam settings should you change to improve gaming performance?

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (557 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Engadget

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Improving your system's gaming performance involves more than swapping components.
  • While it's a reliable gaming storefront with plenty of community tools, those tools can affect weaker machines or people on slow internet.
  • Steam's in-game overlay is a powerful tool.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

When in doubt, disable the overlay.

Improving your system's gaming performance involves more than swapping components. Software can affect your frame rate as much as the system's hardware. Multiple overlays and background apps can quickly ruin your frame rate in any game. Even if you're selective about what you install, tried-and-true apps can slow your device down if you leave them on their default settings. A great example of this is Steam.

While it's a reliable gaming storefront with plenty of community tools, those tools can affect weaker machines or people on slow internet. By default, Steam starts when your system boots, loads community assets in the background and uses resources to power its in-game overlay. These small features can eat into your FPS and bandwidth, but the good news is you can turn almost all of them off to improve your gaming performance and system stability. The best place to start is Steam's overlay.

Steam's in-game overlay is a powerful tool. It gives you easy access to community guides, friend invites, frame rate limiters and in-game purchases. As useful as that can be, it comes at a cost: stability. Valve's overlay uses few system resources, lowering your FPS by maybe a couple of percentage points at most. However, many gamers can attest to just how buggy some titles are when the in-game overlay is enabled. With the overlay enabled, games might stutter, drop frames, or even crash. Disabling the overlay is generally a good place to start when these issues occur.

In a recent development, open Steam and click the top-left corner, then select the "Settings" option. From here, go to the "In Game" tab to view all of your options with the in-game overlay. If you're experiencing major complications with most of your games, we suggest you toggle the "Enable the Steam overlay while in game" option at the very top of the menu. Your system will no longer use resources to run the overlay's background tools or web browser, saving bandwidth and improving overall system stability.

Industry observers note that if disabling the overlay didn't fix the issue, Steam has a few performance settings you can toggle that should noticeably affect your FPS and bandwidth on weaker hardware. From the same settings menu, head to the "Library" section. There are two settings here that can help: Low Bandwidth Mode and Low Performance Mode. If you are having issues with graphical performance in general, we recommend enabling both and testing your in-game FPS. Should your frame rate improve, try disabling Low Bandwidth Mode and test again.

Low Bandwidth Mode disables Steam's background loading of community assets — community guides, artwork and video content. While this doesn't affect FPS directly, Steam can use a surprising amount of background bandwidth when this setting is disabled. For video games with online components or always-online requirements, leaving this setting on can improve your game's stability and frame rate.

According to recent reports, the other setting, Low Performance Mode, disables some of the advanced graphic effects you'll find in Steam's library tab. It disables category transitions, game selection, and various icons to save system memory. This frees up system resources for whatever game you're playing, though it won't make a night-and-day difference on most systems. Pair this with disabling the in-game overlay to maximize your FPS.

#201. How the world’s fires changed while humanity hit pause

📅 15 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1412 w)

How the world’s fires changed while humanity hit pause

📅 15 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1412 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Ars Technica

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Wildfires occur worldwide, and they can sometimes become serious threats to people’s lives.
  • Many things can cause wildfires, but humans are the only factor that can also make preventative efforts.
  • A team led by Jianghao Wang, a professor at the Chinese Academy of Sciences, recently published a study in Cell Reports Sustainability comparing the COVID-19 era with other years.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Wildfires occur worldwide, and they can sometimes become serious threats to people’s lives. A series of massive bushfires from 2019 to 2020 swept across southeastern Australia and destroyed thousands of homes. Recently, the 2025 Los Angeles wildfires spread widely across the city, resulting in massive damage to local communities.

Many things can cause wildfires, but humans are the only factor that can also make preventative efforts. Measuring people’s impact on fire is difficult because of the mix of human and natural influences.

A team led by Jianghao Wang, a professor at the Chinese Academy of Sciences, recently published a study in Cell Reports Sustainability comparing the COVID-19 era with other years. Data from the 2020 lockdowns suggest that lower human activity at this time had the net effect of lowering average fire activity.

Fire doesn’t just happen anywhere. Although plenty of flammable materials exist in natural settings, not every place experiences wildfires. Some prairies burn almost every year, while many forests go without big fires for hundreds of years. Researchers explain these differences in terms of fire regimes, which are patterns describing when, how often, and how widely and intensely fires occur.

Weather is a major factor affecting fire regimes. An abundance of rain helps grow grass and trees that can become fuel for fires. Whether they do or not, however, can depend on the moisture inside plants; plants with enough moisture do not burn easily. By contrast, dry conditions make them more likely to catch fire. When a drought lasts, vegetation becomes increasingly flammable. Strong winds also accelerate fire growth and spread enormously.

According to recent reports, human activity often combines with weather conditions to cause fires. Even routine outdoor recreation can accidentally start a fire. More people venture outdoors during sunny, drier times of the year, increasing the risk of accidental fires when dry vegetation is more likely to be present.

The double-sided role of humans in fire also adds to the difficulty. Humans do start fires, but they also put them out. Firefighters contain fires that could have gone worse if no action had been taken and can keep them from spreading. Humans can also take preventative actions, such as clearing flammable material.

Sometimes the line between starting fires and preventing them becomes blurred. One way to clear out flammable material is to intentionally set fires to make future fires more manageable. However, these fires are hard to distinguish from other fires through satellite monitoring.

An experiment is one way to find out how humans affect wildfires. If everyone stayed home under the same weather, their impact on fires would be revealed. This is why Wang’s research team focused on the COVID-19 era. It was what’s called a “natural experiment,” in which experimental conditions arose without any action by researchers.

Industry observers note that wang explained: “Human activity and climate normally vary together, because seasons, farming calendars, and weather all shape both fire and human behavior. The early-2020 lockdowns produced an abrupt, large-scale drop in human mobility, and the timing differed across countries while the weather did not change in the same way. This gave us a natural experiment.”.

The researchers defined the period of restricted mobility by checking regional lockdown orders and mobile phone location data. Data from NASA and the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration’s Suomi NPP satellite helped the team track fires. Its VIIRS sensor detects heat signatures from fires at a spatial resolution of 375 meters. Each hot spot the satellite detects counts as an active-fire detection, meaning one large fire can appear as multiple spots. However, the satellite records both wildfires and prescribed burns without distinguishing between them. As a result, the intent behind each fire remains unknown.

In the study, detections during the 2020 restriction periods were compared with those from the same weeks in 2013–2019. Weather conditions weren’t exactly the same as in past years, which was accounted for.

Recent findings suggest that the results show that areas under lockdown in the first half of 2020 had about 12.3 percent fewer active-fire detections than the recent-past average. The drop varied by vegetation type. In forests, fires decreased by about 27.7 percent, while grasslands decreased by 8.4 percent. Shrublands, savannas, and croplands didn’t show much difference. The researchers interpret this to mean that humans are a major cause of fires in forests and grasslands.

Controlling for weather factors was important in the study. Without adjustments, the drop was only 5.8 percent, which was not statistically significant. After controlling for weather, however, the estimated decline increased to 12.3 percent. If weather in 2020 were more favorable to fires than in previous years, it might have masked some of the human impact.

The 12.3 percent decrease in fire detections doesn’t mean that humans directly caused this share of fires. Restricting human activity shrank both humans’ impact on starting fires and likely limited their impact on extinguishing them. The 12.3 percent figure is the net effect after these two opposing forces partly cancel out.

Wang noted, “The 12.3 percent is a net effect, not the share of fires caused by humans; opposing changes in ignition and suppression mean it does not capture the full magnitude of human influence.”.

It has been revealed that in regional data, some areas experienced a considerable increase in fire after human mobility was restricted. Most of South America, southern Africa, and northeast Asia saw an increase in fire during the COVID-19 lockdowns. Notable increases include 31.4 percent in Colombia, 25.4 percent in India, and 70.7 percent in Honduras.

There are no direct field data showing why this occurred. The researchers inferred that diminished fire suppression capacity resulted in more fires in these locations, but Wang acknowledged, “It is an inference, not a direct observation.” That inference was based in part on earlier studies that suggested that weaker fire management in Colombia and Madagascar contributed to increased fires.

Recent findings suggest that one line of evidence is how fires reacted to different levels of mobility loss, based on fire counts in 0.5-degree grid cells. In countries with fewer fires, fire declined in almost a straight line as mobility decreased. But countries that experienced more fires highlighted a slow increase that leveled off at about 27 percent on average as mobility fell. The researchers interpreted this as a sign that different mechanisms were at work. The steady decline fits fewer human-driven ignitions, while the gradual rise points to weakened suppression. But Wang mentioned that there could be other reasons, such as changes in local land use.

Mobility restrictions may also have disrupted fire management activities, which could mean that fewer fires were set for management purposes. The researchers examined 12 countries with records of prescribed burning. The area burned by prescribed fires in 2020 decreased by about half compared to the 2013–2019 average. Of course, the locations and sizes of prescribed burns also shift from year to year with fire return intervals and land-management cycles, which complicates this analysis.

When areas subjected to prescribed burning were excluded in those 12 countries, the decline in fires there shrank from 45.3 percent to 27.8 percent.

This research has limits partly because it relied on mobile phone data to track human movement. This kind of data might not capture human activity in rural areas where coverage may be limited. Also, the analysis focused only on the first half of each year, so the impact on regions where fires happen more frequently in the latter half of the year, such as the western US, may not have been fully captured.

Wang explained that this quasi-experimental design provides strong associational evidence but is not a controlled experiment.

According to recent reports, wang emphasized that the study is not an evaluation of fire policies. The analysis does, however, suggest that there’s no single ideal policy response. Where fires decreased, human ignition seems to dominate. In those areas, reducing accidental ignitions through public education and maintaining beneficial prescribed burning can be important. On the other hand, areas where fires increased might need to address reduced monitoring and suppression. Maintaining firefighting and patrol capacity during disruptions can be important there.

Recent findings suggest that wang added, “Overall, a uniform policy is unlikely to work, and strategies should be tailored to local human-fire relationships.” Fire-risk projections might benefit from accounting for human behavior. That way, more accurate fire projections can be made even as weather and society change.

Industry observers note that cell Reports Sustainability, 2026. DOI: 10.1016/j.crsus.2026.100860.

  • For Thorsten Leiduck, SVP and global head of SAP Business AI Platform Ecosystem, that shift begins with treating AI as an enterprise platform rather than a collection of disconnected projects.
  • That foundation also determines which AI applications are worth pursuing.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that for years, enterprises have approached AI as a series of discrete experiments. Now, as AI agents begin to move into the workflows that run the business, that model is starting to look inadequate. Organizations moving from isolated pilots toward AI agents and autonomous workflows are confronting a deeper challenge: rethinking how data, business processes, governance, and people fit together, turning AI from a collection of tools into part of the enterprise operating model.

For Thorsten Leiduck, SVP and global head of SAP Business AI Platform Ecosystem, that shift begins with treating AI as an enterprise platform rather than a collection of disconnected projects. “AI is absolutely dependent on the data foundation,” he says, arguing that companies need a connected, semantically rich layer that reflects their business before they can reliably deploy AI across processes. The stakes also change as AI moves into mission-critical workflows. For some everyday applications, “80% might be good enough,” he says, but in areas such as supply chains or financial close, that level of accuracy is “a very terrible result.”.

That foundation also determines which AI applications are worth pursuing. Satinder Pal Singh, associate VP North America for SAP BAIP and SAP AI Strategy at Infosys, frames AI agents as “digital coworkers” and recommends evaluating potential use cases through three lenses: impact, feasibility, and scalability. Companies should identify where an agent can move meaningful business metrics, determine whether their data and talent can support the use case, and then establish whether successful applications can be replicated. “A pilot that can't scale is just an experiment,” he says.

Industry observers note that scaling also brings governance into sharper focus. Clear policies, access controls, monitoring, and oversight are necessary to ensure agents remain trustworthy and aligned with business requirements. “The absence of governance doesn't speed up AI adoption,” Singh notes. “It creates a risk backlog” that can ultimately force a more disruptive stop and audit.

Recent findings suggest that those considerations will become more important as AI agents take on more responsibilities as digital coworkers. Both executives see a future in which agentic systems coordinate work across applications, while customer-specific knowledge graphs and governed data become critical enterprise assets. For Singh, the longer-term opportunity is a shift from AI as a productivity tool to “AI as a decision-making partner,” helping leaders understand what is happening, anticipate what comes next, and determine how to respond.

#196. Hands-on (and off) with Mercedes-Benz's upcoming MB.Drive Assist Pro system

📅 16 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1336 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Engadget ↗ Open Full Page

Hands-on (and off) with Mercedes-Benz's upcoming MB.Drive Assist Pro system

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1336 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Engadget

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The streets of San Francisco are increasingly littered with oddly shaped cars festooned with bulbous sensors on the outside and no drivers on the inside.
  • When it comes to cars you can actually own, various manufacturers are making meaningful strides toward autonomy, but all in the form of driver assistance.
  • Next year, Mercedes-Benz is taking its own step forward with advanced driver assistance in the form of Hands-Free Highway Assist and MB.Drive Assist Pro.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Benz takes us another step towards self-driving.

The streets of San Francisco are increasingly littered with oddly shaped cars festooned with bulbous sensors on the outside and no drivers on the inside. You can't go two minutes without seeing a car from Waymo or Zoox buzz by, proof that the autonomous revolution has hit the Bay Area. Still, those are all limited-use cars, summoned via smartphone, taking you to your destination, then disappearing from your life as swiftly as they arrived.

When it comes to cars you can actually own, various manufacturers are making meaningful strides toward autonomy, but all in the form of driver assistance. These systems do some of the driving some of the time, but under the active supervision of the driver behind the wheel.

Next year, Mercedes-Benz is taking its own step forward with advanced driver assistance in the form of Hands-Free Highway Assist and MB.Drive Assist Pro. To get an early look, I visited that haven of autonomy for some laps of the Bay in the best that Mercedes has to offer.

Recent findings suggest that my first go was behind the wheel of a GLS, Mercedes-Benz's largest and most luxurious SUV. In the high-performance AMG flavor, it's also reasonably fun to drive, but my job for the morning was to sit back and take my hands off the wheel.

Recent findings suggest that hands-Free Highway Assist is an upcoming feature that will let the driver go hands-free on limited, designated, divided highways. The driver will need to keep paying attention — an eye-tracking camera ensures that — but they can at least sit back and let the car handle the highway drone at speeds up to 85 mph.

Industry observers note that I started in Alameda and made my way up to the 880, a highway still littered with the remains of the morning gridlock. Once there, I just turned on cruise control and waited for the visual indicators on the gauge cluster and heads-up display to change from a green steering wheel with green hands to a green steering wheel with gray hands.

Industry observers note that that subtle cue proved to be the first problem. In the bright California morning sunlight, I struggled to spot the subtle color change on the HUD. On the gauge cluster, the indicator is positioned up in the corner, blocked by the steering wheel.

It has been revealed that but eventually I spotted the signal, took my hands off, and that was that. The SUV and I just kept on going. It was entirely uneventful, which is exactly how these things are supposed to go. That didn't mean it was a completely passive experience, though. Traffic was thick and moving at various speeds across many lanes, and before long the GLS started to pick its way through, moving with intention and even aggression at times to maintain my chosen speed.

As my exit approached, it even changed lanes to the right, ensuring I was in as good a position as possible to get where I needed to go.

The automatic lane changes in the GLS generally worked well, but there was one moment when the SUV failed to detect a rapidly approaching car in the left lane and tried to change directly into its path. I had to grab the wheel to override.

Overriding is easy to do. There's none of the wrestling for control that some other assisted driving systems require. You just take the wheel and do what you like. The only matter I had was that after overriding the system, it often took 10 to 20 seconds before I could take my hands off the wheel again.

That's a far cry from other systems already on the road, like GM's Super Cruise. With that system, you just take the wheel, change lanes, then let go again. BMW's latest Highway Assistant in the new iX5 operates in much the same way, even applying the turn signal for you.

The other concern I had on the highway was frequent disengagements, where the GLS SUV would suddenly demand I put my hands back on the wheel even though there wasn't much going on.

Sources indicate that later in the day, I went out in an S-Class for a lap over the Bay Bridge, and things were even worse. I had at least a half-dozen disengagements during a roughly 45-minute loop. I was told that the system is being quite conservative to start, handing over control early whenever it sees a complicated situation is ahead. Hopefully that improves rapidly, because the constant hand-offs made using the system more annoying than relaxing.

Industry observers note that after my highway time, I got to meander through downtown San Francisco in a GLC SUV equipped with Mercedes-Benz's upcoming MB.Drive Assist Pro feature. This system works exclusively off the highway and requires hands on the wheel. You don't have to exactly be locked in at ten-and-two, but at least some constant contact with the steering is needed.

It has been revealed that do that, and the car basically drives itself, working its way through traffic, navigating intersections and roundabouts, avoiding jaywalkers, and basically doing everything needed to do to survive in a bustling place like SF. Plug a destination into the integrated nav system, and it'll even handle all the turns.

I got a preview of this system last year while driving the CLA, but this year I got behind the wheel. San Francisco isn't perhaps the most manic city on the planet, but it's up there, full of double parkers and a remarkable number of people making U-turns with no warning.

In a recent development, the GLC, seeing the world through 10 cameras plus five radar sensors, handled it all without glitch. It calmly navigated pedestrians (whether they be in or out of the crosswalk), cyclists and all manner of bad drivers. During my journey, which took nearly an hour, I only needed to intervene once, tapping the accelerator at one point when the car got stuck sitting at an intersection.

In terms of driving behavior, the only weirdness was the SUV occasionally stopping at an intersection, creeping forward and then stopping again. Otherwise, it was faultless. Conservative at times, moving cautiously through complicated situations, but never so slowly that I felt like a road hazard.

I was told that Mercedes is considering making this configurable, a sort of aggression slider that would allow you to tailor the behavior of your car to your mood at the moment. Starting on the slow-and-steady side, though, seems like the right approach.

I was hugely impressed by how well the hands-on, point-to-point system worked. It took all the stress out of driving on city streets and worked with an ease and assurance often lacking in a certain other point-to-point driving system with a misleading name.

In a recent development, I was less impressed on the highway. The frequent disengagements and limited operating domain mean that Hands-free Highway Assistant is well behind competing offerings from BMW, Ford and General Motors, despite not being released yet. It is coming soon, though. Look for it in the spring of 2027 on compatible cars, which right now includes the 2027 S-Class, GLS and AMG GT 4-door Coupe. It'll also be available as an option on the 2027 CLA, GLB, C-Class, GLC and GLE as part of the MB.Drive Assist system.

The MB.Drive Assist Pro point-to-point navigation feature is slated for release next year for 2027 CLA Electric, GLE, GLS and S-Class models, with the company promising more to come in 2028. Some California customers will get a chance to enter an early access program later this year. Specific costs for these features have not been finalized.

That might feel a little slow and limited since this tech is already prevalent on many other brands today. However, given the safety-related aspects of these systems and what can go wrong, sometimes being a little late to the party sounds just about right.

#195. Breaking: The iPhone Duo Is Getting a Limited Version of Face ID

📅 16 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 2m • 📖 Standard (457 w)
📖 Baca
Gadgets ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 WIRED ↗ Open Full Page

Breaking: The iPhone Duo Is Getting a Limited Version of Face ID

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (457 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: WIRED

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that apple's most expensive smartphone—the iPhone Duo—lacks one of the company's hallmark features: Face ID.
  • It has been revealed that that's changing now in a software update.
  • Recent findings suggest that the HomeView personalizes the display content for up to six people in a household, with its camera recognizing people who step in front of it (it also uses voice data for recognition when someone asks Siri a command).
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that apple's most expensive smartphone—the iPhone Duo—lacks one of the company's hallmark features: Face ID. The folding phone is already jam-packed with a hinge and multiple display layers, leaving no room for the TrueDepth sensor required for biometric face authentication. The Duo relies on Touch ID instead.

It has been revealed that that's changing now in a software update. On Monday, Apple announced that it's bringing facial recognition to the iPhone Duo as part of the iOS 27.3 update. But since it can't rely on the tried-and-true Face ID system without those crucial components, it's borrowing the feature from the company's recently launched smart display, the HomeView.

Recent findings suggest that the HomeView personalizes the display content for up to six people in a household, with its camera recognizing people who step in front of it (it also uses voice data for recognition when someone asks Siri a command). This “person recognition” technology is protected by the Secure Exclave—different from the Secure Enclave chip that houses Face ID data—a memory-protected space in Apple's A20 Pro processor. As WIRED's Lily Hay Newman writes, it's still not as comprehensive as Face ID, and could be more susceptible to attacks.

At launch, the iPhone Duo relied on Touch ID for biometric authentication.

In a recent development, rumors abound that Apple is racing to add proper Face ID to the second-generation iPhone Duo. Still, tight development cycles might mean the feature may not arrive until the third generation in 2028. That also points to limitations in the Duo's new facial recognition tech.

Sources indicate that you cannot use it to authenticate payments or unlock sensitive content, like your banking app. You'll still need your thumbprint or passcode to approve Apple Wallet purchases. Instead, it's designed to unlock the foldable without tapping a finger on the Touch ID sensor. There is also a time-based limitation. For face recognition to work, it needs a recent Touch ID or passcode authentication within a 45-minute window. This capability is also restricted to the front screen and camera—it doesn't work if the iPhone Duo is unfolded. Also in iOS 27.3, Apple has a new toggle that lets you lock your iPhone Duo when you close it.

Google's newer Pixel folding phones are the only ones on the US market with secure facial authentication, though it's not as effective in the dark as Apple's Face ID. Samsung's facial biometrics on its Galaxy phones aren't strong enough to protect sensitive content and are largely used to unlock the device.

Apple’s willingness to roll out a watered-down version of Face ID is a rare compromise for the firm—and shows just how much of a friction point Touch ID has become for Duo owners.

  • As AI tools become more capable, people are asking chatbots to help design things they can hold, wear, or install in their homes, from custom jewelry and household gadgets to metal parts built around precise measurements.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The next wave of AI projects might just arrive in the mail.

As AI tools become more capable, people are asking chatbots to help design things they can hold, wear, or install in their homes, from custom jewelry and household gadgets to metal parts built around precise measurements.

In a recent development, welcome to "vibe manufacturing." The phrase borrows from "vibe coding," where people describe the software they want and ask AI to help create it. Here, the goal is a physical object, with AI helping develop a design that can be printed at home or sent to a manufacturer.

The appeal is easy to understand. Most people have encountered a product that would be perfect if it were a little smaller, worked differently, or fit that one awkward space. These tools offer a starting point for making their own version. Getting it right, though, still takes more than a good prompt.

Vibe manufacturing loosely describes using conversational AI to help design and build physical things. Someone explains what they want, supplies measurements or reference images, and works with an AI tool to develop it. Depending on the project, that could involve generating a digital model, choosing components, writing software for a device, or figuring out assembly.

The bridge between the conversation and the object is often CAD, short for computer-aided design. CAD software creates precise digital designs for physical objects, and AI tools can help translate everyday requests into the code or geometry behind them.

Sources indicate that entrepreneur Greg Isenberg outlines the process in an Oct. 4 explainer on X. "You describe what you want. An AI turns it into a precise design file. A printer on your desk tests it overnight," he writes.

In a recent development, tools such as the open-source text-to-cad project support that process, providing workflows for creating models with AI agents, producing engineering drawings, and checking designs for fabrication. The resulting files can go to a printer or an outside shop with the equipment to make the parts.

Some of the projects getting attention solve problems that are deeply specific to their creators.

In October, entrepreneur and former X head of product Nikita Bier posted that he'd used AI to design a dog door with a Wi-Fi-controlled lock, customized to his house. Despite having no background in metal fabrication or electrical engineering, he said it was being manufactured for almost the same price as a mass-produced alternative. "We are now entering into an era where any product can be created exactly to a consumer's preferences & needs," he wrote.

Other makers are tackling repairs. In a post on r/ApolloScooters, one Reddit user described using Claude to modify an existing design file after their scooter’s rear fender broke. They ordered a replacement through a 3D-printing service and shared a photo of the result, while noting that they would make the next version shorter.

In a recent development, around the house, customization can be decorative, too. An employee for AI modeling tool Meshy, Jessica Bergau, used the tech giant's AI tool to design cabinet knobs, then asked Claude to generate a script that added screw threads to the models. A blog post documents her plastic prints and the work needed to get an actual screw to fit. Some people are taking their AI-generated ideas to professional craftspeople. In an Instagram post, Dubai-based jeweler AV Creations said a client brought in an AI-generated design that its team recreated as a bespoke gold dog tag pendant, complete with geometric engravings, diamond detailing, and a sculptural carved cube.

Others are experimenting with more complex systems. In a post on X, Ruben Kostandyan shared that he'd asked GPT-5.5 to design an industrial mini HVAC system using ForgeCAD.

And some projects start with wanting a device that doesn't quite exist on store shelves. In a recent Business Insider report, David Plakon described using AI to help build a homemade answering box so his children could leave messages for their grandparents.

The report also featured a sheet-metal robot arm and a custom steel component for securing a camper to a truck.

According to recent reports, greg Isenberg sees a business opportunity in what he calls "the gadgets nobody would build" — products for audiences too small to interest a large manufacturer. He points to accessories for particular bikes or coffee machines, replacement parts for discontinued products, and equipment tailored to an individual business.

"When the design is a file and the factory makes one at a time, the product can fit you instead," he writes.

That vision extends beyond personal projects to businesses serving small markets. Whether those businesses can consistently deliver reliable products at a workable price is a separate question.

Recent findings suggest that turning an AI-assisted design into a physical object often relies on existing manufacturing services: SendCutSend lets customers order custom metal parts, Xometry offers processes including machining and 3D printing, and JLCPCB can manufacture and assemble circuit boards. Each requires files specifying what to build.

But access to production equipment doesn’t guarantee a workable design. "A design can look perfect on screen and be impossible to manufacture," Isenberg writes. He recommends checking a manufacturer’s guidelines, testing a physical prototype, and paying a mechanical engineer to review files before ordering.

Sources indicate that dominic Böttger's account of making a case for an air-quality sensor indicates why. He used Claude Code to develop the enclosure, but early versions had misplaced supports and an opening wide enough for the circuit board to slide out. Getting it right took seven design revisions and three prints, with photographs helping guide corrections. "The feedback loop needs the physical part," he writes.

Industrial manufacturers face the added challenge of making those results repeatable. Technology and manufacturing organization Automation Alley explores that ambition in its March 2026 Integr8 playbook, Vibe Manufacturing: Where AI Meets Additive. Engineers set requirements such as strength, durability, and cost, then use AI to explore designs for additive manufacturing, the category that includes 3D printing.

It has been revealed that "AI explores the options. Additive manufacturing turns those options into physical reality," CEO Tom Kelly writes in the foreword. The report also discusses "Smart Product Recipes," digital instructions intended to standardize production across locations.

In a recent development, as AI tools improve, more people may get the chance to make the products they've been wishing someone would sell. The real test will be how well those ideas hold up once they leave the chat window.
