‘It’s like the 16th-century version of doomscrolling’: the Book of Miracles may fetch £1m at auction

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (910 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Theguardian

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Exclusive: Public institutions get first chance to bid for rare ‘wonderbook’ of apocalyptic visions and extreme weather.
  • In one illustration, five suns blaze down on Leipzig in 1551.
  • Created during the mid-16th century, when earthquakes, storms, floods and other extreme weather events were often interpreted as ominous warnings from God, the Book of Miracles contains 167 paintings of apocalyptic visions, celestial wonders and meteorological phenomena.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Exclusive: Public institutions get first chance to bid for rare ‘wonderbook’ of apocalyptic visions and extreme weather.

In one illustration, five suns blaze down on Leipzig in 1551. In another, blood rain falls on Rome in 1456. In a third scene, dated 1552, monstrous hailstones batter the Dutch city of Dordrecht during a storm so fierce people feared Judgment Day had come.

Created during the mid-16th century, when earthquakes, storms, floods and other extreme weather events were often interpreted as ominous warnings from God, the Book of Miracles contains 167 paintings of apocalyptic visions, celestial wonders and meteorological phenomena.

It is the only known copy. To this day, no one is sure why it was created.

Now, public institutions will have their first chance to bid for the Book of Miracles since scholars learned it existed. It is expected to fetch between £700,000 and £1m when it is auctioned in London on 10 December, as the star lot of the Christie’s valuable books and manuscripts sale.

Members of the public will also have a rare opportunity to see it in person for six days before it goes under the hammer.

For nearly half a millennium, scholars were unaware of its existence. Found in the library of a small baroque castle in southern Germany nearly 20 years ago, the manuscript, which is from 1550s Augsburg, was put up for auction alongside the castle’s furniture, carpets and tankards in 2008 and sold for just over £100,000.

Shortly after the sale, the manuscript entered the private collection of Mickey Cartin, one of Connecticut’s biggest contemporary art collectors.

Eugenio Donadoni, Christie’s international specialist in medieval and Renaissance manuscripts, said the book was an “exceptionally rare” German wonderbook.

Sources indicate that “German wonderbooks functioned as the sensationalist mass media of their day,” he said. “They were used by Lutheran theologians such as Martin Luther and Philip Melanchthon to further their Protestant eschatology, but crucially – with all the depictions of comets, cosmological events, natural disasters, all verified by witnesses, with exact dates and geographic coordinates – they laid early foundations for empirical observation and reporting. They mark a shift from medieval to Enlightenment.”.

He expects the sale will attract collectors of both historic and modern art because some of the scenes, which are painted in watercolour and gouache, are “super surrealist … almost Dalí-esque”.

“If it weren’t for the little captions, which are obviously 16th-century German, some of them look so vividly modern … it’s really jaw-dropping,” Donadoni remarked.

The scenes depicted include a plague of locusts arriving in Poland on a “terrible wind” in 1527 and the North Sea flooding the coast of Frisia – in what is now the Netherlands and Germany – in 1230.

Other pictures are of fiery comets and eclipses, while scholars think an illustration of “wondrous dragons” flying across the sky over Bavaria in 1533 depicts the northern lights.

Underneath each scene, a German picture caption describes what is happening and where and when the event took place.

“All of these events are portentous,” said Donadoni. “The artists of the Book of Miracles, relying on contemporary broadsheets, chronicles and histories, have condensed into pictorial form the concerns of an age that was gripped by an anxiety – and learned curiosity – about the future.”.

The book records how uneasy people felt about climatic anomalies at a time of doctrinal disunity, when there was growing interest in documenting and cataloguing visible, tangible scientific phenomena, he said.

“It’s really fascinating … it is a window into how Europeans were dealing with the impending end of the world, political uncertainty and extreme – and strange – weather events.”.

Industry observers note that the five suns over Leipzig, for example, is thought to depict the optical illusion of a parhelion, more commonly known as a sun dog. “You see in the sky various different rings of light and it looks like suns,” Donadoni remarked.

It has been revealed that “Blood rain” occurs when high concentrations of red-coloured dust particles, usually from the Sahara, mix with water droplets in rain clouds. “Many of these things have actual rational scientific explanations to them,” Donadoni said.

He noted he imagined that leafing through the pages of the book in the 1550s was similar to bingeing on bad news on social media today: “I think it could be a little like the 16th-century version of doomscrolling.”.

Industry observers note that in this way, the book straddles a momentous turning point in history. “We’re right at that period where the superstition of the middle ages turns into the age of scientific discovery,” Donadoni noted.

Industry observers note that till-Holger Borchert, the director of the Suermondt Ludwig Museum in Aachen, has studied the manuscript and mentioned the first time he saw it, his reaction was: “Wow”. “It’s one of a kind,” he said. “It grabs you by your heart or your soul or your belly.”.

According to recent reports, he noted he thought £1m was a “very conservative estimate” of its value. “It [the final price] could possibly be much more,” he said.

A facsimile of the manuscript was published in 2013 that got people “really excited” about it, Borchert added, and since then the Book of Miracles has become “a kind of icon for people who are interested in apocalyptic things”. It would be wrong to value it merely as an historical document: “It’s more than that. It speaks to us, to our generation.”.

How to stream Twitch on your TV

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that twitch is one of the largest streaming platforms for gamers and content creators alike.
  • But before you go through the hassle of fishing out a Chromecast or a gaming console, make sure your TV doesn't already have Twitch as an available app.
  • Recent findings suggest that twitch offers support for cross-device streaming.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Casting Twitch to your TV has never been easier.

It has been revealed that twitch is one of the largest streaming platforms for gamers and content creators alike. Millions watch their favorite creators across PCs, laptops and mobile devices. It's the perfect platform for streaming on a larger screen, yet many TVs don't have Twitch built in. Thankfully, several methods let you stream Twitch to your television, from video casting to third-party streaming devices.

But before you go through the hassle of fishing out a Chromecast or a gaming console, make sure your TV doesn't already have Twitch as an available app. Most modern smart TVs have an app library where you can download apps like Twitch. If you haven't already, check your TV's app store to see whether you can install Twitch. If your TV doesn't have an app store, fret not. Casting your device to your television is a great alternative that nearly every TV supports, though you might need a streaming device to begin casting.

Recent findings suggest that twitch offers support for cross-device streaming. You'll need a TV that supports streaming or a device that enables it, such as Google's TV Streamer. Casting to your television varies slightly depending on how you're using Twitch. If you're using the Twitch app on your mobile device, casting Twitch to your television is as easy as tapping the cast button on your favorite stream. If you don't see the option, make sure your phone and television are on the same Wi-Fi network and that both devices have the latest firmware. It's also worth checking your Twitch settings to ensure that you don't have any unwanted security settings, such as AI training, enabled.

Streaming Twitch from your computer is a little different but still fairly easy. Use Google Chrome as your web browser, since it lets you stream your screen to another device. Once you've loaded Twitch, click on the three dots on the top-right of your browser to bring up an options menu. Select the "Cast, Save and Share" ribbon and click on "Cast." Select your television to begin casting. As with the mobile device method, make sure your computer and television are set up on the same Wi-Fi network or the option won't appear. If casting the specific window doesn't work, you can also try casting your entire screen.

Sources indicate that if casting content doesn't work, you can always use a streaming device. Gaming consoles are the best option here since most have a Twitch app you can install. Boot up the Twitch app from your preferred console and watch your favorite streams. Previous-generation and modern-gen PlayStation and Xbox consoles include a Twitch app; the Switch and Switch 2 do not.

It has been revealed that consoles aren't the only devices that can stream. You can also use an Amazon Fire Stick, a Roku device or Apple TV 4K to watch Twitch on your TV. The Fire Stick has an official Twitch app you can install; the Roku doesn't, but it does support casting and screen mirroring. If all else fails, you can also connect your laptop or desktop directly to your TV via HDMI or DisplayPort. Play Twitch on the connected device, then switch your TV's input to that device to enjoy the stream. Remember, you'll need to switch streams on the connected device, not on your TV.

Mercedes' clever new driving assist handles complex traffic like a champ

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (979 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Ars Technica

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • SAN FRANCISCO—When Ars first drove the new Mercedes-Benz CLA last year, the automaker also gave us a sneak preview of its next driver assist.
  • Industry observers note that while most automakers want a reputation for safety, Mercedes has long used passive and active technology to do so in its products.
  • “Level 2” assisted driving, where the car also controls the steering as well as the acceleration and braking, got famous with Tesla Autopilot.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

SAN FRANCISCO—When Ars first drove the new Mercedes-Benz CLA last year, the automaker also gave us a sneak preview of its next driver assist. Called Drive Assist Pro, it’s for collaborative partially assisted driving, and from the passenger seat at the time, the demo was impressive. Now the automaker is getting ready to start rolling out Drive Assist Pro to customers with cars running the new MB.OS operating system here in the US and in Germany, and it let us have some time behind the wheel.

Industry observers note that while most automakers want a reputation for safety, Mercedes has long used passive and active technology to do so in its products. It was one of the first OEMs to introduce airbags, and a decade later started adding active safety systems like anti-lock brakes, electronic stability control, and adaptive cruise control. And so, by giving the car’s electronics the ability to control the brakes and throttle, we arrive at the first level of assisted driving—called “level 1” in automotive engineer-speak.

“Level 2” assisted driving, where the car also controls the steering as well as the acceleration and braking, got famous with Tesla Autopilot. But the first lane-keeping assists predate it by almost a decade in passenger cars, when Toyota introduced a system in 2004. The human driver behind the wheel is still in charge, responsible for situational awareness (and anything that arises from a lack thereof), with the idea that long drives become less tiring and a little more effortless when the car does the boring job of keeping a constant speed or a constant distance to the car ahead and between the white lines.

The next step, numerically at least, should be level 3, where we move from assisted driving to partially automated driving; here the car takes over the task of driving fully under some circumstances, like heavy traffic. But that’s getting ahead of ourselves—the main developments over the past few years have been the inelegantly named “L2+” systems that combine more advanced driver monitoring with a higher degree of assistance, usually on geofenced highways.

General Motors’ Super Cruise was the first of these, allowing hands-free operation as long as the car can tell the driver has their eyes on the road. Now many automakers offer something similar: Ford has BlueCruise, BMW has Highway Assistant, and Mercedes is about to add a hands-free highway assist next spring to its MB. Drive Assist system, which will be standard on the 2027 S-Class and AMG GT 4-Door Coupe and an option on the 2027 CLA, GLB, C-Class, GLC, and GLE.

I tested that system while in San Francisco in a 2027 S-Class, and it’s competent within its operational design domain. The user interface is a little more subtle than Super Cruise’s massive green LED in the steering wheel; instead, the icon on the dash changes, with the hands on the steering wheel going from green to gray when it’s safe to remove them. Like other systems, MB. Drive Assist has been programmed to make automatic lane changes if the car decides that’s quicker—these can be canceled with the turn signal or simply by resisting the car steering into the next lane.

Sources indicate that MB. Drive Assist Pro takes that idea and brings it to lower speeds and much more complex traffic situations—“level 2++” (we really need to stop letting engineers name things). Instead of hands on the green steering wheel icon, there’s a large green arrowhead, showing you’re in point-to-point mode—compared to the various configurations of the highway assist, I found this much less likely to engender mode confusion. (Did the green hands mean I could take my hands on or off the wheel? On, but see what I mean?).

Recent findings suggest that the driving behavior was about exactly as cautious as I would want on surface streets. The electric GLC was as smooth accelerating and braking as the entirely autonomous Waymo robotaxi I rode in the day before, and the car’s electronic brain was able to safely pass double-parked cars—waiting patiently for an oncoming bus first—and stopped for stop signs, red lights, and pedestrians on crosswalks (while making a left turn at the time). The system is collaborative—steering or accelerating won’t end the automation, but unlike BMW’s fresh iX5, any use of the brake will turn it off.

Industry observers note that some customers in Germany and California will be part of an early access program for Drive Assist Pro from next month, with a wider rollout in the first half of 2027 for model year 2026 CLAs, as well as the model year 2027 CLA, GLC Electric, GLE, GLS, and S-Class, and more coming in model year 2028. (The system is already live in China.).

It has been revealed that the unifying factor is the MB.OS, the automaker’s latest operating system. Like other automakers, Mercedes has embraced the software-defined vehicle paradigm, replacing dozens or even hundreds of discrete ECUs with a handful of powerful domain controller computers that oversee vehicle dynamics, occupant comfort, infotainment, and automation.

According to recent reports, drive Assist Pro combines 10 cameras, five radars, and 12 ultrasonic sensors, all stitched together by a domain controller that uses Nvidia’s Orin processors. I’m told that in China, cars are now advertised with processor and RAM specs rather than boring information like range or performance: In that spirit, Mercedes says it can deliver 254 tera operations per second, uses a 2.5 Gbit Ethernet network, and has more than 70GB of RAM.

The driving decisions are made by Nvidia’s Alpamayo end-to-end tokenized stack that picks your driving trajectory, with a rules-based system running alongside as a safety check. That’s reassuring, as is the knowledge that Nvidia’s stack has been certified by Germany’s TÜV, which takes a less lackadaisical approach to safety than the current incarnation of the US Department of Transportation.

Suspected Chinese spy balloon was able to transmit information back to Beijing

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The Chinese spy balloon that transited the US earlier this year was able to capture imagery and collect some signals intelligence from US military sites, a source familiar with the matter tells CNN.
  • The balloon was able to transmit information back to Beijing in real time, the source stated, and the US government still does not know for sure whether the Chinese government could wipe the balloon’s data as it received it.
  • Still, the intelligence community has not been overly concerned about the information the balloon was able to gather, the person said, because it is not much more sophisticated than what Chinese satellites are able to glean as they orbit over similar locations.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The Chinese spy balloon that transited the US earlier this year was able to capture imagery and collect some signals intelligence from US military sites, a source familiar with the matter tells CNN.

The balloon was able to transmit information back to Beijing in real time, the source stated, and the US government still does not know for sure whether the Chinese government could wipe the balloon’s data as it received it. That raises questions about whether there is intelligence the balloon was able to gather that the US still doesn’t know about.

Still, the intelligence community has not been overly concerned about the information the balloon was able to gather, the person said, because it is not much more sophisticated than what Chinese satellites are able to glean as they orbit over similar locations.

A US intelligence official told CNN on Monday that “although analysis of the wreckage of the High Altitude Balloon remains ongoing, thus far, its flight over the United States does not appear to have provided critical latest insights to the People’s Republic of China.”.

The US also knew what the balloon’s path would be and was able to protect sensitive sites and censor some signals before the balloon was able to pick them up, officials have said.

As CNN has reported, the US intelligence community last year developed a method of tracking what it indicates is a fleet of these Chinese balloons operating across the globe, controlled by the Chinese military.

The FBI is still examining the balloon, but so far officials have been able to glean additional information about how the device worked, including the algorithms used for the balloon’s software and how it is powered and designed.

Industry observers note that CNN has reached out to the National Security Council at the White House and the Pentagon for comment. NBC was first to report on the new intelligence.

It has been revealed that the balloon first crossed into US airspace over Alaska in late January before passing through Canada and down into Montana, where it hovered for a few days, leading the US to believe it was trying to surveil sensitive military sites, like Malmstrom Air Force Base in Montana. It was eventually shot down by the US off the East Coast on February 4, and the incident further escalated tensions between Washington and Beijing, including the postponement of a diplomatic visit by US Secretary of State Antony Blinken to China.

A senior State Department official said in February that, as the balloon floated across the US, it “was capable of conducting signals intelligence collection operations.”.

Sources indicate that gen. Glen VanHerck, the commander of US Northern Command and NORAD, stated at the time that the US “did not assess” that the balloon “presented a significant collection hazard beyond what already exists in actionable technical means from the Chinese.”.

The surveillance program, which includes a number of similar balloons, is in part run out of the small Chinese province of Hainan, officials told CNN. The US does not know the precise size of the fleet of Chinese surveillance balloons, but sources tell CNN that the program has conducted at least two dozen missions over at least five continents in recent years.

Roughly half a dozen of those flights have been within US airspace, although not necessarily over US territory, according to one official familiar with the intelligence.

China has maintained that the balloon was actually just a weather balloon thrown off course, and the US has been assessing the possibility that it was not deliberately maneuvered into the continental US by the Chinese government, CNN has reported.

Still, China did maintain some ability to maneuver the balloon, officials believe. And once the balloon was over Montana, China appeared to take advantage of its position to loiter over sensitive sites and try to collect intelligence.

This story has been updated with additional reporting.

CNN’s Alex Marquardt contributed to this report.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

French actor apologises to two women he was convicted of assaulting on a film set in 2021.

The French actor Gérard Depardieu has dropped his appeal against a conviction for sexually assaulting two women on a film set, and has for the first time apologised to the victims.

Recent findings suggest that “I was found guilty. I hear it and I accept this conviction,” Depardieu, 77, said in a written statement. “I address my deep and sincere apologies to those who suffered.”.

The actor, who has made more than 200 films and TV series, wrote: “For a long time on film sets, I hid behind provocation and ribald humour.”.

He said he accepted that remarks and “some of my gestures” were not “without consequences”, particularly because he held a powerful position in the entertainment industry.

Depardieu said he had never intended to hurt the women he encountered but had “come to understand that intention changes nothing about the harm caused”.

He mentioned times had changed and that he belonged “to a world that no longer exists”.

At a trial last year, Depardieu was found guilty of sexually assaulting a 55-year-old set dresser and a 35-year-old assistant director during the shooting of the feature film Les Volets Verts (The Green Shutters) in Paris in September 2021.

His suspended sentence will now stand and his name must be added to France’s sex offender register.

The set dresser, named in the media as Amélie, said outside the Paris appeal court on Monday: “I waited for years for this apology.” She said she would have preferred if Depardieu had attended court to deliver it in person.

The assistant director, named in the media as Sarah, mentioned: “The monster of cinema has fallen.”.

According to recent reports, depardieu’s conviction last year was a turning point for the #MeToo movement in France. He became the biggest figure in the French film industry to be convicted of sexual assault after years of criticism of the country’s reluctance to take women’s claims of abuse seriously.

Depardieu had previously denied all allegations of sexual assault. He told last year’s trial that the media had used allegations against him to damage his reputation.

He attacked the #MeToo movement as well as women who had staged protests outside venues during his concert tour at the time of the allegations. “This movement is going to become a terror,” he said.

The trial also set an key legal precedent when the judge ruled that Depardieu’s defence lawyer, Jérémie Assous, had been “excessively harsh” to the two women in court, saying they were not real victims and were liars.

Assous had stated the women were working for the cause of “rabid feminism” and called their lawyers hysterical, “abject and stupid” and described them as having an “unbearable voice”.

The judge awarded the complainants compensation for being further victimised by Depardieu’s defence during the trial, ordering Depardieu to pay each woman €1,000 (£835).

The court had heard there was a “system of impunity” around Depardieu, with film industry insiders staying silent to keep cashing in on his name.

Sources indicate that depardieu has appealed against a separate decision requiring him to face trial on charges of raping and sexually assaulting the actor Charlotte Arnould at his Paris home in 2018. Appeal judges will rule this month on whether to uphold his appeal or allow the trial to go ahead next year.

In an open letter to Le Figaro in October 2023, Depardieu denied all allegations and remarked any encounter with Arnould had been consensual. “Never, ever, have I abused a woman,” he wrote.

In December 2023, when Depardieu was under formal investigation for rape and sexual assault in the Arnould case and also facing scrutiny over sexist comments revealed in a TV documentary, the French president defended him, saying “he makes France proud”.

Asked at the time about stripping Depardieu of a state award, Emmanuel Macron stated: “You will never see me participate in a manhunt … I hate that type of thing.”.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

For 33 years, Nvidia had only one CEO. Now, just days after the chipmaker announced Jensen Huang's resignation, some of the country's biggest names are already want him back — from OpenAI CEO Sam Altman to President Donald Trump.

The decision ultimately belongs to Nvidia's board, which has appointed longtime finance chief Colette Kress as interim CEO.

Industry observers note that the calls for a comeback follow a week of mounting scrutiny over Huang's intimate extracurriculars. On Nov. 8, Huang had told employees he’d been unfaithful to his wife after reports of a relationship with Alice Huang, a former executive at Megaspeed, a Singapore-based cloud computing firm that buys Nvidia chips. U.S. officials suspect she had ties to Chinese intelligence, an allegation Beijing has denied. The same day Huang emailed employees, Nvidia's board declared an independent investigation into reports that he had been targeted by a foreign intelligence effort. Reuters also reported that Huang had relationships with two Nvidia employees, including one who reported directly to him. Inhales.

In a recent development, it's a lot. But that doesn't mean everyone thinks its enough to get rid of the co-founder permanently. On Nov. 15, Huang was already talking to people close to him about a possible return, according to the Financial Times. One ally told the paper they were getting tech executives together to lobby for his reinstatement and would seek support from the White House.

Sources indicate that on Monday, Trump gave that effort some encouragement. "I would certainly not mind seeing that," he told reporters before leaving Washington for the Philippines and China. He mentioned he thought Huang had "learned a big lesson" and questioned whether Alice Huang had worked for Chinese intelligence.

A day earlier, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent told Larry Kudlow on Fox News that Nvidia should hire its next CEO from outside the organization, saying it needed a "dramatic shake-up.".

Huang's supporters are also making their case online. "Thirty-three years deserve an answer," reads the Stand With Jensen petition, which demands that Nvidia's board reinstate its co-founder while the independent investigation is underway. "We are concerned that Jensen was removed without meaningful due process," it adds. If directors think Huang should stay out of the job, the letter asks them to explain what evidence led them to that decision and why it serves Nvidia's interests. It also calls on the board to disclose what the investigation will cover, when it expects to finish, and how Huang will get a chance to respond. It has been revealed that by Monday afternoon, the campaign's website highlighted more than 185,000 signatures, including more than 9,300 from people who identified themselves as current Nvidia employees. The site also lists Tesla and SpaceX CEO Elon Musk, Epic Games CEO Tim Sweeney, and Replit CEO Amjad Masad among the signers.

According to recent reports, the push to bring Huang back is familiar territory for OpenAI CEO Sam Altman. OpenAI's board fired him in Nov. 2023, and he returned days later after employees and investors rallied behind him. At Semafor's Silicon Valley & the World event on Monday, Altman mentioned he sympathized with Huang and had long seen him as a hero. When asked whether Huang should get his job back, Altman said, "I don’t think I know enough to answer that question." He added: "it's hard to imagine the AI revolution without Jensen Huang.".

Altman also sounded confident in Nvidia's ability to back the data centers that AI companies depend on. "Nvidia is, like, a behemoth of a organization," he said. "I think people still trust their guarantees very much.".

Sources indicate that openAI has a stake in that confidence. At an Ohio data center campus where an OpenAI affiliate is leasing capacity, Nvidia has agreed to guarantee up to $105 billion in certain lease and power payments if the tenant defaults under conditions spelled out in the deal. The campus is set to run on Nvidia hardware, with limited exceptions.

Industry observers note that for now, Kress is running Nvidia on an interim basis while keeping the CFO job she's held since 2013. The board, led by longtime director Harvey C. Jones, says it will consider internal and external candidates. It has already approached Arm CEO Rene Haas, the Financial Times reported.

The next chance to hear from Nvidia's fresh leadership comes Tuesday at 5 p.m. ET, when the company holds its first earnings call since Huang's departure.

Industry observers note that there was a reason, 11 years ago in Paris, that world leaders set themselves a target to keep the global rise in temperatures below 1.5 degrees Celsius compared with preindustrial levels. Beyond that, climate scientists say, warming will dangerously change our way of life.

We got a taste of it this year, as temperatures rose above the threshold for several months. Heat waves. Wildfires. Flash floods. And with a super El Niño year unfolding, next year might be worse. As one climate expert put it to me: This El Niño will effectively offer a time machine to the 2030s, showing what will happen if we don’t radically cut carbon emissions.

My colleague David Gelles, host of the Climate Forward newsletter, has been following the much diminished U.N. climate talks in Turkey. Today he writes about the death of 1.5 degrees and what that means for the planet.

It was the climate movement’s unifying slogan for the past decade: “Keep 1.5 Alive.”.

The tagline referred to the central ambition of the 2015 Paris climate agreement, in which almost every country pledged to try to limit global warming to 1.5 degrees Celsius.

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • These apps are being shut down after just 14 months.
  • Microsoft is sunsetting three Office taskbar apps just 14 months after their initial release.
  • Industry observers note that these three taskbar tools were primarily for those using Windows 11 on employer-managed devices.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

These apps are being shut down after just 14 months.

Microsoft is sunsetting three Office taskbar apps just 14 months after their initial release. The People, Files and Calendar Companion apps, which Microsoft designed to increase user productivity and focus, will no longer work as of December 16.

Industry observers note that these three taskbar tools were primarily for those using Windows 11 on employer-managed devices. These companion apps weren't added to all versions of Windows, so if you have Windows 11 Home, for example, you likely never had these apps in the first place. Microsoft automatically added the companion apps for those with commercial Microsoft 365 and Office 365 licenses. So if you see these apps on your computer, it's time to remove them and use existing alternatives instead.

Industry observers note that in its support post announcing the companion app retirement, Microsoft didn't share why it made this decision. But it's possible the taskbar apps simply didn't get enough active consumers for Microsoft to continue to maintain them. After all, these apps are redundant to existing Windows tools, so some users may have not found them necessary. Others might have seen the apps as another example of Windows bloatware and removed them from company devices.

Industry observers note that the People companion app was for finding people at your firm or in your contacts promptly. It let you start Microsoft Teams calls, see shared files, see someone's spot in the company's org chart, view online or offline status, share the person's contact information, see profiles and skills, check whether someone is in a meeting or send someone an email in just a few clicks. You could also "favorite" people, like your boss or immediate team members, so they're pinned to the top. And of course, Microsoft added a Copilot connection too so you could ask the AI about what projects a specific person at your company is working on.

In a recent development, the Files companion app let you quickly access and create shared links to Microsoft Office files with coworkers. It also let you search for files using keywords and sort by file type, which feels a bit redundant considering the main Windows Search bar has always let people do this.

And lastly, the Calendar companion app was another way to see your Microsoft 365 calendar and join meetings. It let you see and edit calendar events, copy meeting links or search your calendar for a specific event.

Sources indicate that was all of this intended to be Microsoft's answer to Slack beyond Teams? It's unclear. These 365 companion apps offer some similar features, but Slack offers more device and platform compatibility than three separate pop-up apps that only work on select Windows devices.

If you're looking to stay within the Microsoft ecosystem, the Outlook app for Windows has tabs for Calendar, Contacts and email to replace the Calendar companion app. Teams offers some of these features from People and Calendar as well including instant messaging, calendar viewing and video calls. And instead of using the Files tool, just use the Windows Start Menu search bar or Microsoft OneDrive, which is available as a desktop app or in the web browser.

Of course, there are also other options for replacing these tools beyond Microsoft's walled garden. Slack and Google's Workspace suite are among the most popular for businesses looking to enable remote work productivity across devices, instant messaging, file-sharing, video and audio calls and more.

According to recent reports, if your Windows computer is being managed by your employer, your IT admin will likely remove the retired apps from your device on your behalf. Otherwise, go to Windows Settings > Apps > Installed Apps, then search "Microsoft 365 companions," click on the three dots and then select "Uninstall" to remove them.

Because these companion apps rely on data from SharePoint Online and Exchange Online, part of the 365 cloud, you don't have to worry about losing anything when they're uninstalled. Microsoft's support page confirms that this data is kept in your Microsoft 365 services files, not within the companion app files.

In a recent development, removing apps you don't use, including retired ones, is a best practice for optimizing device security, storage and performance. If you want to take things one step further, there are other things you can do to improve your Windows 11 experience, too.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Whole areas of Derna have been entirely rebuilt.

Recent findings suggest that "It was joy when I moved in. I could finally relax," states Abdulwahab Damdoum, surveying his luxurious newly introduced apartment overlooking the Mediterranean Sea, in the eastern Libyan city of Derna.

Just three years ago he was clinging in terror to the roof of a house as the world's deadliest flood this century surged around him.

Now the 27-year-old port worker, his wife and two young daughters have been given a upcoming, free, 300-sq-m home in a showcase development commissioned by a son of Khalifa Haftar, the warlord who controls eastern Libya.

It is part of a rapid $2bn (Â£1.5bn) rebuilding of Derna that the powerful Haftar family hope will serve as a model for development throughout Libya, increasing their influence across a country presently split between east and west, with rival governments in charge.

According to recent reports, the money comes from the state coffers of the oil-rich country, allocated by its parliament. But there are no published records of how it has been spent, raising questions about accountability and possible corruption.

Damdoum, like many flood survivors, simply thanks the head of the Development and Reconstruction Fund, Belkacem Haftar, for what has been achieved since the early hours of 11 September 2023, when lashing rain from Storm Daniel burst two dams above Derna, sending a wall of water 7m (23 ft) high cascading down onto the sleeping city.

It has been revealed that the exact death toll will probably never be known. Some estimates have been as high as 6,000, though 4,000 now seems a more likely figure. Many bodies are still unidentified.

Abdulwahab Damdoum lost his father, brother and sister in the flood.

In a city of about 100,000 people, that means almost everybody lost someone they loved. The 14 relatives and neighbours on the roof with Damdoum â including his father, brother and sister - all drowned.

Sources indicate that he survived, but his home was destroyed, and he had to find temporary accommodation. "It was rent, rent, rent," he says. "Now, no-one can take this [fresh flat] from me. I thank Engineer Belkacem. God sent this person who picked the city up from disaster.".

Portraits of Belkacem, widely known simply as "the Engineer", his younger brother Saddam, a military chief also involved in reconstruction, and their father Khalifa are on hoardings all over Derna and the region.

"Since 2011, Libya has not built big projects like this," indicates Hussein el-Mansory, project manager of the "2,000 Apartments" complex where Damdoum now lives. "I feel very happy and proud and I'll tell my children: 'I made this.'".

The complex includes a upcoming mosque, hospital, shopping mall and schools. New roads, bridges have also been built in Derna. But while many survivors have been rehoused, some are still waiting.

In a recent development, among them is Izz al-Nasr Ibzeou, a marine science lecturer at the university. His wife Salima, her mother Mouna, and all the couple's seven children, aged between one and 11, drowned.

His family home was ruined, but the authorities have not yet fully restored it because Ibzeou also has an undamaged apartment in another part of town.

He returns every day to his old house, now an empty shell, to see his children's possessions, which he has kept in dust-covered piles.

"This is my son Moez's bike. He played with it every day. And this is my daughter Fawzia's dress. She wore it whenever she went to a wedding," Ibzeou says. "Even if I decide not to come to remember them, my feet will bring me here of their own accord.".

To this day, he has not found their bodies. In Derna's vast latest flood cemetery, most graves are marked only by numbers, not names, because the process of matching survivors' DNA with corpses is still not completed.

Industry observers note that "I go to the cemetery and try to guess where my family are," he claims. "This has burned my heart too much. Thank God, I'm patient, but I'm still waiting just to read the Qur'an [at their graves] and say hello to them.".

Izz al-Nasr Ibzeou visits his former home every day, to remember his children.

Belkacem Haftar has now extended the work of his reconstruction fund to Libya's second city, Benghazi, and other parts of Libya his father controls.

Libya's parliament, based in the east, last year allocated him a further sum of nearly $11bn, to be spent over three years, in addition to the $2bn it had already given him specifically for Derna.

According to recent reports, building in Benghazi has included new skyscrapers, hospitals, housing developments and a refurbished football stadium that last year hosted a friendly between Inter Milan and AtlÃ©tico Madrid. Officials have talked in the past about turning the city into a version of "Dubai on the Mediterranean.".

Tim Whewell reports from eastern Libya, where a vast reconstruction programme led by the Haftar family is transforming cities and reshaping the country's political future.

Belkacem tells the BBC he has accomplished more than any previous Libyan administration.

In a recent development, "Libya went through the Gaddafi era, 40 years of neglect and poverty," he stated. "The interim governments [post-Gaddafi, based in Tripoli] wasted a lot of money without providing anything the people could touch. I have never made promises to the people. But I have provided them with what they need.".

International human rights organisations have repeatedly accused the authorities in eastern Libya and Libyan Arab Armed Forces headed by Khalifa Haftar of serious abuses, including secret executions, arbitrary detentions and forced disappearances.

The Haftars and the Benghazi-based government deny the allegations. Belkacem told the BBC there was complete freedom of speech in eastern Libya.

Posters of Khalifa Haftar and his sons are a common sight in Derna.

Critics also say the Haftars have a top-down approach to development, with little public participation in planning decisions, and no transparency.

"There is absolutely zero accountability. We've never seen any financial statements of the Reconstruction Fund, for even the legal on-the-table disbursements of funds," says Claudia Gazzini from the International Crisis Group (ICG) think-tank.

Industry observers note that belkacem says the fund is independently audited and that all contracts are drawn up to high international standards. Dismissing concerns about transparency, he says: "What we've done in Derna was almost impossible. What we care about is the reality, what we do on the ground.".

In a recent development, he agreed to show the BBC the audits. But he has not provided them, despite repeated requests.

Jalel Harchaoui, a Libya expert affiliated to the Royal United Services Institute think-tank in London, who has talked to some of the foreign partners awarded construction contracts. He says they are usually obliged to work alongside a private Libyan company linked indirectly to the Haftar family or other powerful political figures.

He claims: "What those foreign companies say off the record, is that they do the overwhelming majority of the work and the Libyan partner is often almost an empty shell, in a context where the money is split very often on a 50-50 basis, which indicates that a lot of those facilities and bridges and towers are overcharged, twice as expensive.

According to recent reports, "It's a form of overpricing within a context that is utterly opaque, and this is not some fairy coming from the sky that funds these reconstruction efforts. Everything is funded using the public wealth of Libya.".

Belkacem Haftar denies the suggestion of corruption in reconstruction projects.

He has noted the reconstruction funding was processed through the Central Bank of Libya, which operates on behalf of both the UN-recognised government in the capital Tripoli, in the west of the country, and the government in the eastern city of Benghazi.

"The Haftar authorities used Derna as a showcase for what they were pitching to the rest of Libya," says Gazzini from the ICG.

Belkacem Haftar, the son of strongman Khalifa Haftar, denies the suggestion of corruption in reconstruction projects.

International efforts to reunite the country have included a proposal by Donald Trump's envoy, Massad Boulos, for a power-sharing deal with Saddam Haftar as Libya's president.

It has been revealed that in Derna, there is no proposal to rebuild the broken dams, so another disaster on the same scale is unlikely. But there is still a possibility of future flooding.

Gazzini says the authorities failed to take up offers of advice from international experts on ways to reduce the risk, for example by creating flood plains along the river which flows through the town.

"I would have expected a holistic project about how you manage the water flow," Gazzini says.

It has been revealed that "But that did not happen. The Libyan side responded more to people's needs, was more interested in having a quick solution to the destruction of the city.".

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Traffic temporarily restricted on key connection after bridge targeted during overnight drone barrage by Ukraine.

Ukraine has hit the Kerch bridge connecting occupied Crimea with Russia, in a symbolic blow that temporarily paralysed road traffic and left thousands of drivers stranded.

A Ukrainian kamikaze drone crashed into one of the bridge’s arches at 5.38am local time, local channels reported. Earlier drones could be heard buzzing above the structure, as Russian air defence units opened fire.

Industry observers note that the extent of the damage was unclear. One report stated the arch was listing at a 15-degree angle and “looked tired”.

The Kremlin-appointed governor of Crimea, Sergey Aksyonov, confirmed the “enemy” had rolled out an attack. “As a result, traffic will be restricted, likely until the afternoon,” he wrote on Telegram.

Sources indicate that russian officials stated the crossing would remain closed while experts assessed its condition. About 2,000 vehicles were reportedly stuck in traffic jams on both sides.

It has been revealed that in a call with reporters, the Kremlin spokesperson, Dmitry Peskov, downplayed the incident. He said: “Minor damage is being assessed. ⁠Traffic across the bridge continues.”.

Ukraine says the bridge is a legitimate target for its armed forces, and has made at least two previous attempts to blow it up.

Industry observers note that in 2022 a truck laden with explosives damaged part of the road section. A second strike using a “sea baby” drone took place the following year. Russia has subsequently strengthened air defences and installed metal barges and boom barriers.

Overnight Ukraine released 1,336 drones, in what the Kremlin says was one of the biggest attacks so far this year. About 600 were intercepted on their approach to Moscow, claimed the capital’s mayor, Sergei Sobyanin.

The barrage took place days before a summit in Shenzhen between China’s president, Xi Jinping, Donald Trump and Putin. US officials say the talks will not focus on the war in Ukraine, where Russia’s military offensive has largely stalled.

Ukraine claims its retaliatory strikes are justified retribution for Russia’s own missile and drone barrages of its cities and energy grid – attacks that have killed hundreds of civilians and regularly knock out power and heating for millions. In recent weeks Russia has repeatedly hit two critical bridges in Kyiv over the Dnipro river.

Recent findings suggest that diplomatic efforts on ending the almost five-year war have so far gone nowhere. After a fresh round of talks in Abu Dhabi last week, Putin reiterated his hardline territorial demands and mentioned any deployment of foreign troops would be seen in Moscow as a “continuation of war”.

The Ukrainian president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, noted on Friday the Trump administration had proposed that Kyiv gives Russia the eastern Donbas region – including towns and villages Russia does not control – in exchange for Nato membership or Nato-like guarantees.

Zelenskyy ruled out handing over territory. The details of possible US security guarantees were vague and did not feature American troops on the ground, he stated, citing conversations with Trump’s son-in-law Jared Kushner and the real-estate developer Steve Witkoff. The emissaries last week saw Putin in Moscow.

Jensen Huang is considering a comeback as Nvidia’s chief executive, as allies in Silicon Valley pressure the company’s board to reinstate him days after the tech executive resigned over reports he had affairs with a suspected Chinese spy and a subordinate.

Huang has discussed with confidants the possibility of returning, according to multiple people familiar with the matter—even as an independent probe by Nvidia’s board investigates the conduct that led to a spectacular leadership crisis at the $4 trillion chip tech giant this week.

One Huang ally told the FT they were putting together a “war room” of Silicon Valley executives to lobby for the former Nvidia chief’s return and would try to garner support from the White House.

“Everyone that matters in tech outside the frontier labs loves Jensen,” they noted. The efforts had Huang’s support, they added.

In a recent development, A public campaign to reinstate Huang has gathered steam over the weekend. Tesla and SpaceX chief Elon Musk and Epic Games chief executive Tim Sweeney were among executives backing a public letter demanding that its board “Bring Jensen Back.”.

Huang continues to command fierce loyalty from some employees, several of whom have gone public in calling for his return in the days since he resigned and have signed the open letter.

The effort to reinstate Huang is likely to face pushback from key policymakers in Washington, with Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent on Sunday calling for a “dramatic shake-up” in leadership at the company after Huang’s departure.

Huang, who lacked the controlling shareholding of other founder-CEOs and was therefore unable to overule any board decision, also faces a board and a management team now led by interim chief executive Colette Kress that is aiming to steady the organization ahead of quarterly results on Tuesday.

Huang’s affair with Alice Huang, an executive at Singapore-based Megaspeed, has triggered deepening scrutiny of Nvidia’s compliance measures when selling its AI chips to customers in Asia who have potential links to China.

Sources indicate that even allies were unsure how to rehabilitate Huang’s reputation. “Having an affair with a subordinate is a fireable offense,” acknowledged one person involved in efforts to reinstate Huang.

According to recent reports, the FT reported on Friday that Arm chief Rene Haas has been approached by Nvidia’s board as a potential successor. Nvidia’s board said no “formal” process had been initiated.

Altimeter Capital founder Brad Gerstner and Atreides Management boss Gavin Baker—who are Nvidia shareholders—published an open letter to the board on Friday urging them to leave “all options on the table, including the potential return of Jensen Huang.”.

The pair, both large investors in the tech giant, cited “the extraordinary success of Jensen Huang’s leadership over a long period of time and given the massive uncertainty associated with recent events surrounding his departure” as reasons for clemency.

#157. Your smart home hub placement is more notable than you'd think

📅 16 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 3m • 📚 Deep Dive (541 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Engadget ↗ Open Full Page

Your smart home hub placement is more notable than you'd think

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (541 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Engadget

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Whether it fits your home's aesthetic or not, that hub may need to be front and center.
  • A robust smart home system makes it easy to control the many devices keeping your household in the 21st century, but there are many ways that system can fail.
  • Many hubs feature controls for all of your connected devices, so it makes sense that you'd keep them in a central spot.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Whether it fits your home's aesthetic or not, that hub may need to be front and center.

A robust smart home system makes it easy to control the many devices keeping your household in the 21st century, but there are many ways that system can fail. Like any gadget, smart home devices are prone to concerns that have no clear cause and can be frustrating to diagnose. Among those potential causes is something you may never guess: placement. As the center of your setup, capable of receiving signals from all directions, you'd think you can place your smart home hub anywhere, but it's not as simple as that.

Many hubs feature controls for all of your connected devices, so it makes sense that you'd keep them in a central spot. But if you control your devices from separate apps or just don't need to make manual adjustments often, it can be tempting to hide the hub out of sight. But since it needs to send and receive signals from all your home's devices, it's vital to ensure they aren't blocked or being impeded.

While not all smart home devices run on Wi-Fi, it's helpful to treat the hub the way you would a Wi-Fi router. The most important part of placing a smart home hub like Anker's MindBase is making sure signals aren't being physically obstructed. Wi-Fi and other forms of wireless communication can be blocked by walls, furniture and doors, so try to keep as clear a path as possible between the hub and the devices communicating with it. Because you're likely controlling devices throughout your home, some will inevitably have a weaker connection than others, but placing the hub in a central place will help minimize problems. If your hub has visible antennas, try to also point them toward your smart home devices.

Hubs can also experience interference from other communication devices, like Wi-Fi routers. It's impossible to completely eliminate this kind of interference, especially if you're living somewhere with a lot of Wi-Fi traffic, like an apartment building. You should place your hub close enough to a router so that it's still receiving a strong signal, but they should never be right next to each other to avoid interference. Modern routers have settings that allow them to change to less crowded frequencies, and turning that on or setting your router and hub to different bands can help cut down on congestion as well. Other electronics like phones and microwaves can also interfere with smart home hubs, and the only solution here is to keep them away from each other.

If you're limited on placement options, you can create a linked network for Zigbee or ZWave connections to travel to the hub. Keep in mind that the signal they use has a fairly short range. Because these devices form a mesh network, each device repeats the signal it receives, letting you form a chain of devices through your home. That means that the signal from your hub only needs to reach one other device to be effective, but the signal does get weaker across multiple devices. So, even for a network that branches across devices, the closer to the hub a device is, the better.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Some British sausages have faced barriers to being exported to the EU.

In Boston, Lincolnshire, a supplier of ready meals to Marks & Spencer (M&S) manufactures thousands of portions of spaghetti bolognese to be sent to the retailer's shops in the Republic of Ireland.

Every plastic pallet is meticulously individually tagged with a green-grey label âEireâ.

It has been this way since Brexit.

Every truck full of food sent to European Union countries requires hundreds of pages of forms, checks by vets, expense and delays.

It has cost M&S millions of pounds and is part of that reason the British business shut down 11 French stores in 2021.

Many smaller exporters stopped sending their goods to the EU entirely. Some produce, including sausages and certain types of seafood, were entirely stopped.

All this was the predictable consequence of former Prime Minister Boris Johnsonâs 2020 deal prioritising regulatory freedom over freeflowing goods trade.

That will end with a Brexit "reset" that Prime Minister Andy Burnham is set to sign with the EU on Friday.

The government claims it could boost the economy to the tune of Â£5bn a year and cut the cost of food for households.

But will the agreement mean a return to frictionless trade for food with the EU or are there trade-offs and quid pro quos the UK will have to make?

EU affairs minister Hamish Falconer, who is a key negotiator with the bloc, acknowledged a âchoiceâ is being made.

In exchange for being able to export produce such as Lincolnshire sausages to the 27 countries, the flipside is the extent to which the UK will be able to influence EU food policies.

The UK will have a "voice in the room", noted Falconer, but no vote. Critics have said a reset will make the UK "a rule taker", not a rule maker.

But Falconer stated the UK will be involved in a process to shape the rules.

A Brexit reset would not involve any upfront payments, said Falconer, but made it clear there could well be an "exit clause" in case a future UK government reversed the closer alignment.

He said this was "reasonable" to consider what would happen if a future Conservative or Reform government wanted to undo the new arrangements. Both parties have said they would if they were in power.

"The EU is worried about that and you can see why," he mentioned.

The BBC understands that the clause is a result of EU concerns about the possible cost of having to rebuild facilities for border food safety checks which were put in place following Brexit.

The reset means they will be dismantled.

The prime minister has stated he believes there is a "win-win" deal to be had with the EU.

Speaking at a Marks & Spencer food court in central London, Falconer said reducing the cost of importing food "will mean less cost for supermarkets, and I hope that less cost then turns into cheaper produce on the shelves".

He mentioned companies have to currently deal with "pages and pages" of form-filling.

Some exports are rejected for having the wrong colour of ink on forms, or an inaccurate Latin name for cooked meats.

The reset could also mean "tearing up" checks that were introduced on goods flowing from Great Britain to Northern Ireland, following Brexit, he stated, as well as separate "Not for EU" labelling.

The whole deal to be signed on Friday is calculated to add 0.4% to UK GDP.

Minister for EU relations Hamish Falconer.

Tom Bradshaw, president of the National Farmers' Union, welcomed reduced border inspections and paperwork but mentioned that for the NFU it was "a moment of opportunity and risk" with farmers waiting to see what carve-outs and transitional arrangements would be included.

Trade volumes in food exports to the EU had "fallen significantly - by over a third" since 2019, he noted.

But the UK should take a "pragmatic" approach to implementing any latest rules.

He raised pesticides and precision breeding - or gene edited crops - as areas where he hoped some compromise would be found.

UK firms are, for example, developing tomatoes engineered to contain extra vitamin D.

Historically the EU has had much stricter rules on gene-editing, but this year relaxed regulations.

Falconer remarked people would have to "wait and see the detail" in this area.

Another contentious area has been crisp flavourings, with concerns raised that stricter EU rules on certain ingredients might limit the sale of some popular snack flavours in the UK.

"I want to take this opportunity to absolutely stamp down on misinformation about smoky bacon crisps," Falconer mentioned.

Post-Brexit the UK had stayed "pretty closely aligned" to European food safety standards, he remarked.

Two leading snack brands had already adapted their recipes to accommodate EU rules, an example of the kind of alignment that would happen whether or not there was a reset of UK-EU relations.

"The truth is, almost every business in this country that wants to export food or drink will be aligning with EU rules because it's our biggest market.

"Lots of people, like the good people at Walkers and Frazzles have made these changes already, so I would want to reassure people, particularly smoky bacon fans, it's okay," he said.

Could smoky bacon crisps really be banned?

Ten years on, Brexit's economic impact is becoming clearer.

Tech Report: Freshworks alums raise $53M to take on Salesforce, HubSpot with AI-native CRM

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (863 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: TechCrunch

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Dreamteam, a startup founded by former Freshworks executives, has raised $53 million to challenge Salesforce and HubSpot with its AI-native CRM, betting that AI can finally shake up a market where established players have so far proved difficult to dislodge.
  • Industry observers note that the funding comprises seed and Series A rounds, led by Together Fund and Accel respectively, with participation from Premji Invest.
  • Traditional CRMs depend on salespeople to manually record customer interactions and keep deal information up to date.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Dreamteam, a startup founded by former Freshworks executives, has raised $53 million to challenge Salesforce and HubSpot with its AI-native CRM, betting that AI can finally shake up a market where established players have so far proved difficult to dislodge.

Industry observers note that the funding comprises seed and Series A rounds, led by Together Fund and Accel respectively, with participation from Premji Invest. The San Francisco-based startup declined to disclose the size of each round or its valuation.

Traditional CRMs depend on salespeople to manually record customer interactions and keep deal information up to date. That often leaves businesses with incomplete or outdated information. Dreamteam aims to eliminate much of that work by automatically capturing context from sources including emails and customer conversations. It also uses AI agents to handle tasks such as follow-ups, meeting preparation, and pipeline monitoring.

Dreamteam co-founder and CEO Anand Venkatraman (pictured above, right) told TechCrunch that he had repeatedly encountered problems with traditional CRM platforms over more than 25 years in enterprise software, including at Salesforce and Freshworks. Salespeople spent considerable time updating records, yet managers still struggled to get a reliable picture of their business. “In all these years, I have never come across an instance where I could click a button and get a forecast from the CRM,” he stated.

That experience led Venkatraman to co-found Dreamteam in 2025 with Senthil Kanthaswamy (pictured above, center), who spent more than nine years at Freshworks, most recently as a product leader at Freshservice, and Ramesh Parthasarathy (pictured above, left), who previously worked on AI and platform engineering at Freshworks.

At the heart of Dreamteam’s CRM is what it calls the Tech giant Brain. This acts as virtual memory, pulling together information from emails, meetings, and other customer interactions to build a shared record of customer relationships. Four built-in AI agents use that information to research prospects, draft follow-up emails, flag potential risks to deals, and configure CRM workflows, with sales teams retaining control over what gets sent to customers.

In a recent development, dreamteam has signed up more than 100 customers across 13 countries in the three months since it began actively selling its product, with most paying for the service, Venkatraman said. The startup has also replaced established CRM platforms at several businesses, including Salesforce at healthcare company DMS Health and HubSpot at other customers.

Recent findings suggest that the advertising sales team at media streaming organization Plex also chose Dreamteam over HubSpot and other AI-native CRM alternatives, Venkatraman told TechCrunch. Plex’s co-founder and chief product officer Scott Olechowski noted Dreamteam’s ability to integrate with AI tools already used across the company was a “game changer.”.

According to recent reports, replacing established CRM platforms at scale may prove more difficult. In a blog post earlier this year, venture capital firm Andreessen Horowitz (a16z) argued that while AI could transform how businesses manage customer relationships, existing CRMs are likely to remain the systems where customer records are stored, with a newly introduced generation of AI-powered tools capturing much of the value by working on top of them.

Venkatraman acknowledged that Salesforce and HubSpot are unlikely to disappear anytime soon, but noted that their entrenched positions do not guarantee they will dominate the next generation of CRM software.

“We see this as an electric-car moment for systems of record,” he stated, adding that AI requires a fundamental rethink of how CRMs are built — not simply adding new features to existing platforms.

Kanthaswamy believes startups have a window of two to five years to gain ground before established CRM providers can fully adapt to AI. Rebuilding software around a fundamentally different architecture takes time, he stated, giving newer companies an opportunity to attract customers while incumbents work to overhaul their existing products.

Sources indicate that dreamteam also prepares to expand beyond sales into other parts of the customer lifecycle, including onboarding, customer support, and upselling. The startup already has a feature called Magic Apps that allows customers to create custom applications and dashboards within the CRM using natural-language instructions, without writing code.

Industry observers note that currently, Dreamteam employs more than 35 people, with its engineering team based in Chennai and its go-to-market operations in the United States. Kanthaswamy said the startup aims to reach eight figures in annual revenue by the end of 2027, though he declined to disclose the startup’s current revenue.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Backdown is one of several premier Chris Minns has announced in recent weeks as state prepares for election in March.
  • Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast.
  • The Minns government has mothballed laws intended to protect homebuyers from underquoting after the premier noted real estate agents in his Sydney electorate had raised concerns about their effect amid a housing market downturn.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Backdown is one of several premier Chris Minns has announced in recent weeks as state prepares for election in March.

Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast.

The Minns government has mothballed laws intended to protect homebuyers from underquoting after the premier noted real estate agents in his Sydney electorate had raised concerns about their effect amid a housing market downturn.

Changes due to come into effect on Tuesday would have banned agents in New South Wales from lowering the advertised price of a property beneath a written offer previously rejected by a seller, with fines of up to $110,000 or three times an agent’s commission, whichever was greater.

But the laws and fines will be paused for up to a year after a last-minute intervention by the premier, Chris Minns, who flagged on Monday morning that concerns had been raised by agents in his south Sydney electorate of Kogarah.

“It has come across my desk from real estate agents in my electorate,” he told reporters, after he was asked about fears the laws could prevent sellers from advertising at a lower rate now that the market has fallen. Home values in Sydney have dropped by 10.1% from their 2026 peak, according to data from Cotality.

“I do think it’s [an] unforeseen [consequence], but it is something we’re going to have to deal with because it’s not the seller or the agent’s fault if the price of real estate is dropping, and the legislation at least intuitively believed that the prices would always rise,” noted Minns.

In a recent development, the changes, which were passed in June, were modelled on laws already in effect in Victoria. Under additional transparency measures which came into effect in Victoria last month, sellers must reveal their reserve price at least one week before a sale, and agents must publish sale prices after a transaction is completed.

The decision is a potential embarrassment for NSW fair trading and corrections minister, Anoulack Chanthivong, who has previously been overruled by Minns on rental and prison reforms.

The minister faces a preselection battle in his seat of Macquarie Fields, but Minns would not say on Monday if he would intervene on Chanthivong’s behalf.

As recently as 1 November, Chanthivong had praised the laws as “important reforms to put the hammer down on underquoting and stop homebuyers being taken for a ride”.

On Monday afternoon, a spokesperson for the Minns government provided a statement from Chanthivong, who said the laws had been passed “at a different time and in a different economic and housing market”.

“We introduced these laws to crack down on underquoting, protect homebuyers from misleading practices and ensure a fair and transparent property market for buyers and sellers,” he said.

“People are already doing it tough, and the last thing we want is for laws designed to protect homebuyers to inadvertently make it harder for them to buy a home.

“That’s why the government has made the decision not to proceed with the implementation of these changes today.”.

It is the latest of several reversals in recent weeks by the government, under pressure ahead of the March state election from One Nation and the Coalition, with the cost of living and pressures on small businesses among the key issues.

Last month, the government dropped parts of plastics legislation which would have required cafes to offer customers who dine in the option of mugs and glasses instead of takeaway cups.

Polling conducted internally by the Labor party has suggested that One Nation could win more than 20 seats in the lower house. The party was polling at 26% of the primary vote in NSW according to a Sydney Morning Herald Resolve poll in October, behind Labor on 30%, but ahead of the Coalition on 23%.

One Nation revealed four more candidates on its six-person upper house ticket on Sunday, but has so far only announced one lower house candidate, NSW party leader Mike Newman.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The enrollment of fresh international students at American universities dropped once again this fall, fueled by deep uncertainty about visas and job prospects.

A survey released Monday found that latest international student enrollment plunged by 15 percent, a figure that was particularly worrisome for higher education executives following a precipitous 18 percent decrease last year.

Including preexisting students, international student enrollment declined 9 percent this fall, according to the survey, adding to last year’s drop of 3 percent.

According to recent reports, for years, American colleges and universities had attracted growing numbers of international students, who often paid full tuition, indirectly subsidizing tuition for domestic students. But President Trump’s crackdown on immigrants, which has occasionally swept up foreign students, along with confusing visa policies and a trade war with China, one of the top suppliers of international students, have stoked fears that the United States is no longer a welcoming place to study.

Ted Mitchell, president of the American Council on Education, a large education trade organization, characterized the combined two-year downturn as “likely historic,” noting that international students had been a growth sector for higher education.

Industry observers note that he pointed to departures among international students who were already enrolled as a worrying sign. “These are people who’ve already started, and they’ve said, ‘No, the risk is too high. I’m not going back,’” Dr. Mitchell said.

#149. Is India rethinking its short-term military recruitment scheme?

📅 16 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1276 w)
