General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Co ↗ Open Full Page

Is India rethinking its short-term military recruitment scheme?

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1276 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Co

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • There are currently 300,000 Agniveers serving in India's defence forces.
  • For generations of young Indians, joining the armed forces offered something few other jobs did - a steady career, financial security, the promise of a pension after retirement and the pride of serving their country.
  • According to recent reports, in 2022, the government upended that arrangement, announcing a latest reform scheme under which young men and women entering the military would serve for just four years.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

There are currently 300,000 Agniveers serving in India's defence forces.

For generations of young Indians, joining the armed forces offered something few other jobs did - a steady career, financial security, the promise of a pension after retirement and the pride of serving their country.

According to recent reports, in 2022, the government upended that arrangement, announcing a latest reform scheme under which young men and women entering the military would serve for just four years. Only a quarter would be allowed to stay on permanently. The rest would return to civilian life with a lump-sum payment, but without the pension and other benefits that had long made military service an attractive career.

Now, as the first batch of recruits prepares to complete its four-year term, the government is offering them a chance to stay longer, in a significant shift in a policy that has been fiercely debated since its introduction.

On 4 November, Chief of Defence Staff General NS Raja Subramani declared that recruits who failed to secure permanent positions under the Agnipath, or "path of fire", programme would be offered another two years of service at higher pay. They would then get a second opportunity to join the regular forces, provided they met the selection criteria.

Gen Subramani stated the decision followed feedback from the forces and insisted that Agnipath would continue.

In a recent development, but the timing is significant. More than 18,300 recruits from the first batch are due to complete their initial tenure by the end of 2026. Officials say the fresh arrangement will be offered to more than 300,000 Agniveers - as recruits under the scheme are known - presently serving across the army, navy and air force.

Whether future batches will also be covered remains unclear. The BBC has contacted the defence ministry for clarification.

The ministry has defended , externalAgnipath, saying internal assessments found the recruits to be physically fit, motivated and technologically adaptable. It also noted the scheme had widened recruitment across districts and made the process more standardised.

But the extension has brought renewed attention to the trade-offs at the heart of the policy - and whether its original ambitions were realistic.

Those selected are trained for months before being inducted into regiments.

When the government introduced Agnipath, it argued the scheme would reduce the average age of the armed forces, lower long-term salary and pension costs and create a younger, more technologically adaptable fighting force.

But military experts and opposition leaders have questioned whether a four-year contract could replace what had traditionally been a coveted, long-term career in the armed forces.

"Being a soldier in the armed forces was a chance for these young men to make a life for themselves, to get their families out of poor or lower-middle-income conditions," says retired Maj Gen Yash Mor, a vocal critic of the scheme.

These concerns were also amplified by the timing of Agnipath's launch. Recruitment had been suspended for nearly two years during the Covid pandemic, leaving thousands of aspirants waiting for vacancies to reopen.

The changes were greeted by massive protests across the country, with many saying the career path they had spent years preparing for had fundamentally changed.

This sentiment was felt most in states and cities that have traditionally been major recruitment hubs, where military service has been a family tradition for generations.

Kulbeer Singh Chaudhary, who runs a recruitment training institute in Dehradun city, states interest in joining the armed forces fell sharply and he stopped conducting Agniveer training batches.

The latest announcement, he hopes, would reverse that trend.

"The possibility of a longer engagement and eventual absorption into the forces may offer young candidates greater assurance," he states.

The changes also come at a time when the armed forces are facing personnel shortages. In November last year, The Indian Express reported, external that the army alone faced a shortfall of nearly 180,000 soldiers and was considering increasing recruitment.

Many young men from small towns spend months preparing for the selection process to join the defence forces.

Sources indicate that but the debate over Agnipath goes beyond what happens to recruits after four years. Critics also question whether that is enough time to turn them into experienced soldiers.

Sanjiv Krishan Sood, a former additional director general of the Border Security Force, has argued, external that the shorter training period is particularly problematic for technical roles requiring specialised skills.

Retired Maj Gen Mor states military effectiveness depends on experience and trust built over years.

"It takes eight-to-nine years to turn a raw recruit into a dependable, seasoned soldier - someone capable of handling a tank crew, an artillery gun crew or a small detachment," he says.

"Over those years, a soldier develops the ethos, camaraderie, brotherhood and fighting spirit that bind a unit together. These qualities cannot be built overnight.".

Sood claims the additional two years could help improve recruits' skills, particularly in handling specialised equipment.

Senior military leaders have also welcomed the extension. Air Vice Marshal Shekhar Yadav told news agency ANI, external it would allow the forces to retain trained personnel for longer.

But the change could create fresh challenges within military units.

Regular soldiers, Agniveers on four-year contracts and those serving an additional two years could find themselves working alongside one another despite differences in pay, promotion prospects and post-service benefits.

Experts warn that these disparities could affect unit cohesion.

Indian soldiers are deployed through the year at the country's borders with China and Pakistan.

Industry observers note that there is also the question of whether the changes will undermine one of the government's central objectives: reducing spending. Almost half of India's defence budget, external goes towards salaries and pensions, leaving less money for modernisation and new equipment.

By limiting the number of personnel eligible for long-term benefits, Agnipath was expected to ease that burden. But critics argue that savings should not come at the expense of military effectiveness.

"We are not against making changes, but there are ways and means to go about it," notes Mor, adding that the government could instead reduce annual recruitment while retaining soldiers for longer periods.

He also points to India's tense borders with Pakistan and China, where troops remain deployed year-round, placing sustained demands on manpower and operational experience.

Retired Major-General Birender Singh Dhanoa, meanwhile, questions whether shorter service makes financial sense when the military is investing in training to operate increasingly sophisticated equipment.

"The amount of time it takes to train, and the financial outlay for training, is much higher for modern equipment. So shouldn't you get the best bang for your buck?" he asks.

Many retired officers had proposed a different approach when the scheme was confirmed, he says.

Recent findings suggest that "We suggested that if you want to reduce your financial burden, you increase the terms and conditions of service. Take these guys for eight-or-nine years and retain a larger number after that.".

The announcement also comes at a politically sensitive time. Elections are due soon in Punjab, Uttar Pradesh and Uttarakhand - states that have traditionally supplied large numbers of soldiers and where military recruitment remains an key source of employment.

The opposition Congress party has called the revision a "u-turn", alleging that the government is responding to fears of losing votes.

It has been revealed that for young recruits approaching the end of their contracts, the changes offer some reassurance, but few guarantees. Two more years of service could mean more money, greater experience and another chance at a permanent career.

But for many, it also means putting their futures on hold, without knowing whether they will eventually be allowed to stay.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The app will become even more of a shopping mall, just in time for Black Friday.

Meta has a fresh gift for Instagram creators just in time for Black Friday and the holiday shopping season. The company is making it easier for influencers to promote Amazon affiliate products directly in their posts without having to rely on a link in bio service.

Recent findings suggest that US creators who are also in Amazon's influencer program will now be able to add dozens of affiliate links directly to their Reels and Instagram posts, Meta unveiled. The links will take viewers directly to the Amazon app and creators will earn their usual commission from any purchase made via their content.

In a recent development, instagram has enabled product tagging and shoppable posts for some time. But the company previously required that tagged products in Reels already exist in Meta's commerce catalog. Now, creators can instead link their Amazon account directly to Instagram and add up to 30 products in a single video (there's a 20-product limit for feed posts). The Instagram app will also show creators what commission to expect for each item.

For creators, the timing of the upcoming feature is particularly good. Commission from affiliate links is a central part of how many Instagram influencers earn money from their accounts. And posts with products linked directly can generate twice as many clicks as bio links, according to Meta. And while the tech giant won't take a cut of creators' commissions, these links are no doubt a valuable source of data to Meta about what their users are interested in.

According to recent reports, the revision is the latest way Meta has made it easier for Instagram influencers to direct people off-platform. The company has also started allowing creators to add clickable links to captions and Reels if they pay for certain Meta One subscription aims. Those paid tiers also come with expanded link pages. Up to now, the company's restrictions on link-sharing have led many creators to depend on separate "link in bio" services. Now, it seems Meta is increasingly interested in offering those tools to creators directly.

In a recent development, for now, Amazon affiliate linking is only available to creators in the United States who have a professional account on Instagram and are 18 or older. The company hasn't mentioned if it prepares to expand the feature to creators in more countries.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Health officials in Pennsylvania and Wisconsin announced two more measles deaths late last week, bringing the national tally of confirmed measles deaths this year to 10. The total includes the deaths of at least four infants: two in Pennsylvania, one in New York, and one in Wisconsin.

Wisconsin health officials said the latest measles death—the second for the state—was in a child. Pennsylvania’s health department did not reveal the age or other details of the latest death—the state’s seventh—besides revealing it was of an unvaccinated resident in Montour County. Overall, the seven deaths in Pennsylvania include two in Jefferson County, three in Lancaster County, and one in Mifflin, in addition to the fresh death in Montour. An eighth death was reported in Franklin County, but state health officials have not confirmed it.

In a recent development, for all the states with deaths so far, health officials have noted that they’re the first deaths in decades. Multiple outbreaks are underway across the country, pushing the national tally of cases to nearly 5,500 across 47 states and jurisdictions, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. Pennsylvania’s case count alone is over 1,500, and Wisconsin is reporting nearly 650.

In a recent development, with outbreaks that have been smoldering and flaring since last year, the US has reportedly lost its measles elimination status—as medical and public health experts have widely expected it would. A panel of experts for the Pan American Health Organization (PAHO), a regional branch of the World Health Organization, convened last week to review US measles data and assess its elimination status. The PAHO is set to announce its conclusion and the review’s other findings on Tuesday, November 17. But sources broke the news to The Wall Street Journal on Friday that the panel had found that the US had indeed lost its status.

In a recent development, an elimination status is determined by international health authorities after a country has gone more than 12 months without continuous spread of a virus. The status is lost when epidemiological and laboratory data indicate that a chain of transmission involving a viral strain with an identical genotype and lineage has continued uninterrupted for 12 months or longer.

Industry observers note that the US earned its elimination status in 2000 after hard-fought vaccination campaigns over several decades. But US vaccination rates have slipped below protective levels in recent years, fueled by the rise of anti-vaccine rhetoric and vaccine misinformation from fierce anti-vaccine advocates, including current US Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. As vaccination rates slipped, measles cases skyrocketed. The current case tally is the highest seen since 1991.

It has been revealed that in reporting the PAHO’s determination, the Journal quoted Noel Brewer, chair of an independent US committee who presented findings about the country’s measles outbreaks to PAHO, on the country’s lamentable status: “Runaway measles outbreaks in the United States, as well as the needless deaths, are all due to low measles vaccination coverage. We’ve gotten comfortable letting children be stopped by a deadly disease and die from it.”.

The US Department of Health and Human Services did not immediately respond to requests to comment about the loss of the elimination status or to answer a question about how anti-vaccine rhetoric and misinformation, including that from Kennedy, has contributed.

Industry observers note that medical and public health experts continue to sharply criticize Kennedy’s and the Trump administration’s poor handling of the ongoing severe outbreaks. The CDC has not held press briefings in efforts to halt the vaccine-preventable illness and promote vaccination. Instead, Kennedy reportedly ordered the CDC to remove measles death data, and the CDC director declined to approve an urgent health alert about the life-threatening risks of measles during pregnancy.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Geothermal heat pumps, which use the ground as a heat source in winter and heat sink in summer, have been around for decades, but they’re underutilized.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Dig deep enough, and the temperature of the ground remains steady year round, a fun trivia fact that has the potential to improve efficiency and slash costs for heating and cooling across the country.

Geothermal heat pumps, which use the ground as a heat source in winter and heat sink in summer, have been around for decades, but they’re underutilized. Just a fraction of all buildings in the U.S. use them in part because it’s expensive to drill into the earth. But one startup, Bedrock Energy, claims its AI-directed rigs can slash drilling times by up to 80%, significantly reducing costs.

In a recent development, that time savings recently helped Bedrock raise a latest $24 million funding round, the startup told TechCrunch. Previously, it raised a $12 million Series A in 2025 and an $8.5 million seed round in 2023.

Bedrock has focused mostly on commercial properties to date, since they benefit from deep, accurate boreholes which maximize the use of their small footprints. But the startup has also been talking with data center developers, Joselyn Lai, co-founder and CEO of Bedrock Energy, told TechCrunch. Some might use it for cooling server racks, but others are interested in the technology’s flat load profile — deploying it on neighboring properties can open up significant capacity on the grid.

“We had someone in Michigan say, if we could free up a few megawatts, I think we might be able to operate that many months or even a year earlier,” Lai said. “A year of revenue for a data center is very meaningful.”.

Sources indicate that bedrock says its modernized approach to shallow geothermal drilling — up to 1,000 feet or so — sets it apart. Most geothermal heat pump drillers use rigs that are similar to those used for water wells. They work fine, but they’re crude instruments.

According to recent reports, instead, Bedrock uses directional drilling techniques borrowed from the oil and gas industry, guiding them using its own models of the subsurface. That combination allows them to optimize drilling and placement, the organization states, helping to ensure performance and longevity. Sensors in the boreholes help to refine those models.

The startup at the moment operates in Utah, Colorado, Upcoming York, Alberta, and its home state of Texas, and the new round will help the tech giant expand into New England, New Jersey, the upper Midwest, and additional states in the West, Lai remarked.

Sources indicate that to power that expansion, Bedrock will add more rigs to its fleet to serve customers in those regions. Presently, it has drilled boreholes in nine sites, and it has secured payments from new customers in anticipation of drilling in the next year or two, she added.

According to recent reports, once up and running, a geothermal heat pump requires far less maintenance than traditional HVAC systems. “You only have to install it once and then it works for a very long time, which is very good for infrastructure from a financial perspective,” Lai stated.

The fresh round was led by Clean Energy Ventures and Clearvision Ventures, with participation from GVP Climate, Susquehanna Sustainable Investments, Catalytic Capital for Climate and Health by Temasek Trust, MUUS, Great Wave Ventures, Autodesk Foundation, Titanium Ventures, Energy Impact Partners, Wireframe Ventures, Elemental Impact, and SFV Capital.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The feature was teased during Google I/O earlier this year.

In a recent development, one of the less visible risks of conversational AI is its flattening effect on a culture's unique dialect and accent. Humanity speaks with a thousand voices, but assistants often just respond in a nicely generic transatlantic monotone. Now, Google is doing something about it by adding 66 regional dialects to Gemini to help it better relate to the people using it. The feature was first teased at Google I/O earlier this year, and starting today, the Android and iOS apps will be able to speak to owners in a variety of voices from different countries.

For instance, UK people can set Gemini to speak in a Geordie, Scouse and Brummie accent to better engage with people from Tyneside, Merseyside and Birmingham. The list also includes Scots, Welsh, Northern Irish and Multicultural London English, among many others. And it's not just the UK that gets this treatment, with tailored dialects for India, Brazil, Indonesia and Korea also in the mix.

Google notes it worked with native speakers to ensure the voices were authentic and clear, rather than exaggerated and stereotypical. It added that Gemini isn't going to suddenly fill its responses with "street slang," but instead focus on sounding more "like a local." Given how much pride people put into their accent as a signifier of their heritage, it'll be very interesting to see how well these voices are received by the people intended to use them.

According to recent reports, to activate the voices, you'll need to access the voice settings in the Gemini app or tap the three-dot menu. Google suggests a good way to test their authenticity is to ask for a recommendation for local food to better hear the "warmth and rhythm of each voice.".

Anthony Albanese will attempt to walk a tightrope in his relationship with Donald Trump when the two leaders meet on Tuesday, arguing for a speedy resolution to the wars in Iran and Ukraine while urging the US to engage in the Indo-Pacific.

Sources indicate that the Quad leaders’ summit in the Philippines’ capital of Manila will be Trump’s first, in either of his presidencies. The US president, fresh from a crushing midterms result, will take centre stage in gatherings of Asian leaders and prepare for historic three-way talks with Xi Jinping of China and Russia’s Vladimir Putin this week.

Underlying the diplomatic swing are efforts by the federal government to avoid angering China, as the Quad leaders gather for the first time since 2024 – and after Australia joined countries, including the US and Japan, in an agreement for new protections around key AI technologies.

Designed to firm up supply chains for chips and critical minerals components, the San Francisco Declaration was crafted to promote cooperation in the face of China’s efforts to control areas of AI development.

It has been revealed that part of the Pax Silica international accord, officials stated the agreement would help ensure Trump worked with partners to set standards in AI, rather than relying on others for leadership. Signatories include the UK, India, Israel, South Korea and Singapore.

Albanese told the Asean-Australia summit on Monday that the region needed friendship, mutual trust, and optimism to prosper.

“At a time of global instability, the cooperation we demonstrate here will help us to confront the challenges we share at home and in our region,” he mentioned.

Federal government sources told Guardian Australia the intense international efforts, including Albanese’s attendance at the Apec leaders’ meeting in Shenzhen, China at the end of the week, was about maintaining engagement with Trump in the final two years of his presidency and stopping the US from withdrawing from global leadership.

Asia Society senior fellow Premesha Saha noted the Quad talks would focus on critical minerals, maritime security and energy security.

“For Australia, keeping the United States engaged in the Indo-Pacific is a core strategic interest, and the Quad is one of the few settings where the president is tied into a regional agenda alongside three close partners,” Saha mentioned.

“After a year in which Washington has been engaged elsewhere and has opened its own channel with Beijing, getting Trump to a Quad leaders’ meeting in the region matters to Australia.”.

Saha said Albanese’s objectives included keeping Washington engaged in the region and building a Quad capable of delivering results, even during shifts in US policy and interest.

Recent findings suggest that “Beijing will criticise it, as it always does, and will cast it as bloc politics. But I will be cautious about overstating how much this will anger China,” she noted.

“The Quad isn’t a military alliance, and Washington has gone out of its way to say it isn’t an anti-China coalition.”.

Jennifer Parker, a non-resident fellow at the Lowy Institute, noted criticism of Albanese’s involvement in the annual international summit season was shortsighted.

“Our relationships in the region are essential to our security in an increasingly chaotic world, and our security is the backbone of our national prosperity,” she stated.

“It is important for Australia to be seen on the international stage and advocate for our national interests.”.

Parker disagreed that Australia was working to keep the US engaged in the Asia Pacific region.

In a recent development, “The US has enduring interests here, both economically and strategically. But sometimes it pays for Australia to remind them of that,” she mentioned.

Albanese announced a new Asean-Australia digital economy program on Monday, to support AI safety and intelligence standards and digital trade standards.

He said humans must remain in control of AI, shaping the technology “rather than let it shape us”.

Albanese also held one-on-one talks with the Philippines president, Ferdinand Marcos Jr.

He told his Laos counterpart, Saleumxay Kommasith, that Australia remained very concerned about the deaths of backpackers Bianca Jones and Holly Morton-Bowles, who died after drinking methanol-laced alcohol at a hostel in Vientiane in 2024.

Albanese said Australia remained concerned about the seriousness of charges over the deaths. Investigators said they did not have enough evidence to do more because autopsies were not carried out.

Albanese called the case a “tragedy” and mentioned it remained a serious problem in Australia.

Kommasith said the Laos government had attached importance to the case and officials were “trying our best to put an end to this by bringing those perpetrators into justice”.

Robert Pattinson starred in 2022's The Batman, which was described by critics as a grim, gritty, and gripping super-noir.

Born in Barnes, south-west London, Pattinson grew up with his father, a classic car trader and mother, who worked at a modelling agency, and two elder sisters.

His interest in acting started while he was still at school, when he joined the Barnes Theatre Club.

"I wouldn't be acting if it wasn't for that little club," he told Your Local Guardian in 2008, external.

"I went originally because a lot of pretty girls went there," he noted. "I worked backstage and I started acting when all the good people left and I was the only one tall enough to play the lead.

"In a weird sort of way, that stuff was probably the best I've done and the stuff I am most proud of.".

In a recent development, he landed his first major film role more than two decades ago, playing Cedric Diggory in 2005's Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire. A relatively minor character, but it was enough to get him noticed.

Robert Pattinson and Kristen Stewart starred in five Twilight films from 2005 to 2012.

Three years later, he had a starring role in the first of five Twilight films, along with Kristen Stewart, in which they played star-crossed lovers - vampire Edward Cullen and mortal-turned vampire Kristen Stewart.

Based on Stephanie Meyer's hugely popular young adult books, the films globally grossed more than $3bn (Â£2.2bn) by 2012, and established Pattinson as a heartthrob.

He spoke in his early career of finding his often adoring, screaming fans hard to deal with.

"Although is part of the job, it feels like they have been paid to turn up and scream at me at 7.30pm," he stated.

"Nothing I don't think can prepare you for the fans. I don't know why I'm not getting used to it but I'm completely overwhelmed every time.".

In 2010, Time included him in their list of 100 people who "most affect our world", external, saying perhaps prophetically that "we haven't seen a tenth of what he can do on screen".

After such mainstream success with the Twilight franchise, Pattinson was able to branch out.

He went on to work with several acclaimed independent film directors including David Cronenberg, starring in his film Cosmpopolis in 2012, as well as working with Werner Herzog in 2015's Queen of the Desert and The Lighthouse (2019), directed by Robert Eggers.

Pattinson told Screen Daily why he took the role in psychological horror film The Lighthouse, external, saying he told Eggers: "I just want to do something weird.".

Pattinson and Zendaya have appeared in three films together this year - The Drama, The Odyssey and Dune: Part Three.

The following year though, he was back in big-studio territory, with Odyssey director Christopher Nolan, in sci-fi thriller Tenet, and again in 2022 with The Batman, directed by Matt Reeves and co-starring Zoe Kravitz and Paul Dano.

Industry observers note that pattinson told Screen Daily why he returned to major-budget films, explaining: "I guess I was trying to do the opposite of what I've been doing. I started thinking, 'I really want to do a big thing.'.

Sources indicate that "I hadn't done something with a massive budget for ages. But you approach it exactly the same way.".

The Batman got generally positive reviews, re-establishing Pattinson with a broader range of fans.

By 2025, when he was on the red carpet for Parasite director Bong Joon Ho's sci-fi black comedy, Mickey 17, he mentioned it was "quite strange" to have a fanbase that was now dominated by men, external.

"There's like a bunch of guys, which is a upcoming one for me!" he told the Associated Press.

Pattinson's private life has often created interest in the press, not least his previous relationships with Stewart, and then the singer FKA Twigs.

Recent findings suggest that since 2018, he has been in a relationship with model Suki Waterhouse. They got engaged in December 2023 and had their first child, a daughter, in March.

Robert Pattinson and Suki Waterhouse have been a couple since 2018.

With his latest role as James Bond, Pattinson will be extremely busy, not least because the forthcoming Batman sequel is reportedly due out in 2028.

But the actor will have a head start as 007, having already worked with Bond 26 director Denis Villeneuve, who also helmed Dune: Part Three.

Pattinson was full of praise for him on their most recent film, despite the strain of working in the furnace-like heat of the desert.

"The scale of this stuff is just unbelievable, you're having your own Dune theme park, where the gimbal is going upside down and flying, and this is not like work at all," he told the Newly introduced York Times, external.

"There are no negatives. Apart from having your sweat drained out of the top of your head, and getting like bulbous sweat bubbles. But even then, I didn't even really notice them.

"He's so easy to work with, Denis, it's never really a stress.".

Sounds like Pattinson will have the cool head needed to juggle his forthcoming roles - including James Bond. You could even say he may end up being shaken, but not stirred.

Industry News: US moves to cut China’s remote access to AI chips

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1270 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Ars Technica

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • On the heels of the Nvidia scandal, the Trump administration is preparing to crack down on foreign data centers that are fueling China’s advancements in artificial intelligence by allowing remote access to otherwise restricted high-end chips necessary for AI training.
  • In a summary of the rule change, the Commerce Department stated it was closing a loophole that previously allowed foreign rivals like China, Russia, and Iran to bypass export curbs on certain advanced computer chips by instead renting access to those chips from data centers in Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand, and Brazil.
  • In a recent development, US rivals could possibly use that access to train and run advanced AI models “capable of supporting military- and intelligence-related activities that could threaten US national security or foreign policy interests,” the Commerce Department noted.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

On the heels of the Nvidia scandal, the Trump administration is preparing to crack down on foreign data centers that are fueling China’s advancements in artificial intelligence by allowing remote access to otherwise restricted high-end chips necessary for AI training.

In a summary of the rule change, the Commerce Department stated it was closing a loophole that previously allowed foreign rivals like China, Russia, and Iran to bypass export curbs on certain advanced computer chips by instead renting access to those chips from data centers in Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand, and Brazil.

In a recent development, US rivals could possibly use that access to train and run advanced AI models “capable of supporting military- and intelligence-related activities that could threaten US national security or foreign policy interests,” the Commerce Department noted. Among threats, the US fears rivals could use advanced AI to develop “more effective weapons of mass destruction and advanced conventional weapons, coordinated cyber-espionage and targeted cyber-disruption, algorithmic theft, and weaponized disinformation.”.

Now, the rules have been tightened up so much that the South China Morning Post reported that, “as a result, any advanced chips made for a Chinese firm are assumed to be restricted, and factories must ask the US government for a license before shipping them.”.

It has been revealed that the rule change takes effect 90 days after it’s posted to the Federal Register. Moving forward, companies headquartered in any of those countries deemed to “present a higher-than-normal risk of diversion” to China, Russia, and Iran must apply for a license with strict know-your-customer controls when transferring high volumes of advanced chips. If a license is granted, companies will have to “perform robust due diligence,” submitting monthly reports on transactions that thoroughly detail all parties involved, as well as their parent companies, and the final destination for chips sold.

In a press release Sunday, the Commerce Department described the rule change as “designed to ensure that existing restrictions on access to sensitive American technology cannot be circumvented through remote computing arrangements involving data centers in third countries.” An exception was carved out for companies providing computing power “exclusively used for commercial recommender systems.” The Department said it was acting to “prevent certain foreign actors from leveraging advanced computing power based on US technology to threaten US national security and foreign policy interests.”.

Without the intervention, officials fear that China could develop a military or economic edge, The Fresh York Times reported.

Recent findings suggest that nvidia CEO Jensen Huang resigned after admitting to an affair with a woman, Alice Huang, suspected of serving as a Chinese spy. Congress is probing if Alice Huang used her personal relationship with Jensen Huang to help her former tech giant, Megaspeed, become one of Nvidia’s biggest customers, then used that position to smuggle Nvidia’s restricted AI chips into China. China has denied that Alice Huang was a spy, and Megaspeed has denied that smuggling occurred, while launching its own internal probe.

Industry observers note that megaspeed is a Singaporean data center firm whose primary business is cloud computing and AI infrastructure. Prior to the rule change, selling remote access to AI servers to customers in China was perfectly legal, NYT noted. But now, the Commerce Department has given firms like Megaspeed 90 days to either obtain licenses or face future export restrictions.

Sources indicate that whether or not to add more chip curbs has been a polarizing debate in the Trump administration. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent reportedly butted heads with Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick. When the Megaspeed news broke, Bessent pushed for curbs, but Lutnick reportedly appeared “too cozy” with Nvidia to move. Instead, Lutnick initially favored looser controls that Nvidia claimed would ensure global dominance of US technology. (A Commerce Department spokesperson told NYT that Bessent has never confronted Lutnick over his handling of Megaspeed.).

Any companies found violating the rules could face a “range of consequences,” the Commerce Department said after reportedly bending to Bessent’s pressure campaign. Those include possibly facing new import restrictions, stricter license requirements, downgrading their status in the US export control regime, or other changes to their firm’s or their base country’s entity-list designations.

Although the summary of the rule change remarked that “Commerce will be actively monitoring for countries that tolerate evasion” of the anti-diversion policy, it’s unclear how aggressively the Commerce Department might enforce the rule, NYT noted.

Bessent has publicly criticized Lutnick for failing to sanction Megaspeed, and NYT reported that ultimately, enforcement of the stricter rules—which Bessent helped draft—“would be up to the Commerce Department.”.

According to recent reports, “The real story here should be: Did Nvidia know their client, and was there a robust effort at Nvidia to make sure that there was no leakage and that they were selling to what were obviously pass-through shell companies?” Bessent said on a CNBC appearance. “I think it’s crucial that anyone at the firm there be held accountable for that.”.

In a recent development, there’s even a push to oust Lutnick over his position on chips, but The Guardian reported that Donald Trump confirmed he has no plans to replace the AI industry-friendly commerce secretary. On Monday, Trump told reporters that Lutnick was right to delay blacklisting Megaspeed, because “if you didn’t delay it… you could have a blow-up with China.”.

Recent findings suggest that at the press gaggle, Trump aligned with China in saying that there’s no evidence yet that Alice Huang was a spy. He also joined a band of prominent tech leaders calling for Jensen Huang’s return to Nvidia, saying that it wasn’t a “bad idea.”.

In a recent development, “Nobody’s proven that she’s a spy,” Trump mentioned. “She may not be a spy.”.

However, US investigators have alleged that they found “Alice Huang used industry contacts and a series of shell companies to access 240,000 chips banned for export into China,” CBS News reported.

China is unlikely to welcome the fresh rules, as it has consistently accused the US of fabricating the spying claims to justify imposing additional chip restrictions.

However, a senior Trump official, granted anonymity to discuss sensitive policy matters, told the NYT that Trump “did not expect countermeasures from China in response.”.

Sources indicate that trump will be in China for an economic summit this week, including a meeting with Chinese President Xi Jinping. The new curbs could potentially disrupt those talks, according to Hong Yuan, a researcher and secretary-general of the Center for American Military Studies at the Chinese Academy of Social Sciences. Hong told the People’s Daily that China will likely view the rule change as politically motivated.

It has been revealed that “Before any judicial causality was established, Washington handed down a political conviction, substituting suspicion for proof, espionage for personal contact, and an industrial embargo for private conduct,” Hong mentioned. “The concern is not the cause of tighter controls, but a political catalyst.”.

According to recent reports, the new policy could hurt the US, experts told the Chinese outlets. Analysts told the South China Morning Post that the policy could “accelerate Chinese companies’ shift to domestic AI chips.” Other experts told the People’s Daily—which is the official newspaper of the Chinese Communist Party—that “the cost of switching back to US platforms will rise” over time. If that happened, it could potentially lock in Chinese technology over America’s in “the world’s largest single consumer market for chips,” experts said.

Sun Chenghao, senior fellow at the Center for International Security and Strategy at Tsinghua University in Beijing, told the People’s Daily that “what US companies stand to lose could be customers and technological influence for years to come.”.

#137. After dodging death, battery startup Our Next Energy is now going public

After dodging death, battery startup Our Next Energy is now going public

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1462 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: TechCrunch

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that it’s never been easy to run a battery startup in the U.S.
  • Sources indicate that not all of them die, though.
  • ONE says it is valued at $600 million pre-money, and it expects the merger with Wen Acquisition Corp.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that it’s never been easy to run a battery startup in the U.S. There have been more failures than successes over the last 20 years, and whipsawing federal policy has caused more than a few battery companies to shut shop.

Sources indicate that not all of them die, though. Our Next Energy (ONE) had some close calls, but soon it will go public via SPAC, the company exclusively told TechCrunch.

ONE says it is valued at $600 million pre-money, and it expects the merger with Wen Acquisition Corp. will bring $400 million in gross proceeds assuming no redemptions. The combined tech giant will trade on the Nasdaq under the ticker “ONEE,” and the pro forma implied equity value is $1 billion.

Over the years, ONE has raised $483 million, according to PitchBook, and at one point was valued at $1.3 billion. It has also received tens of millions of dollars in incentives tied to investments and job creation in Michigan.

Sources indicate that ONE is the brainchild of former Ford and Apple engineer Mujeeb Ijaz, who designed a way for electric vehicles to draw power from two batteries of different chemistries. In ONE’s first setup, it paired lithium-iron-phosphate (LFP) and with a manganese-rich chemistry, which would let each chemistry play to its strengths: LFP could be used day in, day out, while the more fragile but energy-dense, manganese-rich one would work for long, infrequent road trips. An initial prototype traveled over 600 miles on a single charge.

According to recent reports, but the EV market didn’t take off as promptly as anticipated, and automakers wanted to buy at lower prices (usually from China). Both of those reasons helped sink ONE’s first attempt at a Series C in late 2023. The startup had to lay off a chunk of its staff, and eventually vacated its lease for a planned $1.6 billion factory in Michigan.

In a recent development, the rough patch led to Ijaz’s ouster as CEO in December 2023, only to have him return to the position in March 2025 after a newly introduced round of funding closed. (His brother’s investment firm co-led the round.).

Sources indicate that part of the critique aimed at ONE during Ijaz’s first tenure as CEO was that the tech giant spent too much time developing upcoming products instead of focusing on one or two, as most startups tend to do. When Ijaz came back to the helm last year, he said that ONE would leave the automotive market and focus on grid-scale batteries.

In a recent development, ONE isn’t alone in pivoting away from vehicle batteries. American automakers, which had similarly rosy views of EV adoption, also bet major on battery factories and supply chains. When sales didn’t pop in the U.S. like they have in China or Europe, they had to find an outlet for that capacity, and the grid started looking like the obvious target once it started groaning under the weight of AI data centers. Both Ford and GM have confirmed their own energy storage products.

It has been revealed that many fresh grid-scale batteries use LFP, which is safer and cheaper than those used in most EVs in the U.S., and Ijaz saw an opportunity for ONE there as well. “We go back to the origins of LFP in this country and even to some of the factories that are in China,” he said. Indeed, just over a decade ago Ijaz led the automotive division at A123 Systems, the firm that first commercialized the chemistry.

Soon, Ijaz saw other opportunities for ONE’s batteries, including defense and locomotives.

It has been revealed that the defense play isn’t surprising. Nearly every battery manufacturer I talk with these days mentions defense, in part because it’s a market that Chinese companies can’t play in. Building an American supply chain means that a company can sell batteries at a premium, shielded as they are from Chinese competition. It’s a higher-margin market, though much smaller than EVs.

Recent findings suggest that my recent conversation with Ijaz last week was the first time I’d heard a company pitch rail companies as potential customers, though. Ijaz mentioned ONE is “finding a lot of traction in” that market. The company has built a hybrid locomotive that uses a 2.8 megawatt-hour battery, and another he calls a micro-hybrid, which uses a smaller battery to start the diesel engine faster, similar to a stop-start system on a fossil fuel car or truck.

“Our customers are seeing a 50% improvement in diesel fuel consumption, which is a big deal,” Ijaz mentioned.

In a recent development, currently, ONE has three business lines, which could be a sign of its old culture creeping back into the picture. But Ijaz mentioned the addition of defense and rail were driven by the bottom line: Grid-scale battery customers are also “very much like automotive customers, where they were willing to buy from China as long as the price was low enough,” he said.

“Believe me, I would have loved to have made that grid business into the single business of the manufacturer. But the customers would look and then be taken away to a Chinese option because of the pricing, and the tariffs also leading them to that conclusion,” Ijaz remarked. “And so we decided that we needed a more durable market, and we looked for who in the customer base valued an American battery company.”.

Recent findings suggest that today, ONE operates a pack assembly plant in Novi, Michigan, which can put together packs from cells at a rate of 3 gigawatt-hours per year. The plant uses cells from China-based and non-China-based suppliers, as well as ONE’s own cells from a smaller factory nearby, which is currently being upgraded to make 50 megawatt-hours of batteries per year.

In its investor pitch, which TechCrunch has reviewed, ONE distills its business lines into defense and rail. Drones and submarines make up the majority of what ONE sees as a $16.2 billion market. Defense-focused data centers get lumped in there, too, contributing $4.1 billion to the defense business. (That appears to be the main outlet for grid-scale batteries.) The other line, which serves the rail industry, is expected to be worth $28.2 billion.

Both markets are sizable, but they pale in comparison to the EV sector, which is worth about $73 billion today, and could grow to $200 billion by the end of the decade, according to Grand View Research. This year, ONE expects to bring in $30 million in revenue, and hopes to make double that next year. The organization mentioned it has $200 million in binding, multi-year contracts with railroads and defense contractors.

Industry observers note that ONE hasn’t closed the door on the automotive industry, Ijaz said. “Automotive still is a race to the bottom on margins,” he said. “As time goes on, if we win an automotive contract for any purpose, we’ll take a look at it, but not at any cost.”.

ONE’s pitch centers on the so-called foreign entity of concern (FEOC) restrictions: The U.S. government can’t buy batteries made in China or those made using minerals from China-controlled supply chains, so ONE will target them first.

But it’s a pitch that many battery companies are making today. Whether investors buy into ONE’s vision will depend on if they think the company has parted with its tumultuous past and found a focus. It will need both to succeed in the increasingly cutthroat battery industry.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • According to recent reports, for many iPhone consumers, Apple CarPlay has become synonymous with a quality driving experience, from playing their favorite tunes to navigating to their next destination.
  • Sources indicate that I am, of course, referring to sharing your estimated time of arrival (ETA) through Apple Maps.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Let your friends know what time you'll be arriving.

According to recent reports, for many iPhone consumers, Apple CarPlay has become synonymous with a quality driving experience, from playing their favorite tunes to navigating to their next destination. And although Apple continues to upgrade its popular infotainment system, one of its most useful features has been hidden in Apple Maps for years and is critical to letting your family, friends, and, if you are like me, enemies know when you will arrive at your destination.

Sources indicate that I am, of course, referring to sharing your estimated time of arrival (ETA) through Apple Maps. Most customers are probably familiar with Apple's Find My and location-sharing functions, but CarPlay's Share ETA feature is woefully underappreciated. Both simple to use and highly customizable, the feature is a godsend for worried parents and surprise parties everywhere.

It has been revealed that to enable Share ETA, go to Settings > Apps > Maps. From here, scroll down to Share ETA and enable the feature. You can also enable location sharing in Messages, Contacts and Find My. You may also want to turn on Siri to make sharing an ETA more convenient. To do so, go to your iPhone's Settings, tap Siri and enable Turn on Siri.

Sources indicate that sharing your ETA is a simple way to improve your CarPlay experience. If you're using Siri, you can initiate a voice command when you're following Maps directions, either by holding the voice command button on your steering wheel or saying "Hey Siri" if your car supports voice activation. Next, say "share my ETA with (contact name).".

If you would rather not use Apple's voice assistant, you can share your ETA directly in Maps. After you've set off, tap the route card at the bottom of the screen, then Share ETA and choose a recipient. If the contact isn't on the list, you can find them under Open Contacts. To share with more than one person, tap Sharing with at the bottom of the screen, Open Contacts and select your intended recipients. You can also stop sharing your ETA by opening the route card again, tapping Sharing with, selecting Stop Sharing ETA and choosing the contact you want to stop sharing with.

You can also automatically share your ETA with someone by adding their contact to a pinned location. First, go to Maps > Places > Pinned. Next, tap the blue information button > Add Person. Next, tap the desired contact and confirm the selection. Now, whenever you select the pinned location in Apple Maps and tap Go, it will automatically share your ETA.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast.
  • A self-described birth keeper advised a pregnant woman whose baby later died to “go home and rest” after she was given urgent medical advice to present to an emergency department, the Fresh South Wales coroner’s court has heard.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sita Kali was involved in care for two of four babies who died between 2022 and 2024 in Lismore after free births or home births.

Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast.

A self-described birth keeper advised a pregnant woman whose baby later died to “go home and rest” after she was given urgent medical advice to present to an emergency department, the Fresh South Wales coroner’s court has heard.

Sita Tara Kali was involved in the care of two of four babies born in free births or home births who died in the northern rivers region between 2022 and 2024. An inquest into the deaths began in the Lismore local court on Monday. The families of the four babies were not present.

The inquest will examine whether the care was reasonable in the circumstances and whether care by an unregistered support worker was reasonable and appropriate before, during and after the birth.

Baby R’s mother had a distrust of hospitals in general, the court heard. She was aligned with and trusted Kali. She felt that having a home birth would give her a stronger connection to the baby. In a police statement she said she felt threatened by her experiences at the hospital.

Recent findings suggest that at 43 weeks, an ultrasound confirmed that the baby was extremely compromised. The obstetric advice was urgent. She was urged to attend emergency and strongly advised against a home birth, the inquest heard.

She called Kali, who said in a police statement, “she was quite upset and anxious. I advised her to go home and rest. Calm yourself down and consider what you want to do.”.

It has been revealed that baby R was born outside into his father’s hands at 9.51am. Two doulas were in attendance; neither had medical training. The baby was white in colour. He never latched on to feed.

About 14 hours later, the ambulance was called. The umbilical cord and placenta were still attached. Baby R died on the way to a waiting helicopter at 12.22am.

The cause of his death was determined to be unascertained. But an expert neonatologist surmised that it was caused by hypoxic-ischemic encephalopathy resulting from severe post-maturity – being born at 43 weeks.

Prof Hannah Dahlen, a midwifery academic who has attended thousands of births, told the court that this was a baby “I would have been watching closely” as a midwife attending a birth.

She said the difference between a doula and a birthing midwife “is the theoretical knowledge that we add on to that clinical experience, which gives us an understanding and an ability to interpret signs and symptoms and to identify what pathology is going on, or what physiology is not actually working at this time and making a decision”.

The counsel assisting, Ragni Mathur, told the court women were choosing unregulated free birthing because of “traumatic or coercive experiences, fragmented care, lack of trust in clinicians, lack of available clinicians, lack of services in regional NSW, and including child protection notifications and regulatory actions against upcoming lives”.

#133. Russia's mega-rich are already imagining a future after Putin

Russia's mega-rich are already imagining a future after Putin

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 12 min read (2300 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Co

⏱️ ~12 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Hours after launching his full-scale invasion of Ukraine on 24 February 2022, Vladimir Putin gathered Russia's richest men in the Kremlin's cavernous Yekaterininsky Hall.
  • According to recent reports, more than three dozen of them sat huddled along a wall, wearing face masks because of the Covid pandemic.
  • Using his typically coded language, he mentioned he expected them to support the war.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Hours after launching his full-scale invasion of Ukraine on 24 February 2022, Vladimir Putin gathered Russia's richest men in the Kremlin's cavernous Yekaterininsky Hall.

According to recent reports, more than three dozen of them sat huddled along a wall, wearing face masks because of the Covid pandemic. One Russian newspaper reporter described them as "pale and sleep-deprived". On entering, Putin sat down at the opposite side of the hall, creating a vast space between him and the businessmen. As usual, he was wearing no mask.

Using his typically coded language, he mentioned he expected them to support the war.

"I would like to call on you to show understanding of what is going on," he said, "and work together with the government to find the tools which would support production, the economy, jobs.".

In the Kremlin-published video of the meeting, none of the invited billionaires said a word.

That silence has become a feature of the Russian super-rich. Over the decades of Putin's rule, they have learnt that the price of piping up could be high. In 2003, oil magnate Mikhail Khodorkovsky, Russia's richest man at the time, who was funding a number of opposition groups, accused Putin of presiding over rampant corruption. He spent the next 10 years behind bars, convicted of tax evasion, fraud and embezzlement - a warning to other would-be critics. He denied the charges.

The silence of Russian businessmen at a Kremlin summit with Putin in 2022 perhaps demonstrated their fear of the president.

And even if any of the tycoons objected to the war, they have tended to keep their thoughts to themselves.

In a recent development, but even in that silence, there are murmurings: some members of Russia's once-mighty business elite seem to be imagining a Russia after Putin. They are wondering if, once the president has left office or died, the country might look more like it did in the 1990s, when the oligarchs enjoyed the fruits of power - or even if a healthier politics may take root.

The journalist Arkady Ostrovsky, a prominent Kremlin-watcher at The Economist newspaper who recently spent hours interviewing one of Russia's richest men, states he feels that a "historic, political shift is happening" in terms of how the ultra-rich view the future of the country.

The collapse of the Soviet Union in 1991 gave birth to a new, powerful force on the domestic scene: people who took advantage of the end of communism and became extraordinarily rich, and then wanted to control politicians for their own benefit. They were dubbed "the oligarchs", from Ancient Greek for the "few who rule".â¯ They had money, which back then meant power.

It has been revealed that this era of the "wild 1990s" was when the so-called "fresh Russians" burst onto the scene. Huge state companies came up for grabs, and men with the right connections became millionaires - even billionaires - almost overnight. Corruption was rife, cronyism rampant, and contract killings frequent.

But almost immediately after Putin was first elected as president in 2000, he subjugated the oligarchs. He had little interest in sharing power with anyone else. He could afford to stand up to the billionaires because Russia's economy was getting back on its feet, and the central government was getting stronger.

Some oligarchs developed a distinctive dress sense in the 1990s, as later satirised by this St Petersburg artist.

Bill Browder, a financier who used to be the biggest foreign investor in Russia, and was banned from the country in 2005 after campaigning against corruption, indicates the Russian tycoons cowered and wilted in front of Putin - for example at the Davos economic forum, in the pre-war years when they were still welcomed there.

According to recent reports, "I can remember seeing oligarchs walking around like they own the place, the most arrogant and self-confident individuals. And then Putin indicated up, and it was just remarkable to see how these supposedly alpha-male-on-steroids individuals turned into absolutely subordinate, almost desperate schoolchildren," he tells the BBC.

Sources indicate that since the outbreak of war in 2022, the Kremlin has kept Russia's rich businessmen in line with a ruthless policy of carrot and stick. Critics of the war have seen their assets seized, while loyalists have been rewarded with lavish government war contracts: today there are more Russian billionaires than ever (155 in total, according to Forbes magazine). â¯Their collective wealth has reached a newly introduced high of nearly $700bn (Â£525bn).

Recent findings suggest that but even for those tycoons who have stayed loyal and been rewarded, all of that money doesn't seem to be making them happy. Some are growing restless.

Their billions do not go as far as they used to: domestically, they cannot buy much political influence.

It has been revealed that "They have no cards, they have no game," exiled politician and analyst Dmitry Nekrasov states. "They're rich because they've got something to do with Putin, not the other way round.".

And outside of Russia, they are ostracised because of the Western sanctions imposed on Russia after its full-scale invasion.

"They're treated like low-level criminals. They can't fly their private jets. Their yachts can't park in all the best harbours in Europe. It must be very awful and humiliating for them," indicates Browder, the avowed Putin critic.

According to recent reports, and so, quietly, some of their minds are turning to what happens after Putin leaves the scene. That's what I'm told by well-placed analysts, who are immersed in the world of these tycoons.

According to recent reports, there's no immediate prospect of the president's departure, and there's no reason to think he's in bad health. But Putin, who turned 74 last month, has served in the Kremlin for a quarter of a century; people in Moscow know that his exit will come one day. When asked by Reuters last year if he intends to serve until 2036, when his constitutional term technically ends, Putin replied: "Only God knows if we have enough health.".

One prominent oligarch of the 1990s was Boris Berezovsky, who fell out with the Kremlin and lived his later years in the UK.

If Putin resigned or died in office, the prime minister, Mikhail Mishustin, would take over. But Mishustin has not exhibited any presidential ambitions (that's probably a key reason he was appointed). That would create something of a power vacuum.

In that scenario, Russia-watchers I have spoken with envisage a few potential scenarios.

Some in the West, and no doubt within Russia, hope that democracy might flourish in a post-Putin Russia, with government led by the people, rather than by a fresh cadre of oligarchs or a single autocrat. But this seems like the least likely path, analysts say. Key democratic institutions have been eroded or destroyed over Putin's rule. "Russia is so used to violence, it has grown unaccustomed to standard democratic procedures," says Alexandra Prokopenko, an exiled Russian journalist and analyst.

Another path is more autocracy. A different figure could replace Putin and continue his culture of repression. But Prokopenko thinks this wouldn't be another strongman dictatorship - at least not right away. These things take time, she says: at first, Putin's successor would be weaker than him, with fewer resources.

And then there's the third option: tycoons re-assert their power and Russia returns to something resembling a 1990s-style system of oligarchy. Dmitry Nekrasov, a former Kremlin adviser and opposition politician who now lives in exile, notes under this scenario, the country would be governed by a handful of powerful elite clans in alliance with business interests.

It has been revealed that this last option, of course, is the one that many tycoons want. "They'd like to return to a time when they were listened to, when they were not stripped of assets and when they understood the rules of the game," claims Prokopenko, who has spent a lot of time speaking to Russia's richest people.

Though their power has been seriously curtailed since the 1990s, it's still worth listening to the tycoons: given their immense wealth, it seems likely that sooner or later they will try to re-assert their political influence.

In a recent development, already, some are "trying to be friends with the right sort of security officials or ministers", says Nekrasov, the exiled politician. But he says any further steps are "too dangerous to take".

Putin has kept tycoons in line with a ruthless policy of carrot and stick since Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine.

He notes the behaviour of the tycoons in coming years will depend in part on their finances. Those who have lots of liquid cash will be more confident to "play political games" and jockey for position, preparing for a post-Putin country. But those whose wealth is dependent on state contracts or government goodwill will feel too afraid, in case they lose everything, he says.

Recent findings suggest that prokopenko notes there's already been a shift in how the businessmen talk about Putin. They used to nickname him "Nachalnik" (which translates as "boss"), as well as "Perviy" ("first"), or by his initials "VV" - all nicknames that convey a degree of respect. Now they call him "Ded", with what Prokopenko calls "a pinch of contempt". "Ded" translates as "oldie" or "granddad" - a much less reverent name.

Some rich Russians are pining after a "return of politics into people's lives", she notes, with less repression, more open speech, and healthier competition between parties and politicians.

In a recent development, but at the moment, she states, they are too afraid to make that happen due to Russia's stifling atmosphere. Prokopenko interviewed one tycoon who physically sat on his phone during the whole conversation, because he thought it would make digital eavesdropping more difficult for secret police. "I thought that it's an absolutely Stalinistic type of fear. It's absolutely irrational," she says.

An interesting clue for what tycoons might want from a post-Putin future came from Andrey Melnichenko, who is known as the world's fertiliser king and is currently Russia's eighth richest man.

According to recent reports, earlier this year, he surprised observers by giving an interview to The Economist - a rare thing for a rich Russian to do, especially to a publication from a country the Kremlin considers unfriendly. They also published an essay written by him.

Sources indicate that in parts of the interview, Melnichenko repeated Kremlin talking points. He mentioned that Ukraine is a battlefield between Russia and the West, and he thinks the West ignored Russia's security concerns and threatens its sovereignty.

But then it got more interesting. Melnichenko did not call for Putin to go, but - and it's a big but - he argued for a change that would bring about an end to one-man rule in Russia. He said Russia needs to engage more with the world.

Sources indicate that prokopenko thinks the tycoon was trying to stir a public conversation. It was a "call on rich people like him to start talking", she states.

The journalist who interviewed him, Arkady Ostrovsky, tells me the pair had "tense and heated discussions" in "hotels and cafes, mostly drinking coffee, lots of coffee, sometimes smoking". He states the tycoon seemed to be "genuinely thinking" about his answers, rather than giving politician-style spin.

According to recent reports, nothing in Russia is simple, and most observers think the interview probably happened with some form of approval - implicit or explicit - from the Kremlin. We don't know why authorities would have been happy to authorise the unusual call for change; it's possible they were trying to show that some degree of pluralism still exists in the country.

Industry observers note that no tycoons came out to support him. Still, the journalist feels that Melnichenko was not speaking for himself alone, but also for his fellow businessmen.

Some tycoons feel ostracised because of Western sanctions, unable to fly private jets and visit Western resorts like Saint-Jean-Cap-Ferrat in southern France, which used to be popular with rich Russians.

Some of them are hoping that after Putin's departure, the country might become an "oligarchic republic", as journalist Ostrovsky puts it - something like how it looked in the 1990s, with the business elites in charge.

Based on his years of reporting on Russia, Ostrovsky says that many of the country's mega-rich currently feel a "sense of complete dead end, which this war has led Russia toâ¦ [an] absence of the future".

But even if the tycoons are thinking about the future, there's a slim prospect of them acting any time soon, it seems.

Sources indicate that browder, the Putin critic, indicates that although many of them are unhappy, they're unlikely to conspire against Putin while he is still alive. "They understand that if they were to do anything that would challenge Putin, he would kill them. And Putin is a very paranoid little man.".

Mike Calvey, an American financier who used to be a key investor in Russia, agrees. "What can they do besides just go straight to the prison and lose their assets? It's easy for people who are sitting in London to say that, 'why don't you just all go stand up and go straight to prison?' That's really what would happen.".

Sources indicate that russia's richest men used to be able to pull strings at the highest levels of power. Once Putin is gone, there is no doubt they will try to claw back their past influence. The question is: will remnants of the current regime let them?

#131. Industry News: Mazama Energy has a solution for geothermal’s biggest drilling problem

Industry News: Mazama Energy has a solution for geothermal’s biggest drilling problem

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (917 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: TechCrunch

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that success in geothermal energy is guided by two basic goals — drill fast and drill deep.
  • It has been revealed that but while the goals might be straightforward, they’re anything but easy.
  • Those two foes are what led Mazama Energy to develop a fresh technology, called Carbon Chill, that uses carbon dioxide to cool the drill bit and bring cuttings to the surface.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that success in geothermal energy is guided by two basic goals — drill fast and drill deep. Hit both targets, and geothermal startups have a good chance at being cheaper than nearly every other source on the electrical grid.

It has been revealed that but while the goals might be straightforward, they’re anything but easy. Drilling fast generates heat, which damages equipment, and so does drilling deep.

Those two foes are what led Mazama Energy to develop a fresh technology, called Carbon Chill, that uses carbon dioxide to cool the drill bit and bring cuttings to the surface. The technology will not only let the company drill deeper, but also faster. The startup gave TechCrunch an exclusive look at Carbon Chill.

“Our rate of penetration increased 20% over the already very high rates we were achieving,” Sriram Vasantharajan, co-founder and CEO of Mazama Energy, told TechCrunch.

According to recent reports, speed has other advantages in geothermal. Drilling represents about 25% to 30% of the total cost of building a power plant, so reducing drill time can bring costs down significantly.

If geothermal startups succeed in drilling faster and cheaper, they stand to help reshape the grid in the 2030s. Hyperscalers are already planning the facilities that will enter operation at the end of the decade.

Sources indicate that mazama has been working on the problem for years now. In October 2025, the Khosla-backed startup stated it had drilled a well in Oregon that reached 629˚ F (331˚ C), and a more recent well has surpassed 700˚ F, Vasantharajan said. In September, the startup raised $135 million in a round led by Centaurus Capital and Doerr Capital.

Mazama hopes that its new carbon dioxide-based cooling technology will help it prove that geothermal energy from super-hot rock is a viable contender in the electricity market.

In a recent development, already companies like Google and Meta have started to explore the use of geothermal energy, in part because the potential is enormous: A report from the National Laboratory of the Rockies said that geothermal could generate between 26.5 to 57 terawatts of electricity in the U.S. alone. If just 10% of the conservative estimate were developed, it would more than double the U.S.’s peak generating capacity.

Geothermal experts have identified super-hot rock — in which temperatures exceed 752˚ F (400˚ C) — as a promising way to improve the performance of individual wells. At those temperatures, water turns “supercritical,” a gaseous-like liquid state which carries five to 10 times more energy than water from traditional geothermal wells. By harvesting more energy from each well, developers have to drill fewer of them, bringing costs down.

It has been revealed that accessing that heat can be challenging for traditional drilling methods. Most geothermal drillers use “mud” — a combination of water and other compounds to keep the bit cool and clear cuttings from the borehole. But mud can only bring temperatures down so much. Eventually, they become so hot that electronics in the drill bit, which help keep it on course, start to fail.

High temperature-rated electronics exist, but they’d be cost prohibitive, Vasantharajan remarked.

According to recent reports, instead of mud, Mazama injects liquid carbon dioxide down the center of its drill string. As it travels deeper, it gets heated by the rock around it, which turns it supercritical, too. Then, just before it reaches the drill head, Mazama has it flow through a valve that looks a lot like a rocket nozzle. As the gas expands, it escapes through the cone-shaped nozzle and rapidly cools, absorbing heat from the electronics and the drill bit.

“I look at [carbon dioxide cooling] as a binary,” he remarked. “Without such technologies, I am, today, not able to drill these horizontal wells at super-hot rock temperatures.”.

It has been revealed that that capital injection will help Mazama drill more wells deeper. By next year, Vasantharajan said his company hopes to complete a single well that’s capable of generating up to 15 megawatts of electricity.

It has been revealed that “What was just a dream or a quest, I can tell you with confidence is now a promise,” he noted. “We see a path towards this commercial super-hot rock geothermal.”.

Proposed NSW laws to allow coalmine to increase production pose ‘serious corruption risk’
